articles.title: HTTPd (CVE-2026-119618): Detecting heap corruption and RCE in Apache HTTP Server mod_http2
articles.context: Threat Intelligence entries show where affected Apache hosts are running, Vulnerability Management maps to each distribution’s vendor advisory, and Runtime Detections catch what...
articles.full_text:
On November 11, 2026, Apache released HTTP Server 2.4.71 to fix CVE-2026-119618, a critical severity heap corruption flaw in mod_http2 that Apache’s security advisory said can lead to remote code execution (RCE). The flaw sits in assign_headers(), affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and can be triggered over HTTP/2 with no authentication. Red Hat and Amazon have scored the vulnerability 9.8 on CVSS v3.1, though CISA rates it at 8.1.

Two teams found the bug independently, eight days apart. Anthropic's OSS Scanner is an opt-in, model-driven scanner for open-source projects. It reported the bug on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it eight days later on November 3, according to the CVE record.

The day after Apache disclosed it on oss-security, a public proof-of-concept (PoC) was published on GitHub showing the heap corruption, though no PoC has been released for the RCE as of the publication of this blog. Additionally, no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported, and the CVE does not appear in CISA's KEV catalog.

The bug lives in Apache's own HTTP/2 implementation, not in any application the server hosts. Only servers that enable HTTP/2 are exposed. Affected organizations are encouraged to upgrade to version 2.4.71 or turn off HTTP/2 if patching is delayed.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed the publicly available research and simulated a successful exploit to help defenders understand four key details: who is affected, what has been demonstrated versus claimed, what runtime visibility can detect, and what mitigation steps should be taken until a patch can be applied. They also tested and found that Sysdig’s existing runtime detections caught every post-exploitation step.

Timeline

Date

Event

Oct. 26, 2026, 12:00 UTC

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reports the flaw as ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ

Oct. 30, 2026

CVE ID reserved

Nov. 3, 2026, 15:50 UTC

Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reports the flaw

Nov. 9, 2026, 02:54 UTC

Fix committed to the 2.4.x branch as 824beab

Nov. 11, 2026, 12:19 UTC

Public disclosure on oss-security

Nov. 11, 2026, 12:52 UTC

Red Hat publishes its assessment and RHEL 9 and 10 fixes

Nov. 11, 2026, 14:54 UTC

CVE record published

Nov. 12, 2026, 09:54 UTC

Debian DSA-6620-1 fixes trixie

Nov. 12, 2026

A public PoC is posted on GitHub showing heap corruption

Affected Apache HTTP Server versions

The flaw is in mod_http2, the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server. The same module is released separately as mod_h2 on GitHub and also affected.

While the Apache advisory rates the vulnerability as critical. The CVE record, which Apache maintains as the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), doesn’t actually carry an associated CVSS score. However, Red Hat and Amazon both rate the vulnerability as critical and score it at 9.8 on CVSS v3.1 and CISA rates it as a high severity vulnerability at 8.1 on CVSS v3.1.

Red Hat rates its own RHEL 9 and 10 builds Important rather than Critical. Those builds allocate each HTTP/2 stream from "a separate allocator, which substantially increases the complexity of exploiting the flaw."

The severity and prioritization of this vulnerability in an organization’s environment depends first on whether HTTP/2 is on.

Version

Status

Fixed version / What to do

httpd versions 2.4.55 – 2.4.70

Affected

Upgrade to 2.4.71.

httpd versions prior to 2.4.55

Not listed as affected by Apache

No action for this CVE.

Standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 – 2.0.42

Affected. The repository has been archived since June 9, 2026.

No fixed release; 2.0.42 is the latest. Move to httpd 2.4.71's bundled module, or disable HTTP/2.

RHEL 9

Affected (Important)

mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1, RHSA-2026:98981

RHEL 9.4 SAP / 9.6 EUS / 9.8 EUS

Affected (Important)

RHSA-2026:98968 / :98954 / :98982

RHEL 10

Affected (Important)

mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1, RHSA-2026:98978

RHEL 10.0 EUS / 10.2 EUS

Affected (Important)

RHSA-2026:98953 / :98979

RHEL 6, 7, 8

Not affected

No action for this CVE.

The version number alone won’t confirm exposure, check these additional factors:

Distribution packages: Vendors often backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so check your vendor's advisory and not only httpd -v or apache2 -v.

As of November 13, fixes are out for Debian 12 and 13 (2.4.71-1~deb12u1 and 2.4.71-1~deb13u1), Ubuntu 22.04 through 26.10, Alpine, Fedora, Amazon Linux 2 and 2023, and Wolfi and Chainguard.

SUSE, openSUSE, Photon OS, and several RHEL rebuilds were still waiting on vendor fixes.

Downstream products: Vendors that repackage httpd, such as Red Hat JBoss Core Services (jbcs-httpd24-mod_http2) and Red Hat Hardened Images, may be listed as affected on version number alone. Whether you are exposed depends on what the product ships. Check that mod_http2 is actually present and loaded. For example, Sysdig’s scan of the Red Hat Hardened Images httpd image shows it listed as affected, but the image has no mod_http2, so the risk can be accepted. Check the vendor’s advisory for fix status.

Recent upgrades: Servers upgraded to 2.4.67 for the HTTP/2 flaw in May, CVE-2026-23918, are still inside this CVE's affected range.

How the HTTPd RCE flaw works

HTTP/2 carries many requests over one connection as parallel streams and that concurrency is where this flaw lies.

The Apache advisory calls the flaw "Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization" in assign_headers(), and the CVE record lists CWE-362. Red Hat lists CWE-20 instead. Red Hat describes the root cause as "a worker thread writes into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared, lock-free allocator." In practice, two threads can corrupt the same heap.

The fix is a one-line change in assign_headers(). Before the fix, a request with a content type that had already ended had its zero Content-Length header written into the HTTP/2 request's own header table (req->headers). The fix writes it into the per-request table (r->headers_in) instead. The commit message gives no explanation. Red Hat's statement supplies the threading context.

What is reachable

Exposure depends on configuration. Red Hat states that only servers with HTTP/2 enabled through the Protocols directive are affected:

Path

Does it reach the vulnerable code?

Details

Protocols includes h2

Yes

HTTP/2 over TLS.

Protocols includes h2c

Yes

HTTP/2 over cleartext TCP. The public PoC targets this.

Protocols set in a virtual host

Yes, for that virtual host

Check vhost blocks as well as the server-wide setting.

HTTP/1.1 only

No

According to RedHat, servers serving only HTTP/1.1 are not affected.

Red Hat's Bugzilla entry says an unauthenticated attacker triggers the flaw "by sending specially crafted HTTP/2 frames." That puts internet-facing, HTTP/2-enabled httpd in the first patch tier. This table does not cover reverse proxies in front of httpd.

HTTPd RCE exploitation: What's been demonstrated vs. claimed

According to Red Hat’s CVE page, public research has shown "a reliable exploit against a default-configured server." However, without a researcher name or links to details, this can’t be verified. As of the publishing of this blog, no other security researchers or vendors have confirmed exploitation.

As of about 16:00 UTC on November 12, a GitHub search for the CVE returned four repositories: a proof of concept, a patch-status tracker, and two detection or assessment tools.

The PoC reports heap corruption, not code execution. Its README describes the impact as "Heap corruption in an httpd child process; potential remote code execution."

Its evidence comes from a lab build:

Setup: httpd 2.4.70 built from upstream source on a debian:bookworm container, running the prefork MPM with Protocols h2c http/1.1.

Results: The PoC sent 6,080 requests. AddressSanitizer reported five crashes, including a heap use-after-free allocated in assign_headers(). ThreadSanitizer reported 31 allocator races.

Fixed build: A 2.4.71 build showed none.

Trigger: A request that ends without a body and carries a Content-Type but no Content-Length triggers the bug. The fix commit changes exactly that code path.

The README doesn't show control of the corrupted memory, and the author has published no exploit.

The bottom line is that unauthenticated HTTP/2 traffic can crash and corrupt the heap of a vulnerable httpd. Remote code execution is possible, but nobody has publicly demonstrated it yet. Treat the crash as likely wherever HTTP/2 is on, and code execution as a credible risk.

HTTPd RCE impact

Nothing publicly disclosed as of November 13, 2026, shows in-the-wild exploitation, a mass-scanning campaign, or a public RCE exploit. The primary sources do establish the following:

Risk of unauthenticated RCE: Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach the server could execute arbitrary commands with no authentication. Bugzilla adds that commands run as the httpd process.

Worker crashes: The public PoC crashes httpd child processes on a vulnerable build.

Long-lived exposure: The affected range starts at 2.4.55, so servers patched for earlier HTTP/2 bugs can still be exposed.

Paths with no fix yet: Standalone mod_h2 has no fixed release. Several distributions, including SUSE, openSUSE, Photon OS, and CentOS Stream 10, were still waiting on vendor fixes as of November 13.

Detecting HTTPd RCE with Sysdig Secure

Sysdig Secure customers have three layers of coverage for CVE-2026-119618. Threat Intelligence entries show where affected Apache hosts are running, Vulnerability Management maps to each distribution’s vendor advisory, and Runtime Detections catch what a successful exploit does once an attacker enters a vulnerable environment.

Threat intelligence

Sysdig Secure customers have two entries for CVE-2026-119618 in the Threat Intelligence feed. Each entry lists the affected hosts and running Kubernetes workloads. One entry uses the SBOM to find affected versions of Apache HTTP Server, mod_http2, and the vendor packages that contain the module. The other entry lists the assets where Sysdig Vulnerability Management reports the CVE.

Vulnerability management

Sysdig vulnerability management detects CVE-2026-119618 across your environment. To prioritize remediation, start with internet-facing workloads and packages in use at runtime.

Sysdig vulnerability scanning reports this CVE by distribution and release, and each status follows the vendor's own advisory. Rows move from "Waiting on vendor fix" to "Reported" as vendors publish fixes and the feed picks them up. The table reflects status as of November 13, 2026. On SaaS, vulnerability database updates reach scanners automatically, so new advisories need no scanner upgrade.

Runtime detection

The Sysdig TRT simulated a successful exploit inside a vulnerable Apache server, both inside a container and as a host service. Existing runtime threat detections caught every step without rule modifications, including:

Failed exploit attempts that crash web server workers

Commands or a shell started by the web server, including reverse shells

Tools downloaded and run by the web server

The web server process replaced by attacker code

A successful attack would give the attacker code execution as the httpd worker. From there, attackers do what they do after any web server RCE: open a reverse shell, download and run a tool, start a miner, steal cloud credentials, or try a kernel local privilege escalation.

Detecting HTTPd RCE with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP/2 frames. It cannot see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. That includes a shell or unexpected binary spawned by an httpd process, an unexpected outbound connection, or a write to a sensitive path.

Web servers fork helpers legitimately, so rules scoped to httpd need tuning to stay quiet. The post-exploitation strategies above apply.

Recommendations

Patch

Update httpd on every server: Move to 2.4.71, or to your vendor's patched package. On RHEL 9 that is mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1, on RHEL 10 mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1, and on Debian trixie apache2 2.4.71-1~deb13u1. Patching is the only complete fix.

Restart httpd and rebuild images after you patch: A running server keeps the old module loaded. Verify the package version inside the running workload.

Replace standalone mod_h2: The project is archived, and its latest release, 2.0.42, is affected.

Interim mitigations if you cannot patch today

Disable HTTP/2: Apache's advisory and oss-security notice give no workaround. Wiz recommends removing h2 and h2c so the setting reads Protocols http/1.1. That is Wiz's guidance, not Apache's. It matches Red Hat's statement that HTTP/1.1-only servers are not affected.

Apply the change server-wide and in every virtual host.

Restart or reload httpd so the change takes effect.

Test latency-sensitive services first. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1, which can slow multiplexed workloads.

Contain the blast radius

Run httpd workers as an unprivileged user: Limit what a compromised worker can read and write.

Keep secrets out of the server's reach: Use a secrets manager, not environment variables or files the worker can read.

Investigate and audit

Audit your environment: Find every host and workload running httpd 2.4.55–2.4.70 or mod_h2 2.0.8–2.0.42 with HTTP/2 enabled, internet-facing first. Sysdig Secure customers can use the Threat Intelligence entry and Vulnerability Management findings.

Watch for crashing httpd children: Repeated child-process segfaults on an HTTP/2-enabled server match what the public PoC produces.

Review httpd process activity: Look for shells, downloads or outbound connections from httpd workers since public disclosure on November 11.

Enable default runtime policies: Sysdig’s runtime detections will catch exploitation, even when a vulnerability scan has no findings yet.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-119618 is a threading bug in httpd's HTTP/2 module, not a flaw in the applications httpd serves. Heap corruption and crashes are public. Code execution is claimed but not yet publicly shown, but that gap is why reachability should drive patch prioritization. Defenders should start with HTTP/2-enabled, public-facing servers.

The timelines are still important to note for security teams. Two teams reported the bug independently, eight days apart. One “team" was an automated, model-driven scanner, while the other was a human team. By November 12, a day after disclosure, a public PoC that corrupts the heap was on GitHub. The window between “advisory published” and “working exploit” is small, and organizations need to be prepared to respond quickly to these notifications.

In this case, the best course of action is to patch first. Until every server is patched and restarted, disable HTTP/2 where you can and use runtime detection to close the gap. A runtime sensor will not see the heap corruption, but it will catch what a successful exploit does next.

articles.title: New N-able "4EverAble2Shell" zero-day exploited hours after PoC released
articles.context: Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners, with...
articles.full_text:
Hackers are actively exploiting a newly disclosed N-able N-central zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to compromise servers and deploy cryptocurrency miners, with researchers reporting at least 21 affected systems, including 19 running the company's latest security update.

The attacks follow security researcher Sean Bales' release of two new zero-day exploits today, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, which he says allow attackers to gain root-level access to N-central appliances and SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems.

N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely.

The new vulnerabilities were disclosed on November 12, just two days after N-able released emergency security updates to address critical N-central zero-day vulnerabilities that Bales had publicly disclosed earlier this week.

Bales published proof-of-concept exploits for both the 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell vulnerabilities, saying they were tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.1.26 HF2, the security update N-able released on November 10.

The 4EverAble2Shell exploit allows unauthenticated attackers to execute commands as root on vulnerable N-central servers. However, the researcher says exploitation requires the platform's Legacy API functionality to be enabled.

The attack combines an Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436, with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to gain root-level access.

The second exploit, Agent2Shell, targets N-central's agent functionality and is claimed to allow attackers to execute commands with SYSTEM privileges on Windows devices.

The disclosures came after N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week and urged on-premises customers to shut down their servers after Bales published more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities.

Bales has criticized N-able's handling of the vulnerability disclosures and the company's slow response to patching responsibly disclosed flaws.

"It's much much easier for me to just release the research I have and the vendor can decide what they want to do with it, what they do and don't want to fix, etc. :)," Bales told BleepingComputer.

Bales said N-able has not patched two unrelated RCE vulnerabilities in a different N-able product that he previously disclosed to the company in July.

In a November 12 security advisory, N-able said it was implementing additional protections in response to the new disclosures, including restricting certain N-central features and integrations while it develops further fixes.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," N-able said.

"These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The company says it has disabled the Intune integration as a precaution and is urging on-premises customers to ensure Legacy API access is disabled, which is already the default.

The protections have already been applied to hosted environments, but customers are also advised to continue upgrading their Agents and Probes under the previous Hotfix 2 guidance.

In its advisory, N-able said it had seen no signs of compromise using the new flaws, although security researchers have since reported successful exploitation of the vulnerability against production N-central servers.

Hackers already exploiting 4EverAble2Shell

Cybersecurity company Previdian told BleepingComputer that attackers began probing for the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerability on November 12, shortly after the public release of the proof-of-concept exploit.

The company first observed suspicious requests targeting its N-central honeypot at approximately 08:30 UTC, using the same Java class referenced in the publicly released exploit.

While the initial requests were limited to probing for vulnerable servers, Previdian later confirmed that attackers were attempting to execute the complete exploit chain against its honeypot server.

The attacks initially exploit Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 to execute commands as the 'nable' service account, then exploit a separate N-central privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges.

This attack chain matches the POC Bales released on GitHub.

According to Previdian, the privilege escalation stage abuses N-central's privileged setLDFileOwner helper and a symbolic link to make a normally root-owned script writable.

The attacker then modifies the script and invokes N-central's serverControl functionality to execute commands as root, while attempting to restore the modified files afterward.

The payload attempted to download and execute an additional shell script from an attacker-controlled server at 157.20.241[.]16, while sending diagnostic information and command output back to the same IP address.

Previdian is tracking the N-central privilege escalation flaw as VULN-2026-0009 and has added it to its own Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

Cybersecurity company Huntback also reports that attackers have already successfully compromised at least 21 production N-central servers using Bales' publicly released exploit chain.

Huntback saw the same attacker IP address as Previdian probing its N-central honeypots at approximately 08:30 UTC on November 12, with the first attempts to execute the complete exploit chain beginning at 09:16 UTC.

The attacks seen by Huntback exploited the 4EverAble2Shell exploit chain to download a shell script that installed an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner.

The miner was configured to use about half of the available CPU cores, likely to make the mining harder to detect.

Huntback identified other compromised systems through the attacker's cryptocurrency mining pool statistics, where infected systems were assigned identifiers beginning with nc_ followed by the server's IP address.

At 12:50 UTC on November 12, the researchers found 21 active miners using this naming convention, all of which had submitted mining shares within the previous five minutes.

The researchers then checked the associated IP addresses and confirmed that all 21 hosted N-central installations, including 19 running version 2026.4.1.26, the latest Hotfix 2 release issued on November 10.

The compromised servers were located across multiple countries, including the United States, Canada, South Africa, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Sweden.

While the attacks observed so far have been primarily used for cryptojacking, attackers could use compromised N-central infrastructure for additional malicious activity targeting managed customer environments.

Organizations running N-central should ensure that Legacy APIs are disabled and investigate suspicious requests to /dms/services/ServerUI, especially those referencing jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings.

Huntback also recommends checking for unexpected xvd.service systemd services, cryptocurrency mining processes, and files created under /tmp/.xvd or /var/tmp/.xvd.

Because the 4EverAble2Shell attack grants full root access to exploited servers, organizations that detect these IOCs should treat the breach as a full compromise of the server.

articles.title: Apache HTTP Server patches critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaw
articles.context: A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE)
articles.full_text:
A critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server could be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to obtain remote code execution (RCE).

The Apache Software Foundation has fixed the issue, now tracked as CVE-2026-119618, but a significant number of servers are vulnerable and reachable over the public internet.

Discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research teams, the vulnerability is a race condition in the mod_http2 module that can corrupt heap memory.

An attacker successfully exploiting it could run code with the web server process’s privileges in HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and standalone mod_h2 version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Apache describes the problem as “Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE.”

Apache HTTP Server is a free and open-source software that handles requests from web browsers and serves pages, images, and other website content. It is a widely used tool estimated to back roughly one out of five websites.

According to telemetry data from cloud security company Wiz, 64% of the cloud environments have vulnerable resources, and roughly half of them have publicly exposed instances.

However, the numbers do not account for server configuration, which requires HTTP/2 to be enabled (default is off).

Researchers at cybersecurity company watchTowr confirmed this condition and recommend technicians to "patch now or drop h2 until you can."

"Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption," Wiz researchers say.

"This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process."

Wiz assesses the severity of the vulnerability to be critical, although no official score is available. The company says that it is currently unaware of any public exploits or attacks targeting the flaw, but this could change soon.

The latest version of Apache HTTP Server also addresses two additional flaws, CVE-2026-106023 - a null pointer dereference in ‘mod_md,’ and CVE-2026-109163 - a low-severity data overwrite flaw in ‘mod_vhost_alias.’

articles.title: ThreatsDay: 59 Linux Kernel Bugs, Falcon Spyware, GSocket Backdoors + 17 More Stories
articles.context: The attackers have been found to gain access through compromised contractor accounts and leverage AI-generated PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands during later stages...
articles.full_text:
A search result isn't always safe. An access request isn't always harmless. And a familiar account doesn't always mean a familiar person is using it. Simple things to remember. Yet a surprising amount of this week's trouble starts right there.

Attackers are using fake websites, stolen access, and trusted tools to get into places they shouldn't be. AI is helping them build attacks faster, while also giving them new systems to target. Some intruders are staying hidden even after security holes are fixed. Others are moving stolen money through a maze of transactions. And researchers keep finding small coding mistakes that can cause much bigger problems. Different stories, but much of the trouble comes down to making something dangerous look normal.

There is some good news, too. Criminal servers have been seized, and a few defenses are getting stronger. Still, plenty of things are going wrong in ways that shouldn't be this easy. Here's what turned up this week.

The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.

North Korea's crypto laundering network

How North Korea Is Laundering $.64B Stolen from Binance

The North Korean threat actors linked to the record-breaking theft of $6.43 billion from Binance are using a highly complex and clearly automated method to launder the illicit proceeds. "Since the theft it has used more than 20,000 wallets on 16 blockchains, at least 36 services and at least 65,000 transactions," Dr. Tom Robinson, Elliptic's founder and chief scientist, said. "Around $3.0 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly as ETH and BTC. A negligible amount has likely been cashed out." The attackers have also been observed creating six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain network (FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU) to launder a slice of the ill-gotten funds, passing through about $430,000 of the stolen cryptocurrency. The goal is to disguise the path of money and make it harder to trace where the assets eventually end up. Other tactics used to make funds tracing more difficult include moving between blockchains through bridges and cross-chain swap services, swapping between assets on DEXs, hopping through lending vaults and liquid-staking services, and mixing bitcoin through coinjoins, and ETH and SOL through the Privacy Cash privacy pool. The Binance breach is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange, but it is the biggest ever by magnitude. North Korean spokesperson Kim Yo Jong denied the country's role in the attack, calling it an "absurd" effort to "damage the international image of the DPRK."

GSocket detections surge 356%

Attacks Leveraging GSocket Spike in 2026

Microsoft said it has observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open-source remote access tool, on internet-facing Linux servers to maintain access after the original vulnerabilities were addressed, turning a single web application compromise into persistent access. "Because GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block," Microsoft said. "Defenders should look for GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections on affected hosts, not treat application patching alone as complete remediation." According to telemetry data, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2% from March through August 2026, with most of them associated with PHP web applications, cPanel hosts, and Apache. The majority of targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities.

235 servers seized in Europol takedown

Europol Operation Dismantles GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC Infrastructure

Europol, along with global partners, has disrupted the criminal infrastructure behind GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains. "The operation targeted 'cybercrime-as-a-service' models, where these tools enabled further crimes like ransomware attacks and data theft," Europol said. As part of the operation, authorities have identified over 6 million victim credentials. "The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol added.

Browser-based espionage targets governments

Hackers Deploy Falcon Browser Spyware to Monitor Government Emails and Steal Passwords

A command and control (C2) framework called Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē) has been found compromising victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. Falcon shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with PeckBirdy, another JavaScript C2 framework that came to light early this year. It's assessed that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework. "An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information: passwords, emails, session cookies, [and] communications." Falcon has also been used to deliver an implant dubbed Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel. The activity has targeted government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. "The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives," Unit 42 said.

59 Linux kernel bugs uncovered

Microsoft Flags 59 Linux Kernel Bugs

Microsoft said its scan of a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026 unearthed 26,502 raw findings using MDASH, which subsequently formed the basis for 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. This includes working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, such as CVE-2026-64563. "CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel's shared resizable hash table," Microsoft said. "Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux -- and affected Android with SELinux enforcing -- without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces."

AI-assisted espionage in Central Asia

Silent Lynx Hackers Use AI Agent to Steal 2,000+ Tajik Government Documents

An exposed Silent Lynx server has uncovered cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026. "The directory held the group's tooling alongside data from active intrusions into government and critical infrastructure organisations across the region, and the AI agent the operator relied on to run them," CloudSEK said. "We assess with medium confidence that the operator has a Kazakhstan nexus: the operation runs in Russian, and the operator's own test traffic came from a residential Kazakh connection, which supports existing vendor assessments. The collection priorities, spanning transport, defence correspondence and resource ministries in neighbouring states, point to regional intelligence gathering rather than financial motive."

Contractor access fuels ransomware attacks

Citrus Ransomware Hackers Abuse Contractor Access, VLESS Tunnels, and AI-Generated Scripts

A new Russian-speaking ransomware group called Citrus is targeting Windows systems in corporate environments. The attackers have been found to gain access through compromised contractor accounts and leverage AI-generated PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands during later stages of the intrusion. In an attempt to reduce visibility, the threat actor removes tools and output files after execution, clears command history, and deletes event logs. The group also disguises tools and related artifacts with benign-looking names to make them appear legitimate by using a trusted brand name. The ransomware is a Sn00py-family ransomware variant written in Go. On Windows systems, the malware encrypts user files and appends the .citrus extension, while taking steps to hinder recovery and incident response. Kaspersky said the activity shares several similarities with Toy Ghouls. "Citrus stands out for the way AI-generated content appears to support hands-on intrusion activity on compromised systems," said Stanislav Larinsky, Kaspersky Security Services expert. "In the cases we investigated, the attackers combined third-party account access, privilege-escalation attempts and domain-wide deployment techniques. These incidents show how limited contractor access can become a path to broader compromise if it is not tightly controlled and continuously monitored."

Malicious AI agents exploit OAuth consent

New BluePhishing Attack Tricks Microsoft Entra Users Into Granting AI Agents Cloud Access

Proofpoint has disclosed details of a new technique called BluePhishing that's described as the "next evolution of OAuth consent abuse," enabling bad actors to leverage agent identities like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for initial access. BluePhishing "socially engineer[s] victims into granting consent to a malicious agent blueprint for initial access," it said. "Analogous to app consent phishing where attackers use client credentials to gain initial access to a tenant, BluePhishing extends this technique to the agent ecosystem. By exploiting gaps in visibility and governance around emerging AI agent adoption, attackers can abuse one-time consent links to create agent identities in target tenants, obtain access tokens, and operate with the privileges assigned to those agents."

AI age checks expand worldwide

Meta Expands Teen Account Protections Globally

Meta has announced that it's expanding its AI age-estimation technology globally to automatically place millions of teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. "We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections," Meta said. "As a result, millions more teens across the world who use Instagram will receive these built-in protections, even if they've misrepresented their age." In Australia, Meta has opted to use Apple's age-range signal as another method to help understand age.

OAuth support for Exchange migrations

Microsoft Supports OAuth Authentication for On-Premises Exchange Mailbox Migrations

Microsoft 365 Mailbox Replication Service (MRS) has added support for OAuth as an authentication method when migrating mailboxes between Microsoft 365 and an on-premises Exchange environment. "Once OAuth for MRS is configured, tenant administrators can create an OAuth migration endpoint and use it in migration batches or in onboarding and offboarding move jobs," Microsoft said. "You can use this method in both hybrid and non-hybrid organizations."

NTLM signing hardened against relay attacks

Microsoft Enables NTLM Signing by Default in Windows to Reduce Relay Attacks

In more Microsoft-related news, the tech giant has incorporated additional protections into Windows starting November 10, 2026, that address CVE-2026-118737 (CVSS score: 8.1), a critical remote code execution flaw in Remote Procedure Call Runtime that could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. "These updates represent the first phase of improvements to NTLM message signing," Microsoft said. "These changes help ensure that authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing, reducing exposure to relay attacks." To that end, Windows servers will begin requiring NTLM signing by default starting May 2027.

Exposed cloud credentials lingered 18 months

Entra ID Issue Impacting Planning Inspectorate Disclosed

Details have emerged about a now-patched security flaw affecting the Planning Inspectorate, an executive agency of the United Kingdom's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG). The issue involved a complete Microsoft Entra ID application credential that was committed in plaintext to a GitHub repository. "Although removed from the branch, the commit was orphaned via a force push and remained retrievable via GitHub's raw object CDN for 18 months," ControlPlane said. The client secret was deleted about 20 minutes after responsible disclosure on August 26, 2026.

Fake software sites spread infostealer

SEO Poisoning Campaign Delivers Armorsteal

An SEO poisoning campaign is using fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware called Armorsteal. "The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor," Zscaler said. "The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data."

Localized phishing delivers banking trojan

Grandoreiro Campaign Targets LATAM

A new Grandoreiro banking malware campaign is targeting users across Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru through country-specific phishing lures that are tailored to each region. "The campaign uses localized phishing lures, primarily in Spanish, with some observed using Portuguese even when targeting Spanish-speaking countries," Arctic Wolf said. "The phishing chain relies on recently registered domains and layered redirection to hinder detection. The final payload is retrieved through a Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) seeded with the current date. The downloaded ZIP archive uses a deeply nested folder structure populated with two legitimate PE files and two benign PDF documents. A VBScript file located in the archive's root directory acts as the primary payload, employing junk code and multiple layers of obfuscation before reconstructing and launching a Delphi-based loader." The loader masquerades as a PDF reader and is used to fetch and run the banking trojan.

AI search results targeted by scam sites

Indirect Prompt Injection Campaign for Investment Scam Sites

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said it detected an indirect prompt injection (IDPI) campaign across 26 domains. "These are attempting black-hat Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to game AI-powered search results," Unit 42 said. "Almost all of the 26 pages have very similar content, presenting as AI-powered digital asset trading platforms. These sites appear to be scam sites designed to collect user information. The injected prompt is set to be hidden from a regular web user but likely visible to an AI agent. These attacks intend to poison SEO and manipulate AI agents to eventually get users to visit these sites."

PyPI adds release verification signals

PyPI Announces Redesigned Project Pages with New Security Tab

The Python Package Index (PyPI) has added a security tab to its project pages, giving developers easy access to security signals. "The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from," PyPI said. "PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation."

100+ domains spread credential stealer

REVSTEALER's Growing Distribution Ecosystem

The information stealer known as RevStealer is being propagated as part of an "industrial-scale, financially motivated campaign" that uses game cheats and AI tools as lures. The payload is distributed through more than 100 interconnected domains, trojanized Electron applications masquerading as Anthropic's Claude Opus 5, and hijacked YouTube distribution channels, per Akatsuki Legion. "Once executed, the malware performs a ten-point weighted sandbox-evasion scoring routine, decrypts an AES-256-CBC in-memory payload, and leverages fourteen indirect syscall wrappers and FNV-1a API hashing to bypass user-mode hooks before systematically harvesting credentials from browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Steam, Roblox, Battle.net, EA Desktop, and Minecraft; then exfiltrating the loot as streamed, encrypted typed records over HTTPS, with a resilient Polygon blockchain dead-drop resolver standing by as a fallback command-and-control channel," the independent adversary research group said.

AI infrastructure becomes an attack target

Threat Actors Target AI Infrastructure

Threat actors have increasingly targeted AI orchestration platforms over the past few months, according to Sekoia. This is because "they concentrate API keys, enterprise data, and access to external tools," it added. This includes Flowise, which has been affected by multiple security flaws like CVE-2025-59528 and CVE-2026-41264. In one exploitation attempt recorded in August 2026, a suspected Chinese-speaking actor abused legitimate Flowise functionality to conduct automated reconnaissance and attempted to hijack the LLM agent to serve as an offensive analysis vector against external targets. "The attacker attempted to turn the AI agent into an interactive offensive assistant, submitting real-world reconnaissance data (Nightingale/Redis infrastructure) to generate custom exploitation playbooks and target analysis," Sekoia said.

AI-built phishing kits multiply

Vibe-Coded Phishing Kits Emerge

LevelBlue has disclosed details of a family of phishing kits named BlackApex, DarkApex, SPY, XXX101-TOKEN, OGPARKER1, W1-TOKEN, and ALIBOBO-TOKEN that are used to facilitate device code phishing attacks using shared document lures. The findings once again demonstrate how AI can speed up the development of a convincing multi-brand phishing kit. "Across all of its lures, the source shows traits we associate with AI-generated code, whether from direct prompts to a language model or from a person working alongside an AI coding assistant," LevelBlue said. "The code, endpoints, and interface are the same across all of them. We cannot say whether these names reflect separate operators, resellers or customers of a single kit, but the pattern is consistent with a shared product being rebranded and redeployed."

AI verifies Signal security properties

DeepMind's AlphaProof Code Proves the Signal Protocol Is Secure

Google's DeepMind has introduced AlphaProof Code, which brings together human experts and AI agents to verify software and mathematically demonstrate that it works as intended. The multi-agent AI framework has been used to prove key security properties of libsignal, the Signal protocol's reference implementation, at the machine-code level. "AlphaProof Code consists of a human-guided agent for writing Lean specifications of code, a formal semantics of AArch64 machine code, and a team of autonomous prover agents whose proofs are accepted only if Lean’s kernel checks them against the approved specification," DeepMind said. "Applied to libsignal, our agents generated about 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean proof code, resting on about 26,000 lines of trusted specifications and AArch64 semantics. The proofs cover Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, establishing forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy."

That's the lot for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others relied on old mistakes, trusted accounts, or someone clicking the wrong thing. AI is showing up on both sides, making attacks easier to build while helping researchers find problems faster. The tools keep changing, but attackers still seem happy to use whatever works.

The good news is that some of these threats are being stopped, and defenses are slowly catching up. The bad news is that fixing a bug, removing a file, or blocking an attacker doesn't always mean the problem is gone. Sometimes the damage sticks around longer than anyone expects. Worth keeping in mind before the next batch of headlines arrives.

articles.title: New SignDrop Zero-Day Exploit Turns Windows CLFS Security Feature Into SYSTEM Access
articles.context: Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver
articles.full_text:
Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver.

The proof of concept, called SignDrop, targets a log-authentication feature added to the driver last year. It abuses how clfs.sys creates companion files when a privileged process opens a prepared log, using path redirection to take control of the operation. Microsoft has not confirmed the claimed flaw, assigned a CVE, or released a fix.

The researcher behind the exploit, who publishes under the name MSNightmare, released the code and a detailed writeup on GitHub on Tuesday, the same day the company published its November security updates.

CLFS is a logging subsystem built into Windows. Its driver has been a frequent target for privilege escalation: 10 CLFS flaws appear in CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in attacks, including one used in ransomware campaigns in April 2025.

To reduce that exposure, Microsoft added an authentication check to CLFS log files in updates for Windows 11 25H2, 26H1, and Windows Server 2025 shipped in October 2025. The check attaches a hash-based message authentication code, built from log data and a key unique to each machine.

The driver then parses only log files it wrote. A companion .cnpf file stores recovery data beside each log and is created with the same security attributes as the original, according to the company's logfile authentication page.

SignDrop targets the creation of that companion file. According to the proof-of-concept code, a standard user prepares a CLFS log and container with paths the user controls. When a privileged process later opens that log, the driver creates the .cnpf file in the privileged process's security context rather than the user's.

The exploit uses object manager symbolic links to redirect that file creation to a location the attacker chooses. In the published code, the privileged process is the Defender antimalware service, triggered through its update interface.

"Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the researcher wrote.

Because the .cnpf file inherits the original log's permissions, the result is a file created as SYSTEM that the standard user can write to. The researcher says that can be chained into a SYSTEM shell.

The exploit was tested on Windows 11 26H2, a Windows 11 26H2 Experimental build, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, according to the repository. Systems are affected when the CLFS authentication registry mode is set to 0 (enforced) or 1 (learning). Systems older than 90 days typically move from learning to enforcement automatically, so the default configuration on established installations is the one the exploit targets.

A registry value of 2 or 3 means the mitigation is disabled. That takes the system outside the claimed attack surface, but the researcher and the driver's own documentation both warn against it: disabling lets CLFS parse tampered log files, reopening the memory corruption flaws the protection was built to prevent.

Independent Test

Sungyup Nam, head of research at Korean security firm 78researchlab, reported in a published assessment today that researcher Heewon Song of the firm's PurpleHound offensive content team tested the exploit and found that it works. Song assessed that it does not run reliably enough for operational use, Nam wrote.

Defender must be enabled for the published chain to succeed. Running the exploit changes every UAC prompt to open a standard user shell and a SYSTEM shell, blocking other actions and making the attack noticeable to anyone at the machine.

The repository claims the technique can work against any antimalware engine whose process runs with elevated privileges. That broader claim has not been tested.

What Defenders Can Do

No CVE, advisory, or patch for SignDrop appeared in the November security updates. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog does not list it, and no attacks using the exploit have been reported.

Administrators can check their exposure by reading the CLFS authentication mode at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication, where a Mode value of 0 or 1 falls within the researcher's claimed scope. The vendor's mitigation guidance describes the setting and the risks of disabling it.

The researcher has released a series of exploits targeting Windows and Defender since April. The vendor confirmed an earlier Defender exploit called RoguePlanet in June as CVE-2026-50656 and patched it the following month.

The ShieldBreak bypass followed in August and was assigned CVE-2026-69414. Three of the researcher's earlier Defender flaws have been exploited in attacks.

SignDrop is a different class of issue. Where the earlier exploits targeted race conditions in Defender's file handling, this one targets the CLFS driver's own authentication feature. The vendor's security update guide is the place to watch for a response.

articles.title: Capabilities and vulnerabilities of the Muse AI agent | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: Around the same time, a researcher found a vulnerability that let an attacker take control of Muse and act on the owner’s behalf
articles.full_text:
That’s how the Odyssey might have opened if it were about Muse, Meta’s new AI agent. For now, the agent is available only as an iOS, Android, or macOS app and on the web. Even so, it’s already caught on: according to Meta’s official figures, Muse had been downloaded more than 10 million times by October 21.

The agent can do a lot: read your conversations and calendars, remind you about meetings and tasks, reply to messages and emails, track your spending, make purchases, search the web, generate content, and much, much more. In short, a full-blown concierge service for the chronically busy. Muse’s creators have admitted they drew heavily on the headline-grabbing AI agent OpenClaw, which researchers coincidentally found full of serious security holes.

But soon after launch, the bad news about Muse started piling up. First, a journalist discovered that the agent had gotten into his conversations without explicit permission. Around the same time, a researcher found a vulnerability that let an attacker take control of Muse and act on the owner’s behalf. And then it turned out that the calls the AI was supposedly making were actually being handed off to… human operators.

We look at how all this could happen, and how to use Muse as safely as possible.

When the agent reads more than it should

Journalist Jason Aten installed Muse on his iPhone and Mac, and deliberately didn’t give the agent access to the Messages app. Yet after he exchanged messages with a colleague about the new iPhones, Muse unexpectedly offered to draft a column on that very topic, citing his editor’s message about the deadline. Aten immediately asked the agent how it had acquired that information.

Muse’s explanation was that the Mac app had merely been passing it the text of notification pop-ups, which sounded quite plausible at first glance. But then Aten discovered that Muse had been syncing data directly from the local message database on his Mac. The sync had reached row 187 462 of the database. That number alone doesn’t reveal exactly how many messages were processed, but this was clearly far more than a few notifications.

According to a Meta employee, Muse could read conversations only if the user had separately allowed access to Messages and given the app Full Disk Access. How the agent managed to read the conversations without explicit permission remains unclear. The likely culprit was an opaque permissions interface.

Zero-day vulnerability in Muse

Just as the message-snooping scandal broke, researcher Patrick Wardle found a serious vulnerability in Muse tied to how the app stores and uses its internal settings.

Muse keeps several of these settings locally, and some of them could be changed with hardly any restrictions. One of these settings determines which server receives your voice input for speech recognition. Normally, these requests go to a Meta server, but Wardle found that almost any local app or Terminal command could change the address.

In practice, an attacker could do this in one of two ways: infect the victim’s device with malware, or talk the victim into pasting a specially crafted command into Terminal under the guise of “helpful instructions”. These dangerous instructions are often spread through fake websites or infected browser extensions that alter the content of the web pages people view.

Once the Meta server in the settings had been swapped for the attacker’s, Muse’s voice requests went there instead. Along with those requests, the attacker received an authorization token, which let them impersonate the account owner and control the agent remotely. If the user had already given Muse access to their camera, messages, files, and other data, the attacker could use all that for their own ends: take photos with the camera, write malicious files to disk, read conversations, locate linked devices, and much, much more.

Once in control of Muse, an attacker can use the same features as the agent itself: take pictures with the front camera, view photos, read files and modify or delete them, show notifications… All told, the researcher counted more than 50 such commands. Source

What’s more, the attacker could route Muse’s voice traffic through their server, and quietly slip their own instructions in with the victim’s voice commands. They would pick up the Muse token along the way, so after the first successful attack they could keep their access to the agent and go on controlling it remotely. Meta has already released an update that fixes the vulnerability, but stories like this are far from rare in the AI world.

Meatbags to the rescue

Muse has an experimental feature that calls U.S. businesses on the user’s behalf: the agent can phone a company itself, ask for the details it needs, and then show a transcript of the call. But as Reuters and 404 Media discovered, Meta had also been testing a curious add-on to this feature with its own employees: handing the calls off to trained call-center operators. Fully automated calls weren’t getting the job done: people on the other end simply hung up as soon as they heard a robotic voice. Meanwhile, many Meta employees had no idea their requests were being handed off to real people.

After a barrage of criticism, Meta shut down the human operator experiment. Company representatives said it had been a mistake to run the experiment without warning and promised to improve the feature.

Protecting your privacy: which Muse settings to check

Meta really does process a huge amount of data when people use Muse: conversations with the chatbot, photos, metadata, uploaded and generated files… This also includes information from any third-party apps you’ve connected to the agent. Meta employees can access this data on an as-needed basis.

We recommend checking the following settings and turning off any features you don’t need:

System permissions on Mac

Full Disk Access: full access to the disk and files on the computer.

Automation: lets the agent take actions in local apps, such as sending messages or deleting notes.

Notifications: lets the agent notify you when it finishes a task.

You can separately restrict access to apps that store their data on your Mac itself rather than in the cloud. Muse offers three modes for each app:

Off: the agent can neither read data nor take actions.

Read only: the agent can only read information, at your request.

Read and interact: the agent can read information and take actions in the app.

Action confirmation

By default, Muse is supposed to ask you for permission before taking important actions in third-party apps. Still, relying on an AI’s judgment for, say, shopping or conversations with coworkers is hardly a good idea, so it’s best to limit its autonomy ahead of time. In Muse, go to Settings → Permissions → Connectors, and choose either Ask for some actions (the less secure option), or Always ask. In Manage permissions, review any permissions you’ve already granted under Connectors.

Meta notes that if you use a single account, Muse connects to Facebook, Instagram, and Threads automatically, and that unlinking them cuts off access but doesn’t delete the data already collected; you have to delete it manually.

Website access

You can set up Muse’s internet access in much the same way:

Go to Settings→ Permissions → Web access defaults.

Choose Ask for some actions to have Muse ask for permission before sharing your data or opening an unfamiliar site, or Always ask to have the agent ask before visiting any site at all.

We recommend choosing Always ask and using anti-phishing protection: there’s always a chance the agent will mistakenly decide to open a fake or suspicious site.

Training on your data

Meta claims that the user data used to train Muse is anonymized and stored without being linked to an account. Unfortunately, that doesn’t mean you can’t be identified from context: the emails, messages, documents, and calendars the agent works with contain names, email addresses, home addresses, and other details that give away your identity.

Meta also says it removes certain categories of personal identifiers before training the model. But the more information goes into training, the higher the risk that one day it will surface by accident in someone else’s conversation, or become public because of a bug. Sadly, even internal safety filters sometimes fail.

And, naturally, training is on by default. To turn off training, go to Settings → Data controls → Help improve our AI models and select Turn off.

Permissions on mobile devices

On mobile devices, we recommend reviewing the permissions you’ve given the Muse app. In your phone’s settings, limit its access to your contacts, photos, location, microphone, and camera. Also turn off AI training on your data.

On iPhone, open Settings → Privacy & Security, and check which categories Muse can access. On Android, check Settings → Apps → Muse → Permissions. You can turn off training separately in Muse → Settings → Data controls.

How to use AI agents safely

Revoke permissions you don’t need, and don’t share sensitive data with the agent. The less information the agent can access, the less you risk if there’s a leak or a bug.

Don’t delegate important decisions or actions to agents. Even if the agent asks you to confirm before it buys something or sends a message, check exactly what it’s about to do, and where. Otherwise, you might end up paying for a purchase of non-existing goods or services on a fake website. Muse’s creators themselves write that the agent isn’t fully protected against prompt injections — hidden malicious commands aimed at AI.

Don’t run Terminal commands you don’t understand — especially if a website, email, or pop-up claims they’re needed for a “security check” or to “install an update”. That’s exactly how the ClickFix attacks work: they trick users into running a malicious command themselves. To protect yourself from malware and fake websites, install a comprehensive security solution on your devices.

Keep the app that runs the agent up to date. The developers have fixed the vulnerability Patrick Wardle found, but security problems in AI turn up all the time.

More reading on AI security and privacy:

Dear diary: how OpenAI’s Computer History feature works, and why it’s risky

The pros and cons of AI-powered browsers

Why AI agents need an iron curtain

Privacy settings in ChatGPT

articles.title: Critical Red Hat Quay Flaw Lets Attackers Read and Overwrite All Private Container Images in a Registry
articles.context: A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository
articles.full_text:
A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository.

Quay enables anonymous access by default, and while it is enabled, the attacker needs no account. When it is off, anyone with a valid account can still exploit the flaw, Red Hat said yesterday. The company has released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 (CVSS score: 9.8).

Quay uses keys it trusts to sign the access tokens that allow image pushes and pulls. The flaw lets an attacker add their own key to the keys Quay trusts, with no expiry date. Quay then accepts tokens signed with that key for any repository.

With those tokens, an attacker can retrieve private images and any secrets or credentials stored within them. The attacker can also push or overwrite images, and the change propagates to every system that later pulls those images.

The planted key survives restarts until someone removes it. It can also be used to delete the keys that running Quay instances use, so normal pushes and pulls start failing with authentication errors.

Quay's key server checks that a request to replace a key carries a token signed by a trusted key, with the expected audience and issuer. It does not check whether the token was issued for key rotation. An anonymous token from Quay's /v2/auth endpoint passes: Quay signs it with a trusted key, and the caller chooses its audience.

A second critical flaw, CVE-2026-110697 (CVSS score: 9.9), was disclosed at the same time. It lets a Quay user who can create a namespace steal other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to read, push, or overwrite those tenants' images.

This flaw is in the code that lists robot accounts. It builds an SQL LIKE pattern from the namespace name without escaping wildcard characters, and in SQL LIKE an underscore matches any single character.

So a namespace with an underscore in the right place can match another tenant's namespace and return its robot accounts, with their decrypted tokens. The attacker needs no elevated privileges, and the victim does not have to do anything.

Deleting the attacker's namespace also deletes the corresponding robot accounts, which can cut off systems that rely on them. Where Quay is the integrated registry for OpenShift, stolen robot credentials can be used to inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines, the company says.

Red Hat's Dave O'Connor found both flaws. The logic behind CVE-2026-123710 has been in Quay since its first public commit, according to the bug report for that flaw.

Red Hat lists every version of Quay 3 and Quay 5 as affected by both flaws. For CVE-2026-123710, its guidance names standalone installs, Quay deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift, and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift as affected.

Any Quay instance that untrusted clients can reach is exposed, including internal registries, the company says.

When checked today, the CVE entry for CVE-2026-123710 still showed every Quay package as affected, with no fix, even though each advisory lists the flaw.

The company recommends these steps:

At the proxy or load balancer, block the /keys endpoint for everything except trusted internal components.

Search the audit logs for service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events where expiration_date is null.

Remove any approved service keys you do not recognize.

Install the fixed release. Until it is running, an attacker can add a new key the same way, so deleting one does not last.

"Turning off anonymous access doesn't protect you," the company says in its key remediation article. A planted key also continues to work after password resets and changes to the robot token.

For CVE-2026-110697, the company's CVE page names the same eight releases as fixed, calls updating the only complete fix, and says Quay.io is already fixed. But none of the eight advisories list CVE-2026-110697.

Until an update is in place, the company suggests limiting who can create organizations or namespaces containing an underscore, rotating robot tokens for any namespace that matches an underscore namespace, and watching for pulls or pushes that do not fit normal robot use. These steps reduce the exposure, but the flaw remains.

The upstream fix adds the missing rotation check, requires keys added through the key server to have an expiry date, and stops callers from choosing a token's audience. The same change fixes the robot account search too.

articles.title: New Windows SignDrop zero-day gives hackers SYSTEM privileges
articles.context: Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (also known as Nightmare Eclipse) has released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges
articles.full_text:
Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (also known as Nightmare Eclipse) has released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges.

Named SignDrop, it exploits mitigations Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to defend against authentication attacks targeting vulnerabilities in the Common Log File System (CLFS) driver. Naceri added that attacks exploiting CLFS vulnerabilities dropped sharply after the mitigation, but that Microsoft's mitigation itself introduced this new vulnerability.

According to Naceri, the flaw is in how CLFS handles creating the authentication file (".cnpf") when it creates a new log file. He said that CLFS enforces access checks correctly at the start, but the logic can be abused if a different, privileged process later opens the log file.

He also added that privileged processes such as Windows Defender can be forced to open the files, so the authentication file gets created with SYSTEM privileges, and CLFS creates it with the original file's access permissions.

Naceri noted that Microsoft implemented the mitigation properly but that "the logic allows abuse" and said the technique works against any antimalware engine's self-defense (tamper protection), because the file-creation request appears to come from the engine's own legitimate process.

"If everything is chained correctly, funnily, this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation of privileges. Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the security researcher said.

"What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism, as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR."

​While SignDrop can't be used against all Windows machines, Naceri tested the exploit on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental and estimates that 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable.

Naceri recommends running the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to check if a Windows device is vulnerable to SignDrop attacks or to check the CLFS authentication mode under the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode registry value.

If the PoC exploit spawns a SYSTEM shell, the machine is vulnerable. Additionally, if the registry value is 0 or 1 (learning mode or enforcement mode), the computer is vulnerable.

Naceri added that there is currently no solution except waiting for a patch from Microsoft, since disabling the CLFS mitigation would expose the devices to attacks exploiting memory corruption vulnerabilities.

The security researcher, who says he is a former Microsoft employee, has disclosed a long list of other zero-day flaws in Microsoft Defender, BitLocker, and other Windows components since April, including BigDiskBuster, ShieldCrash, ShieldBreak, LegacyHive, RoguePlanet, BlueHammer, RedSun, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, MiniPlasma, and UnDefend.

Five years ago, Naceri released several zero-day exploits that allowed privilege escalation on various Windows versions.

After Naceri publicly disclosed the zero-days without first attempting to report them privately, Microsoft warned of legal action against anyone engaging in "malicious activity causing real harm" to the company's customers, leading many in the infosec community to see the company's actions as a direct threat to the security researcher.

While Microsoft has fixed some of the security flaws Naceri disclosed since the start of the year (including ShieldBreak, RoguePlanet, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, and MiniPlasma flaws), the other zero-day bugs still lack an official patch.

articles.title: Citrix Patches 12 NetScaler and Secure Access Client Flaws, Including Authentication Bypass
articles.context: Citrix has released patches for multiple critical security flaws impacting NetScaler ADC, Citrix NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console that could lead to denial-of-service...
articles.full_text:
Citrix has released patches for multiple critical security flaws impacting NetScaler ADC, Citrix NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console that could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or an authentication bypass.

The critical vulnerabilities that impact NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway are listed below -

CVE-2026-120868 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Packet Processing can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments)

CVE-2026-107407 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in SMPP traffic can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC configured with a Load Balancing or Content Switching virtual server of type SMPP)

CVE-2026-107408 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory corruption vulnerability in DNS / DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC configured for DNS load balancing and recursive DNS resolution)

CVE-2026-107409 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory corruption vulnerability in DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured with DNS Load Balancing over HTTPS)

CVE-2026-107410 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow in NetScaler Push can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as Load Balancing virtual server of type PUSH)

CVE-2026-107412 (CVSS score: 9.5) - Multiple memory overflow vulnerabilities can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior and DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway or an AAA virtual server)

CVE-2026-107415 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Email OTP authentication can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway configured with an Email Action)

CVE-2026-111344 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Endpoint Analysis (EPA/EPAS) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a VPN virtual server or an authentication (AAA) virtual server with Endpoint Analysis)

CVE-2026-120864 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in ICA proxy can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway VPN virtual server, an AAA virtual server, or a CR virtual server of type HDX)

All the issues have been patched in the following versions -

Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.57 and later releases

Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.39 and later releases of 13.1

Citrix NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.58 FIPS and later releases of 14.1-FIPS

Citrix NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.293 and later releases of 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP

Also addressed by Citrix are a number of flaws in NetScaler Console and Secure Access Client for Windows and Linux -

CVE-2026-120869 (CVSS score: 9.4) - An improper authentication vulnerability in NetScaler Console can allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication controls to access restricted resources on the appliance. (Fixed in NetScaler Console 14.1-74.34 and later)

CVE-2026-118268 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper privilege management vulnerability in Secure Access Client for Windows can allow a low-privileged user to escalate privileges to SYSTEM. (Fixed in Secure Access Client for Windows 26.11.1.6 and later)

CVE-2026-118269 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper privilege management vulnerability in Secure Access Client for Linux can allow a low-privileged user to gain root privileges. (Fixed in Secure Access Client for Linux 26.10.4 and later)

The security updates, Citrix said, follow a deeper review of its codebase by integrating artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted code analysis to detect and resolve vulnerabilities with an aim to harden the products before potential threats could materialize.

The company said it's not aware of any exploits for any of the announced vulnerabilities, but urged customers to apply the updates as they are designed to "enhance the security posture of NetScaler."

articles.title: Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era
articles.context: Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released
articles.full_text: Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone. The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update. Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned. Support for Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended on October 14, 2025, but the company announced an Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in July 2025. The plan was that this program would end on April 14, 2026, by which time customers would surely have made the jump to a later or online version, right? The company said: "This period will not be extended past April 2026 (you do not need to ask)." And... of course it was. As April 2026 rolled around, and it became clear that some customers were still stubbornly sticking with the old versions, Microsoft did the equivalent of heaving an exasperated sigh and offered another six months of paid security updates. Those final weeks also brought a separate treat: a Windows Server update breaking Exchange Server. This time it was serious. Microsoft released the final Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 security updates on October 13. No more patches, no more vulnerability testing, and apparently no more reprieves. According to Microsoft's Security Update Guide, the November update fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server SE, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft isn't testing earlier versions of Exchange for the vulnerabilities. ®
