articles.context: In the observed incidents, the attacker exploited PHP2Shell to gain initial access, then used a local privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges and establish...
articles.full_text:
Check Point Research has identified active, in-the-wild exploitation of PHP2Shell, a vulnerability in PHP that also affects Check Point Security Gateways. In the observed incidents, the attacker exploited PHP2Shell to gain initial access, then used a local privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges and establish persistence.

Security fixes for Check Point Security Gateway and Management were available one week before the attack, on October 23rd. Only a couple of dozen unpatched systems, in a single region, were compromised in the observed incidents. Affected customers were notified in real time. Check Point Research, through its Incident Response teams, worked to remediate affected systems.

We recommend that customers install the November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways as soon as operationally possible.

Overview

As part of BLAST and our Frontier AI Readiness Program, Check Point continues to release monthly security fixes that include fixes for vulnerabilities and security hardening.

Recent security incidents, such as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) and HTTP2Shell, also known as Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), a Brotli decompression vulnerability affecting Node.js and other software, led us to release hotfixes that are now part of the November Jumbo Hotfix.

Check Point is reporting active exploitation of PHP2Shell together with a local privilege escalation vulnerability (CVE-2026-123039). Indicators of compromise are shared below to help customers investigate.

Observed Attacks

Check Point Research investigated the exploitation of a chain of PHP2Shell and the Dynamic CLI privilege escalation vulnerability against internet-facing gateways. Exploitation activity dates back to October 30 and was observed as active until November 4.

Initial access was gained through exploitation of PHP2Shell in the Mobile Access Portal. While a hotfix for PHP2Shell has been available since October 23rd, we included it in this November Jumbo Hotfix. The privilege escalation vulnerability was then required to elevate permissions.

This activity provided initial access to the customer network and, in many cases, led to a foothold in the network. In a limited number of cases, the attack also involved destructive activity and was ideologically motivated.

Check Point Research, through our Incident Response teams, contacted affected customers on the day the investigation started and worked to remediate affected systems.

Recommended Actions

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation on Check Point Gateway
articles.context: TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, a malware framework previously documented in attacks exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities
articles.full_text:
Key findings

Beginning on 30 October 2026, an attacker executed scanning and exploitation activity against organizations with unpatched Check Point Security Gateways, using Mobile Access portals with PHP2Shell as initial access followed by CVE-2026-123039.

The first wave, on October 30, targeted Israeli organizations and included destructive activity against some of them. A broader second wave on November 2 targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors, with no evidence of destructive activity

In the investigated intrusion, PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The attackers then deployed PHP webshells, the persistent TSGA backdoor and its embedded TSProxy networking component.

The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage.

TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, a malware framework previously documented in attacks exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities. Both tools share distinctive code, configuration, and cryptographic material with the framework

Although ESET associated PhiliKit with China nexus UNC5221, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

The note left during the destructive activity uses the Dream Security brand. Dream had recently published research on PHP2Shell exploitation of Palo Alto Networks devices by China nexus actors. While this timing raises the possibility of retaliation, the available evidence does not establish a clear motive.

Introduction

We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.

A second scanning wave on November 2nd targeted some Israeli organizations previously targeted during the first wave, alongside additional organizations worldwide, with no apparent focus on Israel. Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting.

Infection Flow

On October 30, 2026, the first signs of exploitation appeared on the targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways. PHP session artifacts were created under /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/, including session files containing the upload_progress_pwn marker associated with the exploitation activity. During the same window, the portal’s Apache/PHP workers experienced hundreds of segmentation faults, providing additional evidence of repeated exploitation attempts against the service.

Figure 1 – Infection chain

After gaining access to the Mobile Access portal, the attackers escalated privileges to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI interface. With privileged command execution, the attackers placed PHP webshells in <templates>, a directory used by the Mobile Access portal to construct its login pages. These webshells provide a way to send commands through the web portal, establishing a stronger foothold within the compromised environment.

printf <base64 Webshell> | base64 -d > <templates>/zz<random>.tpl

The attacker used multiple .tpl files with names matching the pattern zz*.tpl Each initially received a small command-execution shell, which was then replaced with a more capable version. The expanded shell requires the hardcoded key zz2026 and supports operating-system commands, PHP code execution, and file uploads. Uploaded files are saved to the fixed path /tmp/.up.tpl. The attackers subsequently issued commands to copy that file into the portal’s directory as challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then moved from web-based access to a standalone passive backdoor, launching the TSGA malware (/tmp/CPconfigdaemon) in the background and redirecting its output to a hidden temporary log:

nohup /tmp/CPconfigdaemon >/tmp/.bd.log 2>&1 & printf started

When executed as root, the malware relocates itself and relaunches under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon in the boot persistence directory. The executable also carries a second component, TSProxy: an embedded shared library that it writes to /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. Its injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue. This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services.

The attackers then deployed the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network and continued to move laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, authenticating with the vpxuser service account. On the ESXi host, they staged the destroy_v6 wiper to /tmp/des wiper and executed it. Finally, the attackers left a note that accompanied the destructive activity named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt.

Figure 2 – Destructive activity note

Technical Analysis

Webshells

The expanded PHP webshell requires a hardcoded key to access its command-execution, PHP-evaluation, and file-upload functions. It supports both plain-text and Base64-encoded, XOR-obfuscated commands, and saves uploaded files to /tmp/.up.tpl.

Figure 3 – Webshell code

Wiper

The Linux ELF wiper destroy_v6 accepts a target directory as a command-line argument. The optional -f flag enables fast deletion, while -w specifies a pipe-separated list of directories to exclude. The wiper recursively traverses the target directory, deleting files regardless of extension and skipping excluded subtrees. By default, it attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them, fast mode skips the overwrite step. It also writes DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt to each processed directory. This politically themed note includes a timestamp and explicitly rejects ransom negotiations.

TSGA – slot_CPconfigdaemon

The TSGA implant, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, is a Linux gateway implant with substantial Check Point-specific functionality. It provides encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

TSProxy

TSProxy is a Linux shared-library backdoor embedded in TSGA and dropped as /lib/libcpfwcommon.so and supports encrypted SOCKS-style proxying.

Tools relationship

Both TSGA and TSProxy are Check Point-specific components linked to the previously reported PhiliKit-associated toolset. PhiliKit is a passive backdoor and installer targeting Ivanti VPN appliances and was previously reported following the February 25, 2026 upload of a sample named philistine to VirusTotal.

TSGA and the PhiliKit implant have roots in Tiny SHell, and share a core set of remote-control capabilities. Both implement authenticated, encrypted communications through TCP port 11072 and the Unix socket /tmp/.p_sock. The analyzed PhiliKit build restricts its TCP listener to loopback, whereas TSGA listens on all IPv4 interfaces. Both provide interactive shells with pseudo-terminal allocation, configurable terminal dimensions and bidirectional input/output. Operators can execute arbitrary shell commands and Python or Perl scripts, retrieve their output, transfer files using operator-selected paths, and collect selected or full appliance configurations over the encrypted channel.

TSProxy shares distinctive configuration with libdssafe.so, the networking component embedded in PhiliKit package: identical operator credentials, transport secrets, three matching activation-selector digests, and the same TLS certificate and private key. These overlaps strongly support a shared tooling lineage.

Attribution

The implants delivered to the gateway, TSGA and TSProxy are part of the PhiliKit malware family, which has been associated with the China-nexus group UNC5221 and previous exploitation of Ivanti appliances. In addition, gogo scanner has also been reported in connection with Chinese-nexus threat actors exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities.

The infrastructure IP addresses used by the attacker were hosted on LightNode VPS infrastructure, a service previously associated with activity by Chinese- nexus threat actors.

The scanning activity was concentrated between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to 08:00–17:00 in China and broadly aligning with typical Chinese working hours.

With all the above, the following attributes that appeared in the described campaign do not appear to fully align with known Chinese-nexus groups (and specifically UNC5221) motives and interests:

Destructive operation

Focus on Israel and wiper note in Hebrew referring to the Israeli-Palestine conflict

Philikit name derived from the malware internal name philistine

Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

articles.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
articles.context: Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT...
articles.full_text: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

articles.title: Zoom Fixes Critical Windows Vulnerability Allowing Privilege Escalation
articles.context: If successfully exploited, either vulnerability could allow attackers to increase their privileges without having an account or any special permissions on the affected system
articles.full_text:
Zoom fixes two Windows Workplace flaws, including a critical bug that could let unauthenticated attackers remotely escalate privileges.

Zoom has released security updates to fix two vulnerabilities in Zoom Workplace for Windows. One is critical and could let attackers gain higher privileges on affected systems.

The vulnerabilities are:

CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS 9.6): An input validation flaw that could allow an attacker to gain higher privileges through a network connection, without logging in.

CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS 8.1): An origin validation flaw that could also allow an unauthenticated attacker to gain higher privileges remotely.

If successfully exploited, either vulnerability could allow attackers to increase their privileges without having an account or any special permissions on the affected system. Users should install the latest Zoom Workplace updates to protect their systems.

The first flaw was reported by the internal security team, while the second one was reported by the research shmoul.

CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows releases earlier than 7.1.5, while CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions from 7.1.0 up to, but not including, 7.1.8.

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In August, Zoom patched four vulnerabilities, including a critical zero-click flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-53413. CVE-2026-53413 is a memory corruption issue found by A Security that could allow a meeting participant to execute code on another participant’s computer.

Due to its impact, the researchers dubbed the flaw “Zoomsday,” it affects Zoom clients on all supported platforms and is linked to the proprietary protocol used by the annotation function. Zoom has now begun rolling out security updates to address the issue.

“Ⓐ Security, the Autonomous Offensive Security and Remediation Platform, discovered a critical flaw in Zoom that let an attacker take complete control of another user’s device during a live call. No click, no download, and nothing required of the victim but being in the meeting.” reads the report published by A Security. “The vulnerability is present in every version of Zoom on every device and operating system: Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android and Linux. The vulnerability exists in all versions up to and including 7.0.5.”

The flaw can corrupt memory through a specially crafted message. Attackers could exploit it to target meeting participants, execute code without user interaction, steal data, activate cameras or microphones, and install malware.

In July, Zoom fixed another critical Windows vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-53412 (CVSS score of 9.8), that could allow unauthenticated attackers to hijack user accounts. The flaw affects older versions of Workplace, the Windows VDI Client, and the Meeting SDK for Windows.

At this time, Zoom is not aware of attacks exploiting one of the above vulnerabilities. Users are recommended to apply the latest updates.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-108186)

articles.title: AI found Linux kernel bugs that remained undetected for decades
articles.context: By manipulating memory, an attacker could turn the flaw into a constrained kernel memory-write primitive that, combined with other exploitation techniques, could enable local...
articles.full_text:
A Microsoft research project combining AI agents with human security researchers uncovered 59 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including bugs that had survived in production code for more than 20 years.

While AI dramatically accelerated the discovery process, the researchers found that validating flaws, developing patches, and working with maintainers remained overwhelmingly human-intensive.

The research, conducted by Microsoft’s FORGE Lab under the codename MDASH, generated 26,502 potential findings in approximately two weeks of scanning selected Linux kernel subsystems. Automated screening, proof-of-concept testing, and human validation narrowed these down to 59 public upstream reports, Microsoft said in a blog post.

“We developed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline,” the researchers said in the blog post.

From thousands of findings to 59 reports

Microsoft said it scanned selected kernel components covering networking, filesystems, and security modules. The initial findings were reduced to 11,769 candidates through automated screening. AI agents then attempted to reproduce potential vulnerabilities using QEMU, an open-source machine emulator.

This produced 621 cases with proof-of-concept evidence. Human researchers reviewed these cases to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions, the blog post added.

Of the 621 cases, 59 resulted in public upstream reports. Microsoft said another 266 shared root causes with other findings and could be addressed through the same patch. A further 163 were not reported following review, mostly because of limited security impact, while 133 had already been reported or fixed upstream.

Microsoft said its first public report was submitted on June 27, 2026. By September 1, 55 of the 59 reports had been posted to public mailing lists. The remaining four were reported privately during the same period and routed to public lists by mid-October.

Of the 33 CVEs assigned to the findings, 24 carry a High or higher severity rating, based on CVSS v3.1 scores of at least 7.0, according to Microsoft.

Eight vulnerabilities had working exploits

The eight vulnerabilities for which Microsoft developed working local privilege-escalation exploits affect several kernel components, including IPv4 and IPv6 networking, IPsec routing, encrypted-key handling and the resizable hash-table implementation. Some demonstrations required non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations, the researchers said.

One finding, CVE-2026-64563, involves the kernel’s rhashtable implementation, a shared resizable hash-table library used by different kernel subsystems.

Microsoft traced the flaw to a 2018 code change that allowed a table-walk operation to retain a pointer when paused. Under specific conditions involving table resizing and the removal of an entry, the kernel could subsequently access freed memory through that stale pointer.

The researchers identified an exploitable path through Netlink socket diagnostics, which are accessible to unprivileged users. By manipulating memory, an attacker could turn the flaw into a constrained kernel memory-write primitive that, combined with other exploitation techniques, could enable local privilege escalation, Microsoft explained.

The company said this vulnerability was exploitable on standard Linux configurations without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces. It also affected Android devices with SELinux enforcing.

Across the 59 reports, the average age of a bug was 8.1 years when Microsoft first reported it publicly. One vulnerability, CVE-2026-74544, had been present in the kernel for at least 21 years, the researchers said.

Patching remains a lengthy process

While AI agents helped identify potential vulnerabilities, generate proof-of-concept demonstrations and draft initial patches, Microsoft said human investigation remained necessary to validate findings and work with Linux kernel maintainers.

“Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential,” the researchers wrote.

Fixes for 38 of the 59 reports had been merged into the upstream Linux mainline at the time of publication. Half were accepted with the initial submission, while the others required between one and four revisions. The median time from the first public patch submission to a mainline release was 41 days, with the longest taking 108 days, Microsoft said. Work with maintainers on the remaining reports was continuing.

Microsoft said the initial scans took about two weeks, but converting the findings into validated reports and patches required more than four person-months of work.

“Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance,” the researchers wrote. “For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck.”

The researchers said the project covered only a small fraction of the Linux kernel and that further tuning of the AI-assisted approach could uncover additional bugs. However, they cautioned that finding more vulnerabilities would not necessarily make systems more secure.

“More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system,” the blog post concluded.

articles.title: Google Cloud Warns Three AMD Turin CPU Flaws Could Leak Data Across Processes in VMs
articles.context: AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory
articles.full_text:
Google Cloud VMs on AMD Turin chips need a guest OS patch and a stop-and-start to protect against three CPU side-channel flaws, Google said this week.

The company has already applied mitigations against attacks between VMs, and between VMs and the host. Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel.

The affected machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D,, and G4, including bare-metal instances of C4D and Z4D. Turin is the code name for fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors.

All three flaws are Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA). Two of them, TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350) and TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), were first disclosed on July 8, 2025, for earlier EPYC processors.

AMD now says its Zen 5 processors, which include Turin, are "impacted differently from previously characterized AMD processors." The third flaw, CVE-2026-0004, is new. It may let an attacker who can run code on a system infer data in the processor's L1 data cache.

The Xen Project, which maintains the Xen hypervisor, calls the new flaw TSA-Fill. It also says an earlier statement has been corrected: "AMD had previously said that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1."

Google rates the issue Medium. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory.

As of today, none of the three is in the KEV catalog of exploited flaws kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Neither company reports any exploitation in its bulletins.

What Google Cloud Customers Need to Do

Google's security bulletin gives these steps for each service:

VMs: Install your OS vendor's fix when it ships. Starting this week, the company will update the CPU information that VMs report, so a patched guest kernel can turn on its mitigations. After that update reaches a VM, stop and start it. As the company puts it: "Rebooting the guest OS isn't enough."

Bare metal instances: If you run your own OS or hypervisor on a C4D or Z4D bare metal instance, apply your vendor's fixes when they are available.

Hypervisors inside a VM: The same CPU information update applies, so patched guest kernels can turn on their mitigations. Stop and start the VM once the update arrives.

GKE: Updated node images for Turin-based bare metal instances will be made available, and upgrading nodes picks up the CPU information update. As of today, the bulletin does not yet list them as available.

Cloud Run: No action is needed.

Customers on older Rome, Milan, and Genoa processors got the same stop-and-start instruction in an earlier bulletin at the time of the original disclosure on July 8, 2025.

The company lists nothing to do in the meantime for VMs whose OS vendor has not yet shipped a fix. It also does not say how to tell when the CPU information update has reached a VM.

A kernel commit that mitigates TSA on Zen 5, including the new variant, is in the Linux kernel source tree. As of today, Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch. Its security tracker still lists the kernels in bookworm, trixie, and forky as vulnerable.

For Turin servers on your own hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed to mitigate the flaws fully. The mitigation may affect performance, and administrators should weigh the risk to their own workloads, according to its technical guidance.

The Xen Project has published hypervisor patches in its Xen advisory. It says microcode for all TSA flaws on Zen 5 has been in linux-firmware since September 23.

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.

articles.title: Exploit Attempts for GPUStack Authentication Bypass (CVE-2026-102895), (Thu, Nov 12th)
articles.context: CVE-2026-102895 is a trivial authentication-bypass vulnerability
articles.full_text:
CVE-2026-102895 is a trivial authentication-bypass vulnerability. GPUStack is also an attractive target. It is open-source software that manages clusters of GPUs, which are typically used to run AI workloads. All versions of GPUStack prior to 2.2.0, which was released at the end of June. This vulnerability was not made public until the end of July, and the CVE was assigned on November 4th.

The vulnerability stems from a common pattern: proxies add custom headers, and the recipient trusts them. An attacker can spoof these custom headers, thereby bypassing authentication and/or access control. In this particular case, the header in question is "X-Gpustack-Real-IP". Like similar headers (Forwarded, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP), this header is intended to help identify the IP address from which the request originates. This is all nice and safe as long as no security decisions are made. But this is exactly what happens with GPUStack. If the "X-Gpustack-Real-IP" identifies loopback (127.0.0.1) as the source of the request, Gpustack bypasses authentication (after all, the request originates from a trusted source)

The requests we are seeing right now are pretty straightforward:

GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: [redacted] Accept-Encoding: identity User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 X-Gpustack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1

The IP address we see as the origin of these requests is 144.91.73.103. In the last couple of days, we have seen this IP look for other AI-related resources:

/v1/models /v1beta/models?key=x /v1/messages /models

https://github.com/gpustack/gpustack/security/advisories/GHSA-gj9m-f8ph-pmhr

articles.title: New N-central Exploits Work Against Patched Servers, Enable Root RCE and Windows SYSTEM Access
articles.context: Dewhurst said the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026
articles.full_text:
N-able on Thursday said it's investigating a new public disclosure containing claims of additional vulnerabilities in on-premise versions of N-central running version 2026.4.1 HF2.

"Based on our initial review, the server issue described depends on a non-default configuration in which the Legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet," N-able said in a new advisory. "Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended."

The company is urging customers to disable Legacy API immediately, if not already. It also noted that hosted environments are not affected by this issue.

The incident impacts the following services -

N-central On-premise (Americas)

N-central On-premise (APAC)

N-central On-premise (Europe)

The development comes days after N-able released 2026.4.1.26 to address a number of security flaws disclosed by independent security researcher Sean Bales earlier this week. The vulnerabilities are collectively tracked under the name Able2Shell.

The new shortcoming, also revealed by Bales, have been codenamed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, adding the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits successfully work against N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), the update N-able released on November 10, 2026, to resolve Able2Shell.

According to the researcher, 4EverAble2Shell enables unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on N-central servers. Agent2Shell, on the other hand, leverages more than 10 zero-day vulnerabilities to run commands on managed Windows agents as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID.

Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News that targeted N-central probing has been observed against 4EverAble2Shell within hours following the release of the PoC. The activity has originated from the IP address 157.20.241[.]16. There is no evidence of successful exploitation as of writing.

In the attack chain observed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to achieve initial code execution through a recently disclosed Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8), followed by attempts to escalate privileges to root using 4EverAble2Shell, and then download and execute a shell script from 157.20.241[.]16 using curl.

Dewhurst said the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026.

In a post shared on X, watchTowr also said it's seeing probes for 4EverAble2Shell targeting N-Centrals builds with the Legacy API enabled.

(This is a developing story. Please check back for more information.)

articles.title: PTC Patches Critical Windchill and FlexPLM Flaw That Could Enable Remote Code Execution
articles.context: PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution
articles.full_text:
PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-126325, carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2 out of a maximum of 10.0.

It has been described as a case of improper input validation and deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution via crafted requests.

"A critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability has been reported in PTC Windchill and PTC FlexPLM," according to a description of the flaw on CVE.org. "The vulnerability may be exploited through the deserialization of untrusted data."

The CVE record lists the following versions as affected -

PTC Windchill: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0, 13.1.4.0

PTC FlexPLM: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is hosted by PTC, the patches have been applied on their behalf. No action is required on your part," PTC said in a statement posted on its website.

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is not hosted by PTC, we urge you to apply the patch as soon as possible to help protect your systems."

The disclosure comes nearly five months after another critical remote code execution (RCE) issue in Windchill and FlexPLM (CVE-2026-12569, CVSS score: 9.3) came under active exploitation.

Then, in July 2026, it emerged that threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware operation were weaponizing the flaw as part of a data extortion campaign designed to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate sensitive product data from manufacturing companies and industrial enterprises.

"PTC software is a textbook target for initial access brokers and ransomware operators and a significant enabler of triple extortion campaigns," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"It allows malicious actors to reach far and wide within victim networks, encrypt and exfiltrate proprietary data, and disrupt industrial processes. In many cases, the impact across these environments has downstream implications for time-sensitive manufacturing, logistics, and fulfillment processes, resulting in material costs per hour of downtime."

Organizations running PTC Windchill and FlexPLM products are recommended to patch exposed systems as soon as possible and monitor for signs of code execution, backdoor access, or web shells on the host. If patching is not an immediate option, it's essential to apply network restrictions to limit the risk of compromise.

articles.title: Security Teams Must Shift from Patching to Mitigation in the AI Era
articles.context: This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026
articles.full_text:
Organizations “can’t patch their way out of AI” and should instead focus on mitigation post exploitation, according to Dick O’Brien, principal intelligence analyst at Symantec.

Speaking at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11, he highlighted the rapid closure of the patch window in the past year due to attackers’ use of AI.

This includes AI tools to discover zero day flaws and the ability of frontier models to chain together low severity vulnerabilities together to find an exploit path in a way that humans would not be able to do.

The Zero Day Clock, a live dashboard that tracks the collapse of the time-to-exploit (TTE) window from CVE disclosure to confirmed exploitation in the wild, has estimated that the average time to exploitation following public disclosure of a vulnerability fell from one week in 2025 to one day in 2026. The initiative estimates that in 2027, the average time will be a minute.

“Once you get to a minute, what can you do realistically? We need to start thinking beyond patching to address vulnerabilities,” O’Brien said.

This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026. O’Brien noted that the first reporting exploitation attempts occurred just 19 minutes after the bug was made public.

Amazon also reported that it detected an attempted exploitation attempt of PHP2Shell four days before the vulnerabilities were published.

Agentic AI Orchestration of Attacks

Post-initial access, O’Brien expects threat actors to move to an era of “end-to-end agentic orchestration of attacks” in the next year, shifting away from using AI as an assistant for various tasks towards AI agents undertaking attacks independently.

This will make it significantly harder for defenders to detect and respond to threats in their organization’s environments.

There have been a few examples of this approach taking place so far. One of these was an attack on the Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) in September 2026, where AI agents executed the post-compromise tasks independently, operating at machine speed.

According to an analysis by Symantec of the DIVD’s assessment report, it took 19 minutes for the attack to be detected, but 19 hours before the response began, and a further nine hours to contain the threat.

“This is what we’re dealing with. It’s an excess of 24 hours and you know you’re not going to be able to compete with something operating at machine speed,” O’Brien commented.

Adopt an Assume Exploit Mindset

In this landscape, organizations should assume exploitation is inevitable and prepare for machine-speed post-compromise activity, where attackers can move from initial access to impact in minutes rather than days.

“Stop measuring your mean time to patch and start measuring your mean time to mitigate. Assume an exploit is going to happen and the plan your preparedness for that,” O’Brien advised.

He set out a number of mitigation tasks security teams can immediately focus on:

Behavior blocking

Default-deny for what runs

Least privilege for every agent and token

Inspect data before it leaves the device

Bind every agent action to a named human

“These are all things you can start doing right now before you become aware of a vulnerability,” O’Brien added.

Longer-term, organizations must integrate detection and protection technologies on multiple different control points, which are able to identify behavioral anomalies of rogue or malicious AI agents.

articles.title: Critical Pre-Auth MongoDB Flaw (CVE-2026-118383) Can Crash Lagging Servers on Failover
articles.context: A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server
articles.full_text:
A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server. The crash occurs only if that server is later chosen to take over as the main server while it still lacks some recent changes.

MongoDB, the company that makes the database, released fixed versions earlier this week.

The affected servers are members of a replica set, a group of MongoDB servers that keep copies of the same data. One member, the primary, serves as the main server and handles all new writes, while the others replicate them. If the primary becomes unavailable, the other members hold an election to pick a new primary.

Researchers at Datadog Security Labs reproduced the crash in a lab and published their findings yesterday. On vulnerable versions, turning on authentication does not stop the two requests. An attacker cannot make the targeted member fall behind or win an election, or see when either happens, the researchers said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-118383, is a use-after-free: the server ends up using memory it has already freed. MongoDB rated it 9.5 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 severity scale. The company said it found the flaw itself and was "not aware of any attempts to take advantage of this vulnerability."

Affected members include the shard and config server members of sharded clusters. A standalone mongod, a single server outside any replica set, is not affected.

Each affected branch has a fixed release, listed below and in the CVE record. Every earlier version in a branch is affected, back to the branch's first release.

MongoDB Atlas clusters automatically receive fixed versions during maintenance, the company said in its security announcement. Customers who defer maintenance should apply the upgrade as soon as possible.

Self-managed deployments need the fixed release on every replica set member. After upgrading, check the version each member is running, including members in containers and any that were offline during maintenance.

The 8.2 branch is not among the affected versions listed, and its newest release is 8.2.12. But a proof of concept published on GitHub reports that 8.2.12 still exhibited the bug in a lab test using a test-only setting.

The 8.2 branch reached end of life on July 31, according to the company's lifecycle schedule. Past that date, a version no longer receives fixes, including security fixes.

Until a member can be upgraded, the researchers advise restricting network access to the database to only the systems that need it. That limits who can send the two requests but does not fix the flaw.

A member who wins an election first catches up by applying the writes it missed before it accepts new ones. The flaw is in the cleanup that runs when this catch-up step ends, according to the Datadog researchers' technical analysis.

The two requests are ping commands that carry a readConcern.afterOpTime value. Each asks the server to wait until replication reaches a certain point, and the server records a pending notification for it, called a waiter.

Planting the waiters does not crash the server. They do not expire, and stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back or steps down from primary.

The crash needs the member who received the requests to win a later election, even though it is behind another member. When catch-up ends, the cleanup runs twice, reusing memory that was already freed, and the new primary crashes before it accepts any writes. Once those conditions are met, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race, the researchers said.

In the lab, the researchers caused the member to fall behind and forced a failover themselves by using admin access to pause and stop mongod processes. Only the two requests came from a client without credentials, and that client could not write to the database.

On version 8.0.34, the member crashed with a segmentation fault, leaving the lab cluster without a primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running.

In the fixed version 8.0.37, the server rejected both requests as unauthorized at once, and the member kept running. One part of the fix lets only system users use readConcern.afterOpTime.

MongoDB says the flaw may also result in arbitrary code execution in the server process under certain conditions. In the lab, though, "we did not achieve code execution," the researchers said. Their results also do not show how often the attack would work in other setups.

The proof-of-concept code reproduces the bug in a lab replica set, according to its author. Its reliable mode requires a test-only setting that a remote attacker cannot enable. Its stated impact is a crash or memory corruption, with no claim of code execution.

The second part of the fix stops the cleanup from running twice even when waiters are already in place, the researchers said. They did not test that part themselves.

In the proof-of-concept lab test, which ran with authentication turned off, the fixed 8.0.37 accepted the planted waiters but ran the cleanup only once.

To look for planting or a crash, check the server's structured logs for these signs from the researchers' vulnerable run:

Log event: a COMMAND "Slow query" entry (ID 51803) for an unauthenticated ping carrying readConcern.afterOpTime that ended with MaxTimeMSExpired.

Log event: a member entering primary catch-up (ID 21359), then exiting it twice (ID 21363) in one transition.

Log event: a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock() after those exits.

A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not point to this flaw. The requests may also arrive before the failover, so check earlier logs from the same member too.

Whether the request fields are logged depends on logging settings, and the attr.remote field may show a loopback address instead of the client's real IP.

articles.title: Node.js Fixes 16 Flaws, Including HTTP/2 Bugs That Crash Servers and Leak Other Connections' Data
articles.context: Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22
articles.full_text:
A flaw fixed in Node.js this week lets unauthenticated clients crash servers that use the runtime's built-in HTTP/2 support on the 24.x and 26.x release lines. A second HTTP/2 flaw can cause a server to send a client pieces of its memory, including responses intended for other connections.

Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1.

The crash flaw, CVE-2026-123863, needs only a default HTTP/2 server that replies before the request body has fully arrived. The Node.js project calls that behavior typical. The crash works over both TLS and cleartext connections.

The memory flaw, CVE-2026-123866, affects all three lines. From 24.22.0 and 26.9.0 onward, a client alone can trigger it. On 22.x and older 24.x and 26.x builds, it can still be triggered when the server itself closes a stream partway through a response, for example after an idle timeout.

A separate flaw in Node.js HTTPS servers, CVE-2026-123864, can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, "including TLS private keys and other users' requests," the project says. It affects all three supported lines.

The flaw needs a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body has fully arrived and later calls res.end() with data. Reading the leaked memory also needs a route that sends back or stores a request body. Plain HTTP servers built with node:http are not affected.

The release fixes 16 vulnerabilities in Node.js itself, seven of them rated high. The other four high-rated flaws, and the servers they affect, are:

CVE-2026-123865: a client can make any default HTTP/2 server hold memory and file descriptors permanently, on all three lines.

CVE-2026-123874: a client can corrupt server memory on 24.x and 26.x when the server serves files with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD(). On all three lines, canceling such downloads can also crash the server (CVE-2026-123875, rated medium).

CVE-2026-126051: a client can crash a TLS server on 24.x and 26.x if the server uses the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext().

CVE-2026-123872: on a TLS server with stricter client-certificate rules for some hostnames, a client approved for another hostname can switch to a stricter one during TLS 1.2 renegotiation without meeting its rules. All three lines are affected.

The eight flaws above are all in Node.js's own HTTP/2, HTTPS and TLS server code, so they matter where a Node.js process accepts those connections itself.

Updating to the fixed version for each line is the only fix in the project's security advisory. It lists no workaround for servers that cannot update yet.

End-of-life lines, including 20.x and 25.x, get no fix in this release, and the project says such versions are always affected.

The advisory does not report any attacks using the flaws. It also does not say whether servers that met the conditions for the HTTPS flaw should replace their TLS keys or other secrets after updating.

Five of the flaws, including CVE-2026-123863 and CVE-2026-123864, were reported by Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research, according to the advisory.

articles.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
articles.context: A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server
articles.full_text:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.

Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.

HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.

Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory. That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.

The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1.

Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code.

The Debian rows come from Debian's security tracker, and the Amazon row from the Amazon Linux tracker. Ubuntu's CVE tracker had no page for the flaw when The Hacker News checked it today.

The Apache HTTP Server advisory offers no workaround. In its vulnerability analysis, Wiz advises admins who cannot update yet to remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving Protocols http/1.1.

The standalone mod_h2 project has published no fixed release so far. Its release list on GitHub ends at 2.0.42, the last affected version, and its repository has been read-only since it was archived on June 9. The Protocols change above also applies to servers that use those builds.

The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week.

An earlier HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

articles.title: N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws
articles.context: Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers already are scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security...
articles.full_text:
N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers that broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers already are scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates.

Multiple Zero-Day Security Bugs in N-able

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

N-Central at Risk Again for Cyberattack

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

More recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody says.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he says. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise."

N-able Cyber-Risk Is a Ticking Time Bomb

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

Researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or new scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools."

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody says he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

"Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he says. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations."

articles.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know
articles.context: CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google...
articles.full_text:
A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).

As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.

Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.

According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.

Which products are affected?

The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:

Vendor

Product

Affected Versions

Patched Versions

Apache Software Foundation

Apache HTTP Server

From 2.4.55 through 2.4.70

2.4.71 and newer

GitHub (Open Source)

mod_h2 module

From 2.0.8 through 2.0.42

2.0.24 and newer

Which actions should security teams take?

Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:

1. Upgrade Deployments

Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers().

Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42.

2. Implement Temporary Mitigations

If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.

Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:

# Restrict protocols to HTTP/1.1 Protocols http/1.1

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

References

Apache HTTP Server release notes

articles.title: Microsoft Patch Tuesday November 2026, (Tue, Nov 10th)
articles.context: One of the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook, is already being exploited
articles.full_text:
Microsoft continues its AI-induced patch surge, addressing 1,260 different vulnerabilities this month. 68 of these vulnerabilities are considered critical. 167 of the vulnerabilities are Chromium issues affecting Microsoft Edge.

One of the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook, is already being exploited.

Other vulnerabilities of note:

CVE-2026-119958: A critical RCE vulnerability in Microsoft LDAP.

CVE-2026-109459, CVE-2026-119967, CVE-2026-116710, CVE-2026-119963, CVE-2026-119964: Several critical vulnerabilities in Microsoft Queuing and Queue Manager.

CVE-2026-113859: Windows TCP/IP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. CVSS score is only 7.5.
