articles.title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs, one already under attack
articles.context: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch
articles.full_text: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review. “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

articles.title: November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs
N-able N-central gets emergency fix two days after 33 exploits published
articles.context: N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33...
articles.full_text:
N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2, on Tuesday.

The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security. The release includes proof-of-concept exploit chains that require no authentication and could result in command execution as the service account and, in some cases, root access.

N-able said it has already observed scanning activity associated with the published exploits but has not seen evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited. Censys found 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances, and security firm Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication.

Exploit chains lead to remote code execution

The 33 exploits, which the researcher dubbed Able2Shell, are organized into four attack chains. The most severe requires no authentication and abuses an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in a service-import function to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands as the nable service user. The same chain can create a Default Administrator account with credentials chosen by the attacker, giving them full control of the appliance.

Two other attack chains start from a predictable appliance passcode that lets an anonymous attacker inject malicious patch metadata. When an administrator opens the patch details, a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) payload runs in their browser and invokes a command-execution interface as the nable user. The administrator’s session can also be hijacked through the same flaw to submit a crafted audit-export configuration that runs commands as root.

A fourth chain writes an executable web page into the server’s web directory through a directory traversal flaw in a software repository feature, then escalates to root through a passwordless installer that executes a configuration from a directory the nable user can write to.

Bales tested all of the exploits against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release build, and noted in the repository’s documentation that most, if not all, of the flaws should work on previous versions, including the most up-to-date release.

N-able has not confirmed how many of the 33 flaws it could reproduce, but the new hotfix lists 7 CVEs:

CVE-2026-125883 — Multiple XXE vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878 — Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879 — Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

CVE-2026-125880 — Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

CVE-2026-125881 — Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882 — RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security)

CVE-2026-91000 — Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation

Attacks likely to follow

N-central has been targeted by attackers in the past and the Able2Shell disclosure is the fourth time in 15 months that N-able has been forced to do an emergency response. In August 2025, the company patched two flaws tracked as CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 that were exploited in the wild as zero-days.

In August this year, the company patched an authentication bypass flaw tracked as CVE-2026-18556 that was exploited as a zero-day to deploy ransomware, but the patch was incomplete and attackers quickly found a bypass: CVE-2026-18577. Microsoft attributed the ransomware attacks that abused the flaw to Storm-1175, a financially motivated group linked to China that deployed the StormEncryptor ransomware on MSP-managed systems.

In September, security firm Huntress discovered that a fully patched N-central server had been compromised through a new chain of access-control flaws tracked as CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207. A day later N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale that had also been exploited.

N-able claims more than 25,000 MSP partners and telemetry from more than 11 million endpoints.

What customers should do

With the N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 available, N-able said on-premises customers should upgrade as soon as possible, and all customers — hosted and on-premises — must upgrade their Agents and Probes to restore compatibility between the two.

Security firm Huntress advised N-central administrators to review authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward, look for administrator accounts, scripts, and remote-access sessions they did not create, and assess every client network managed by the server, not just the server itself. Huntress also cautioned that patched servers may not display a new version number, so administrators should verify fixes against N-able’s guidance rather than the version string.

ThreatDefence recommended preserving logs and server snapshots before making any changes, then rotating credentials for administrator and technician accounts, asset-discovery databases, agent registration tokens, and ecosystem agent keys once the server is restored.

articles.title: Patch Tuesday - November 2026
articles.context: 5 does not tell the full story here, since this vulnerability provides value for both commodity attackers working to harvest initial access at scale, and also more targeted...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve.

The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future.

Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month.

Outlook: zero-day spoofing

Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriting, or has this been printed? Probably marketing material.

You put the card in the recycling and, since life is busy, you move on and forget about it. Somehow, you remain entirely unaware that, immediately after reading the postcard, you took out your phone and sent high-resolution images of your front door key to a number you’ve never contacted before.

Is this sketch just some rather questionable science fiction? Yes, hopefully, but what if that non-specific postcard was instead a malicious file in your Outlook inbox? Now we’re talking about CVE-2026-124194, an exploited-in-the-wild spoofing vulnerability. Merely opening a specially crafted malicious file causes Outlook to silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user’s NTLM v2 hash. All supported versions of classic Outlook receive patches.

The relatively low CVSS v3.1 base score of 6.5 does not tell the full story here, since this vulnerability provides value for both commodity attackers working to harvest initial access at scale, and also more targeted campaigns by more sophisticated threat actors.

The NTLM v2 hash can be relayed live to impersonate the user against another service, at least where those services do not implement adequate safeguards such as message signing for SMB or LDAP, as well as Extended Protection for Authentication for Exchange or Active Directory Certificate Services. Alternatively, the NTLM v2 hash can be cracked offline by a motivated attacker to retrieve the underlying credential. The Preview Pane is not a vector, which will help limit the real-world impact somewhat.

Windows Schannel: critical pre-auth RCE

A pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows will always attract attention. CVE-2026-119952 allows an attacker to execute code on a target system by sending specially crafted malicious packets. Since the vulnerable component is Schannel, which is Microsoft’s implementation of Transport Layer Security (TLS), attackers may not have to look very far to find vulnerable endpoints.

The advisory provides some comfort by pointing out that specific conditions are required for exploitability, which reduces the likelihood of broad exploitation, but the advisory still assesses exploitation as more likely, so Microsoft presumably expects that the development of reliable exploit code is feasible. In many cases, there will be no need for an attacker to have an existing foothold on the same subnet.

The execution context likely depends on the vulnerable service, which points to the evergreen need for least privilege architecture, but it also means that we cannot exclude the possibility of pre-auth RCE as SYSTEM in some cases.

Exchange/Windows Search: critical pre-auth RCE

Could someone take control of your Exchange server by sending a single email? In short: yes. Microsoft offers customers tight integration between various business-critical components. Exchange running on Windows is Microsoft on Microsoft, and the Windows Search component indexes email on behalf of Exchange.

An attacker aiming to exploit CVE-2026-116928 relies on this helpful synergy to achieve pre-auth RCE on the server by sending a malicious attachment, which Exchange will process automatically. How’s that for low attack complexity Although the advisory does not specify the context of execution, we should assume SYSTEM, since several of the services which might be involved do run with a high privilege level.

Since the patches are for Windows OS rather than Exchange itself, there’s no need to worry about which version of Exchange you’re running, so long as you are running only Exchange Subscription Edition, since all previous versions of Exchange are now fully beyond end of support.

Microsoft lifecycle update

There are fewer Microsoft product lifecycle changes in November 2026 than last month. As of Nov 11, 2026, .NET 8 Long Term Servicing channel moves past its release end date, along with PowerShell 7.4 LTS, and the 23H2 versions of the Enterprise, Education, and IoT editions of Windows 11.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.context: This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers,...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

articles.title: Git Patches Flaw That Lets Malicious Repositories Execute Code During Recursive Clones
articles.context: A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules
articles.full_text:
A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The Git project fixed it this week in Git 2.56.1, with matching fixes for the 2.50 through 2.55 series in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git.

This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration. Hooks are programs Git runs at set points, so once Git uses that folder, the attacker's code can run.

Submodules matter here because Git refuses to replace a .git folder with a symbolic link, but in a freshly cloned submodule, .git is a file.

The fixed versions, listed in the Git project's release announcement, refuse such extremely long paths before their length can be cut short.

GitHub, which ships Git in its own tools, explained the fixes in a detailed write-up. It advises installing a fixed version from your operating system or Git distributor, and updating any app that ships its own copy of Git.

The company has already applied the fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For GitHub Enterprise Server, they are in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4.

Fixed versions of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app are being prepared. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also get the fixed Git.

Git for Windows had not released a version based on Git 2.56.1 as of Tuesday at 19:09 UTC, a check of its release tags by The Hacker News found.

Until a fixed version is installed, GitHub suggests these steps, which do not replace the fixes:

Clone only from servers you trust.

Do not recursively clone repositories you do not trust.

Do not merge content or tags you do not trust.

Do not process binary patches or fast-import streams from sources you do not trust.

The Git releases also fix five other flaws:

CVE-2026-113408: When someone clones an empty repository over Git protocol v2, a malicious server can send a branch name that contains path traversal. With the files reference backend, a later update to that branch can then write outside Git's reference folder.

CVE-2026-114467: Merging a tag that carries more than two GPG signatures corrupts Git's stack memory and can cause a denial of service. Hosting services that run such merges for users may also be affected.

CVE-2026-114469: A binary patch that expands to a very large size can get past Git's patch size limit of about 1 GiB and crash Git with an out-of-bounds read.

CVE-2026-105437: A very large merge, with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size attribute, can make Git write past the end of a buffer that is too small, corrupting heap memory.

CVE-2026-114466: Three git fast-import features, rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges, could be used to read arbitrary files or to create files and add data to them. Git now rejects them in an input stream unless --allow-unsafe-features is set.

GitLab, which assigned CVE-2026-105437, said code-hosting servers are most likely to be targeted through git merge-tree. A server may run that command to check whether a pull or merge request can be merged.

The conflict-marker-size attribute can be set in a .gitattributes file committed to a repository. If a server reads attributes from the repository, any user who can push branches and open a pull or merge request can trigger the flaw.

As a workaround for this flaw, servers that cannot upgrade yet can add conflict-marker-size=7 to each repository's info/attributes file, or turn off those merge checks for untrusted repositories.

articles.title: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users
articles.context: An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday
articles.full_text:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday.

The attacker could also have seen requests being processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode, the company said earlier this week. That mode processes requests inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) designed to keep them private even from the company itself.

But the TEE "does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment," the company said. SGLang runs inside the TEE, which is how the attacker could reach requests there.

That access has since been closed, but not before the attacker moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated. So far, the company has confirmed that the attacker downloaded account details for about 100 users there. These are email addresses and names, and for some accounts, plan and balance information.

The company found no sign that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files were accessed.

The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older deployment of NEAR AI Agents that did not run inside the company's TEE. From those agents, the attacker took data including chat history, settings and logs.

Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs. The company has revoked both.

After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens and took Private Chat offline. It also deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all of its inference servers, rotated its remaining credentials and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report.

Access to its NEAR AI Cloud service has been restored. The company reported the flaw to the SGLang project. It has not identified the flaw by CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix.

The company has contacted users whose account details or agents it confirmed were accessed. Affected users heard directly from security@near.ai, with the steps that apply to them. As a precaution, the company asks users to be careful with messages about their account or balance that they did not ask for.

In a follow-up post yesterday, it said users who have not heard from it do not need to do anything. It has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted.

In an October 15 technical write-up, Brave, the browser maker, said its Leo assistant runs chats with the GLM 5.3 Flash model inside a TEE operated by NEAR AI.

NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats.

The penultimate month of 2026 bring with it the usual storm of patches from Microsoft and Adobe. I’ve been prototyping some new ways to display this data, but as always, I’m open to suggestions. Seriously – hit me up on Bluesky if you have any ideas.If you’d rather watch the full video recap covering the entire release, you can check it out here:

Adobe Patches for November 2026

For the first part of the November release, Adobe released nine bulletins addressing 110 unique CVEs in Adobe Connect, Experience Manager, After Effects, Audition, Dimension, Photoshop, Media Encoder, Premiere, and Content Credentials SDK.

Here’s this month’s overview table:

Obviously, if you need to prioritize, the Connect patch is the biggest and most severe bulletin this month: 24 CVEs, 18 of them Critical, with a top CVSS of 10.0. It’s Priority 2, and Adobe is not aware of any exploits in the wild. Each of the CVSS10 bugs are reachable over the network with no authentication or user interaction, and each changes scope. The other Critical-rated update for this month is in Experience Manager. It addresses 14 CVEs, which includes four Critical bugs with a CVSS 9.9 rating. Two are incorrect-authorization bugs and two are code injections. All give arbitrary code execution over the network. Each needs a low-privileged account but no user interaction, and each changes scope.

Besides the bugs already mentioned, all other patched from Adobe are a Deployment Priority 3. None of the other Adobe bugs receiving patches this month are listed as publicly known or under active attack at the time of release.

Microsoft Patches for November 2026

Well, at least it’s not a new record for Microsoft. As always, the overall count is a bit confusing, but I see about 1,090 new CVEs released today. At this point, does the exact number actually matter? Regardless of the actual count, it’s huge but less than the 1,400 or so released last month. That’s two months in a row that have exceeded all previous years from Microsoft. As for the products affected by this release, we have Windows and Windows components; Office and Office Components; Windows networking and remote access; Windows graphics, media and printing; Windows storage file systems and drivers; .NET and Visual Studio; Windows Security and identity; Azure, cloud and identity; Exchange Server; Microsoft Dynamics; and Xbox. We’ll see how close I came to matching Microsoft’s “Cohorts” list.

Interestingly, there is only one bug under active attack, and none are publicly known this month. While this is encouraging, it does not mean we’re seeing less exploitation in the wild. It does mean we are seeing fewer 0-days exploited in the wild. This makes sense, as AI is better at reversing patches than it is at finding and exploiting bugs in closed-source software.

Let’s begin by covering some of the more severe and interesting patches released this month.

- CVE-2026-124194 - Microsoft Outlook Spoofing VulnerabilityThis is the one bug under active attack this month. It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests. An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it. Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector, and the CVSS is only 6.5, so don’t let the score lull you. Microsoft marks it as exploited, so this one goes to the top of the list.

- CVE-2026-116928 - Windows Search Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityWe start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server. This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month.

- CVE-2026-119958 - Windows LDAP - Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityThis patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction. Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly.

- CVE-2026-119990 - Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege VulnerabilityUPDATE: Microsoft has revised this bulletin to indicate there is no customer action needed.This is an odd duck. The bulletin says “Customer Action Required: Yes” for this bug, but nothing in the advisory tells customers what to do. There are no mitigations, workarounds, or customer steps. The FAQ says an unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted request over the internet to an affected Azure OpenAI service, with no account or user interaction. The impact is access to orchestration information, workflow changes, or service disruption. Hopefully, Microsoft adds some direction here soon.

- CVE-2026-119952 - Windows Schannel Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityThis flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit arbitrary code over a network without user interaction. Microsoft rates this bug as “Exploitation More Likely”. It is one of only a few Critical-rated patches with that rating. They also list the attack complexity as high, which is why the CVSS score is lower than the others. I would still put this near the top of my list.

- CVE-2026-95962 - Windows Virtual Filtering Platform (VFP) Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityI include this one because it’s in a little-documented component. It’s not the first CVE in VFP, but it appears to be just the second. It’s a use-after-free that allows an unauthenticated attacker to get code execution on affected targets by sending a specially crafted packet to the affected service over the network. No authentication or user interaction is needed. There is a race condition here, but we see those overcome all the time at Pwn2Own. This should be an interesting component to watch.

- CVE-2026-112967 - Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityYou don’t see a lot of Xbox Live bugs, but here we are with a CVSS 9.8. This bug is a heap overflow that doesn’t need authentication or user interaction. Microsoft states the attacker can “gain remote code execution via an in-network attacker calling arbitrary endpoints.” Is this really likely? Probably not, but it’s fun to think of Xbox Live exploits in the wild.

On to those that are Wormable…

Last month saw 59 bugs that fit this definition. This month, it’s a bit less. A total of 30 of the November CVEs fit my definition of wormable. Specifically, 17 contain the advisory language describing an unauthenticated attacker executing code over the network with no authentication or user interaction required. The other 13 use variant wording or have no FAQ, but their summaries and CVSS vectors (AV:N/PR:N/UI:N) describe the same thing.

These bugs are as follows:

Message Queuing (5): CVE-2026-116710, 119963, 119964, 109459, 119967

DNS (4): CVE-2026-81384, 96092, 96177, 88218

Two each (8): Color Management (CVE-2026-96067, 96078), DHCP Server (CVE-2026-88243, 72998), DirectMusic (CVE-2026-95882, 95901) and Xbox (CVE-2026-112967, 66801)

One each (13): Exchange Server (CVE-2026-116928), LDAP (CVE-2026-119958), Schannel (CVE-2026-119952), CredSSP (CVE-2026-119962), Deployment Services (CVE-2026-119951), IIS (CVE-2026-119961), NAT (CVE-2026-113862), RPC Runtime (CVE-2026-118737), Media Foundation (CVE-2026-96157), iSCSI (CVE-2026-88234), Virtual Filtering Platform (CVE-2026-95962), eSCL Scanner (CVE-2026-95956) and Modern Device Management (CVE-2026-119945)

I may be wrong about some of these, since a few advisories are light on detail. As always, I recommend testing and deploying these patches quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange

Microsoft addresses 1093 CVEs in the eleventh Patch Tuesday of 2026.

Microsoft patched 1093 CVEs in its November 2026 Patch Tuesday release, with 63 rated critical, 1029 rated as important, and one rated as moderate.

This month’s update includes patches for 287 products and components. The following table lists the products with the most CVEs patched this month. A full list of patched products is available in the appendix.

Elevation of Privilege (EoP) vulnerabilities accounted for 48.9% of the vulnerabilities patched this month, followed by remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities at 27.1%.

Moderate

CVE-2026-124194 | Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 is a spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. It received a CVSSv3 score of 6.5 and is rated moderate. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by convincing a target to open a crafted Microsoft Office file. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to obtain the target’s valid NTLMv2 hash, which can then be used to impersonate that user in follow-on attacks.

According to Microsoft, this vulnerability was exploited in the wild as a zero-day. Additionally, the advisory credits this discovery to a security researcher that used Claude, the large language model (LLM) from Anthropic, though no specific version of Claude was noted in the advisory.

Critical

CVE-2026-118146 | Windows Active Directory Domain Services remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118146 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Active Directory Domain Services. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Active Directory Domain Services to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Important

CVE-2026-120002 | Microsoft SharePoint Server elevation of privilege vulnerability

CVE-2026-120002 is an EoP vulnerability affecting Microsoft SharePoint Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 9.9 and is rated as important. An authenticated attacker could exploit an incorrect authorization in Microsoft Office SharePoint to elevate privileges over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to gain elevated privileges. It was assessed as “Exploitation Less Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-118207 | Microsoft Exchange Server remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-118207 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.8 and is rated as critical. An authenticated attacker could send malformed input to Microsoft Exchange Server, causing code to execute over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

Critical

CVE-2026-119952 | Windows Schannel remote code execution vulnerability

CVE-2026-119952 is an RCE vulnerability affecting Windows Schannel. It received a CVSSv3 score of 8.1 and is rated as critical. An unauthenticated attacker could exploit an observable timing discrepancy in Windows Schannel to execute code over a network. Successful exploitation would allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected system. It was assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.”

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Xen Orchestra Auth Bypass Flaw to Gain Admin Access
articles.context: French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild
articles.full_text:
French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild.

The authentication bypass flaw, which does not yet have a CVE identifier, is tracked as VSA-2026-062.

"REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}," Vates VMS said in an alert. "REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string."

"The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs."

In other words, the vulnerability can allow an attacker to bypass authentication by sending a specially crafted cookie and perform arbitrary actions with "Admin" privileges, ultimately resulting in arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.

Vates VMS said it's seeing the vulnerability being actively exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain -

91.211.251[.]112:8001, which has been flagged as a RedLine Stealer command-and-control (C2) server on VirusTotal

ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333

It's unclear when the activity started and if the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day.

Other indicators of compromise are listed below -

HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}

A running virtual machine named pivot2

Virtual machines configured using "hvm_serial: file" parameter

Suspicious files named /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6

The issue has been addressed in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 for the stable and latest channels, as well as xo-server versions 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. If immediate patching is not an option, the following mitigations are advised -

Avoid exposing Xen Orchestra instances on the internet

Block the IP address and domain associated with malicious activity

Block the empty token in a web application firewall (WAF) or a reverse proxy

Rotate all passwords and secrets in Vates VMS if indicators of compromise are detected

Filip Magic (@mad31k) and Christoffer Olsen from TDC NET Security have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw.

articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.context: Get an updated version of Git > The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog
articles.full_text:
Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

[Advisory]

Additional hardening

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Protecting GitHub users

We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.

We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.

GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.

Update Git

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Get an updated version of Git >

The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Sandbox-Evading Python Backdoor
articles.context: The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant.

The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026.

The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems.

"However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said.

Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells -

nsmind.jsp, a signed API with command execution and file transfer capabilities using exec, cd, upload, and download parameters

AhsayCBS.jsp, a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory

Keyed command shell, which compares a hard-coded key against its own copy and, if it matches, runs the command via "cmd.exe"

Keyed shell with file write, which expands on the keyed command web shell with the ability to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and deploy more tools

status_<six_random_letters>.jsp or st_<six_random_letters>.jsp (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), which are used to run commands, recursively delete any path provided as input, and delete themselves using cmd, del, and rm parameters.

"[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later."

The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool.

The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine.

It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com").

In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access.

Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups.

"On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said.

"Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

articles.title: Researcher bypassed Meta smart glasses’ safeguards to run her own code
articles.context: Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses
articles.full_text:
We’ve written before about what Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses can see and hear, and who might get to use that information. Those worries focus on how the glasses handle information during normal use. A security researcher has now shown how to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on them.

Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. For the technical details I’ll gladly refer you to her own post about it.

The glasses are controlled by the Meta AI app on the owner’s phone. Developers can add their own apps to the glasses through a developer tool, and the phone sends that software to the glasses to install.

The glasses were supposed to check that the software really came from Meta. In older firmware (up to and including version 126), they didn’t check, so the researcher could swap in an app of her own.

Meta introduced a check in firmware version 127 to verify the app’s digital signature to prove that it came from Meta . The researcher found the on/off switch for that signature check came from a settings file passed along by the phone. The glasses only checked the file was correctly formed, not whether it had been tampered with. Changing a single byte in the file turned the signature check off.

Once her app was running, she could send commands to the glasses from the paired phone over a wireless connection.

The glasses have a camera, microphones and a wireless connection, and they sit on your face all day. A wearable that can be made to run unapproved code goes beyond a privacy-policy question. It becomes a security question about who controls the device. As we’ve seen, some cheaper smart glasses already are a security disaster.

In this case the person running the code would be the person that controls the phone. If malicious software running on the glasses could access the camera or stored recordings, it could potentially send footage to an attacker’s server. Pamoutaf’s research doesn’t demonstrate that scenario, but it raises questions about what that software might be able to access.

In her post she promised a follow-up exploring other potential ways to attack the glasses.

How to stay safe

Keep the glasses’ firmware and the Meta AI app updated, and avoid unofficial apps or modifications.

If smart glasses are just another gadget to you, I’d leave them on the shelf. If you rely on them as an accessibility aid, you deserve technology that helps you without putting your privacy or other people’s at risk.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

articles.title: Introducing JFrog Threat Hub: Turning Vulnerability Intelligence into Blast Radius Analysis
articles.context: A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment
articles.full_text:
A new supply chain attack hits the news. A CVE with a dramatic name starts trending. A malicious package turns up in npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face. Within minutes, your Slack channels fill up, your CISO wants an update, and someone asks the question every DevSecOps professional dreads:

“How are we affected?”

Providing a definitive answer should be simple. In practice it often takes hours, and sometimes even days to get the complete picture.

The pain: awareness is easy, blast radius is hard

Security teams are not short on information. Advisories, research blogs, vendor bulletins, social media threads, and mailing lists all announce new threats faster than anyone can read them. The challenging part is leveraging that information to understand how it affects your particular environment.

Until now, that process usually looked something like this:

Separating the signal from the noise. Relevant intelligence is scattered across dozens of sources. Some of it is vetted, some of it is speculation, and some of it is a repost of a repost. Someone has to read it, judge its credibility, and decide whether it deserves attention.

Translating general threats into actionable responses. A blog post describes an attack. It doesn’t hand you a clean list of the affected packages and versions. Someone has to extract the package names, version ranges, and CVE identifiers, and hope nothing was missed.

Figuring out where affected components are hiding. Today, software applications are assembled from many open-source components. Unfortunately, the vulnerability that was just discovered is rarely a direct dependency. It’s usually buried several layers deep in a transitive dependency which is part of a Docker image, or sitting in a build from last quarter. Your artifacts are spread across multiple repositories, projects, teams, and pipelines, making it difficult to identify all the affected components across the entire software supply chain.

Stitching together a holistic view from disparate tools. One tool tracks vulnerabilities, another tracks builds, and a spreadsheet maps services to owners. Correlating these sources manually is a slow and error-prone process, especially in the middle of a high profile security incident where nobody has the time to do it.

Prioritizing remediation with imperfect data. Published severity scores don’t always match real-world exploitability. A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment. Without context analysis, teams either over-react or under-react because they lack the proper information.

All of the above happens while the clock is ticking. The window between disclosure and exploitation keeps shrinking, and every hour spent hunting for an answer is another hour attackers can use to exploit weaknesses in your application. The real cost is often not the vulnerability itself but the time it takes to figure out the most effective strategy for defending against it.

Meet JFrog Threat Hub: taking you from “what happened?” to “what’s affected?” in a single unified interface

JFrog Threat Hub is designed to close the gap. It brings both publicly published security research and JFrog’s own threat intelligence directly into the JFrog Platform, to help determine how it affects your development environment.

What is JFrog Threat Hub?

JFrog Threat Hub is a detailed threat intelligence dashboard accessed from within JFrog Xray. It includes a daily-updated feed of vetted posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages. Most of the security intelligence is based on reports from the JFrog Security Research team, which monitors public registries such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face, runs automated scanners on every new and updated package, and analyzes CVEs for real-world exploitability. Relevant external advisories are also included in the feed.

Each post includes the name of the source, publish date, CVSS score, and descriptive tags, along with a public label that groups the affected packages and versions. A severity mismatch indicator flags cases where JFrog’s research rates a threat differently from its published score, so teams can prioritize by actual, rather than perceived, risk.

One of the most important features is the Check Impact button. With one click, it runs an impact search across your organization and lists every affected artifact, along with its repository, vulnerable component version, scan date, and runtime status. Teams can export these results, set Xray policies, or move straight into triage and remediation all within a single unified platform.

Threat Hub includes updated CVE advisories and impact search across the entire supply chain

Instead of reading about an attack in one place and searching for exposure in another, Threat Hub brings both steps into one seamless workflow. It not only provides early awareness, but also helps map out the true blast radius, taking you directly from reading about a threat to understanding your exact exposure.

Curated intelligence, delivered where you already work

Threat Hub consolidates security posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages, updates it daily, and then sorts it according to customer preference. In addition, intelligence from the JFrog Security Research Team is integrated as well, including:

Continuous monitoring of open-source repositories such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face for the latest security issues

Running automated scanners across new and updated packages

Deeply investigating suspicious findings

Analyzing new and existing CVEs for real-world exploitability

Disclosing newly discovered malware to repository maintainers

For our customers, this means original, vetted research sits alongside the external advisories that matter, without the noise of an open-ended news feed. Each post shows its source, publish date, and tags such as which ecosystems are affected. When a post is tied to a known attack, it applies a label that puts together groups of affected packages and versions, and may link to a fix or advisory.

Just one click to gauge CVE impact

When working from the JFrog Xray interface, the Threat Hub dashboard can be accessed by selecting Xray > Overview. One of the most powerful features of the Threat Hub console is the “Check Impact” button. Click it, and Threat Hub opens an Impact Search specifically for your organization. If you are affected, it shows the matching artifacts and their scan dates, so you can see where the problem lives across your scanned artifacts and decide what to fix first.

For supported CVE and malicious package posts, there’s no manual extraction of package names, no custom queries, and no stitching together results from separate tools. The research and the results are presented side by side.

CVE Severity you can act on

Published scores don’t always tell the whole story, so some posts also show a Severity Mismatch Indicator when JFrog Security Research’s assessment differs from the severity of a publicly available CVE or advisory. JFrog’s research severity reflects real-world exploitability and impact, not just the published score, which gives you the context you need when prioritizing your remediation strategy.

What this changes for your team

Operations and Security teams gain these important advantages:

Faster incident scoping. The question “How are we affected?” can get an answer faster, with less cross-tool detective work.

Less context switching. Reading the research, understanding the impact, and identifying affected artifacts all happen in one centralized interface.

Improved prioritization. Vetted research and severity context from JFrog’s own researchers helps focus on the threats that are more likely to be exploitable.

More precise communications. When leadership asks for a status update, you can present them with the specific affected artifacts and scan dates instead of “we’re still looking.”

See JFrog Threat Hub in action

The next major supply chain attack is a question of when, not if. When it arrives, the teams that respond best won’t be the ones who read the most blog posts. They’ll be the ones who can understand how a specific threat affects their particular environment in the fastest way possible.

Learn more about JFrog Security and see how you can shorten the path from “What happened?” to “How are we affected” by scheduling a demo with one of our domain experts.

articles.title: Critical vulnerabilities in N-able N-central prompt hosted shutdown
articles.context: Overview On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and...
articles.full_text:
Overview

On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details.

As of November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor has advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it develops and validates a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments remain offline, according to the same notice. N-able's notice does not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026. Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations operating on-premises N-central servers take them offline immediately and keep them offline until the hotfix is available, and the server has been successfully upgraded. Hosted customers should follow the vendor's service restoration updates. N-able is developing and validating a hotfix, with a target of midday November 10 EST.

Affected versions: The researcher reports testing N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. N-able's current notice does not specify the full affected-version range.

Fixed versions: N-able's incident notice does not yet identify a remediation build. Follow the incident notice for release confirmation and installation instructions.

Rapid7 also recommends reviewing N-central servers and downstream managed systems for signs of compromise and engaging incident responders if suspicious activity is identified.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to N-able's security incident notice.

Updates

November 10, 2026: Initial publication.

articles.title: Cloud Vulnerabilities Surge Fourfold in Less Than a Year
articles.context: ” Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds
articles.full_text:
The median number of high or critical vulnerabilities in cloud workloads increased fourfold between May and November this year, due to the impact of frontier AI, Datadog has claimed.

The cloud observability and security specialist revealed the findings in its State of Cloud Security 2026 published on November 10. It’s based on analysis of the cloud security posture of thousands of customer organizations around the world.

Datadog claimed that the median number of high/critical severity flaws in cloud workloads surged from four in May, when Anthropic’s Mythos model was released, to 14 in June and 16 in November.

The data was sourced from analysis of vulnerabilities in third-party libraries used by applications monitored through Datadog Code Security’s Software Composition Analysis (SCA) feature, the report noted.

“This data reveals that the increased number of vulnerabilities in the CVE database isn't a theoretical risk,” it added. “It affects an increasing number of real-world applications running in cloud environments, reinforcing the need for cloud security foundations that limit the blast radius of compromised applications.”

Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds.

The report also highlighted the challenge of long-lived credentials; specifically related to cloud-hosted AI inference services and CI/CD pipelines.

Datadog warned that such credentials are consistently ranked as one of the most common causes of cloud breaches, with automated tools continuously scanning the web for weaknesses.

“Red-team frameworks like Pacu and Datadog’s own Pathrunner along with secret scanners like TruffleHog reliably find over-permissioned credentials and exposed keys at scale,” it said. “That same tooling is available to autonomous attackers, who enumerate for long-lived credentials first because they’re the highest-value, longest-lived prize in the environment.”

The report revealed that nearly half of organizations using Gemini use long-lived Gemini API keys, while the percentage of cloud users with access keys older than three years has reached nearly 30% for AWS IAM and Google Cloud Service Account users.

“Rather than static Bedrock or Gemini API keys, you should access AI inference services through the calling workload’s short-lived identity when supported (IAM role, managed identity, or service account) so the model is reached with the same federated credentials as other cloud resources and not a separate long-lived key,” Datadog explained.

Cloud Dependencies Expose Users to Machine-Speed Attacks

Supply-chain attacks are increasingly run autonomously and at machine speed, with hijacked dependencies one of the most popular routes to compromise, Datadog claimed.

Part of the challenge is the speed with which new dependency versions are adopted by users. If adopted automatically without proper vetting, they can result in the rapid compromise of cloud credentials and services.

Some 60% of organizations Datadog analyzed run versions that were released less than 24 hours earlier, with these versions appearing in more than a fifth (21%) of cloud applications.

The risk is amplified the more dependencies there are, and Datadog found that app workloads running in the cloud have on average 149 software dependencies. The figure across the average organization is 568.

“Organizations should implement dependency cooldowns to lower the risk of malicious dependencies reaching their cloud environments, because the community usually identifies and contains hijacked libraries within a few hours,” the report recommended.

articles.title: Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8
articles.context: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar
articles.full_text: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited. The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight. That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess. Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

articles.title: Update Chrome now to fix a flaw attackers are exploiting
articles.context: A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available
articles.full_text:
On November 9, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. It includes nine security fixes, including one for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.

A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available.

Hong Kong’s Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) rates the overall risk as “Extremely High.” Its bulletin says some of the vulnerabilities address in the update could allow denial of service, security restriction bypass, and remote code execution.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.51 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android on November 9. Google says it includes the same security fixes as the desktop release unless otherwise noted. Android users should check Google Play for the update.

Technical details

Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability.

Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component.

XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

Google only says that it is “aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” It has not named the attackers, the targets, the delivery method, or what the exploit can do.
