articles.title: Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497): Detecting the Node.js Brotli RCE
articles.context: js Brotli RCE Published by: Sysdig Threat Research Team @ linkedin Subscribe to Threat Research Published: October 28, 2026 Table of contents TRT in your inbox Get security...
articles.full_text:
This blog was originally published on October 24, 2026.

As of October 28, 2026, Node2Shell is also tracked as HTTP2Shell and there are four important updates:

The Sysdig TRT added an additional runtime rule called Node.js Process Redirected Network Socket to Standard Stream to Runtime Notable Events. The rule detects the post-exploitation step of Node2Shell.

We previously reported there was no confirmed exploitation. On October 26, ELLIO confirmed exploitation.

Initially, we cited only one RCE reproduction. OtterSec has since reported dozens.

Debian was previously unpatched. Debian 12 and 13 now ship a fixed brotli, and Debian's Node.js uses the system library.

A malformed compressed stream, an ignored error, and a write past the end of a buffer. On October 21, 2026, Node.js shipped fixes for an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder it bundles, versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. One day later, on October 22, Imperva reported running code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Docker image for Linux arm64. The vulnerability, now tracked as CVE-2026-111497, received a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.2 (Critical) and has been widely referred to as Node2Shell.

As of October 23, no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported, and Node2Shell has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. However, public proof-of-concept (PoC) code has been tested, and the gap between patch and PoC was about a day. Security teams should work to uncover all instances where their Node.js services decode Brotli data they don’t control, and begin by patching those first.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed public Node2Shell research to help defenders understand who is reachable, what has been demonstrated versus claimed, what runtime visibility can detect, and what they can do until their organization can begin to patch.

Timeline

Date

Event

Oct. 14, 2026

Node.js pre-announces the release, naming the affected lines and a top severity of high

Oct. 21, 2026, 10:38 UTC

Node.js publishes v22.23.4, v24.22.1, and v26.12.1

Oct. 21, 2026, 15:47 UTC

The first public GitHub repository for the CVE appears, about five hours after the fixes ship

Oct. 21, 2026, ~19:27 UTC

The Brotli project publishes 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1, each listing CVE-2026-111497

Oct. 22, 2026

Google’s CVE record is published with a 9.2 score on CVSS v4.0

Oct. 22, 2026

Imperva publishes research showing code execution on Node.js 24.22.0

Affected Node.js versions

The bug itself is in Brotli, not within Node.js code. Node.js bundles its own copy, so fixing it means updating the runtime itself.

The Node.js advisory rates the vulnerability as high severity. Google scores it as a critical severity vulnerability, at 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. However, severity may depend on exposure, which is determined by whether your code reaches the decoder.

Node.js version

End of life

Fixed version

26.x

Apr. 30, 2029

26.12.1

24.x

Apr. 30, 2028

24.22.1

22.x

Apr. 30, 2027

22.23.4

25.x

Jun. 1, 2026 (ended)

No fix

20.x

Apr. 30, 2026 (ended)

No fix

Node.js states that end-of-life versions are always affected by security releases. Organizations running Node.js 25, 20, or older should treat those hosts as vulnerable, with no further patches coming.

Distribution packages need their own check. Debian’s tracker, read on October 23, lists nodejs 18.20.4 in bookworm, 20.19.2 in trixie, 24.21.0 in forky, and 24.22.0 in sid as vulnerable, and notes that Debian’s nodejs uses the system Brotli library. In that case, the fix lands in the library, not just the runtime.

Debian’s Brotli package is also vulnerable in every release the tracker lists, and the tracker shows no fixed version for any release. The tracker also shows both brotli and nodejs as unfixed in Debian’s development branch unstable. As of October 23, there is no patched Debian package for either component. Debian rates the nodejs entry as unimportant urgency, which differs from the high rating assigned by Node.js, though the tracker doesn’t state why.

The CVE record places the root bug in Google’s Brotli library 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, fixed in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. Any other software that bundles a Brotli build in that range is worth further analysis or vendor inquiry.

But the impact isn’t limited to Debian. Packages for Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, and Alpine may also use the system Brotli library instead of the bundled copy. Therefore, the fix arrives through the distribution’s Brotli package, and a Node.js version number won’t indicate whether a given instance is patched.

According to Aikido, Bun is also affected. All versions 1.4.3 and earlier are vulnerable, and Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix.

How the Node2Shell bug (CVE-2026-111497) works

Brotli is a compression format. Node.js supports it through the native decoder in its zlib module. The CVE record describes a buffer overflow in c/dec/decode.c and lists two weakness types: out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and unchecked return value (CWE-252).

The second weakness explains the mechanism. The crafted stream declares one type of data block, then asks the decoder to switch block types. A correct decoder stops with an error. The unpatched decoder ignores the error and keeps going, writing past the end of its buffer. Semgrep describes the underlying defect as the decoder confusing incomplete input with invalid input and continuing to process a malformed stream.

The fix is small. Node.js cherry-picked an upstream Brotli commit (0ed4268a) that makes the decoder fail immediately on a block switch when the stream declares only one block type. Node.js also added a new error constant, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH.

What is reachable

Node.js does not decode Brotli on its own. An app is exposed when its code, or a library it uses, decompresses Brotli data an attacker controls. Semgrep confirmed several entry points:

Path

Reaches the decoder?

Details

Express 5 with express.json()

Yes, by default

Express 5.3.0 depends on body-parser ^2.3.0. body-parser 2.x decodes br bodies, and its inflate option defaults to true. A bare Node.js HTTP server doesn’t decode incoming Brotli bodies on its own.

Express 4 with express.json()

Not through body-parser

body-parser 1.20.x handles only deflate and gzip and answers 415 to other encodings.

Server-side fetch()

Yes, for attacker-influenced responses

Node.js fetch decompresses a response with the Brotli decoder whenever the Content-Encoding header contains br. Sending Accept-Encoding: identity does not prevent it. Features that call user-supplied URLs are typically targets, like webhooks.

Direct node:zlib use

Yes

createBrotliDecompress() is exposed when it receives attacker-controlled data.

Koa (via co-body)

Yes

Brotli request bodies pass through co-body to inflation. Semgrep also lists @koa/bodyparser, koa-body, Egg and Strapi.

Fastify with @fastify/compress

Yes

Registering the plugin adds request decompression before Fastify’s content-type parsers run.

The inbound path should be prioritized. When mounted globally, body-parser can reach many public body-bearing routes, subject to the content-encoding and parser conditions. However, the outbound path also matters. If an organization’s service fetches from a server an attacker controls, the response can attack the service.

This doesn’t leave Express 4 with a clean bill of health. That reading covers body-parser only. Other middleware, frameworks, reverse proxies, and an organization’s own code may still decode Brotli.

Node2Shell exploitation: What’s been demonstrated vs. claimed

Imperva has demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux arm64, and noted that execution required several attempts. On freshly started containers without a debugger or modified binaries, the test ended with a marker file, and the patched 24.22.1 rejected the same inputs with a format error. Imperva has not released its exploit code.

As far as what the public PoCs do, on October 22 at 20:28 UTC, a GitHub search returned 11 repositories. One lab reported crashes on Node.js 20.19.5, 22.23.3, 24.22.0, and 26.12.0, and says the fixed 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 reject the same input. Another team reported local command execution in three of three runs, but it needed a build that loads an unfixed system Brotli library plus a predictable memory layout. That team says blind remote execution with address randomization on did not work.

However, some of the evidence is thin. Research has argued that no Brotli stream can reach the bad write and the real impact is denial of service. An independent test of the fix commit’s input on Node.js 24.22.0 produced an error on both the pre-fix and patched builds, so that test alone can’t show the write happens. Konfirmity notes that the fix commit itself describes the bug as low severity and not easy to exploit.

Reliable remote code execution (RCE) has been reproduced in only one setup to date. Crashes, by contrast, have been easy for researchers to reproduce. Organizations should treat a crash as the likely outcome everywhere, and the shell as a credible risk wherever their service decodes instances of Brotli that may be attacker-controlled.

Node2Shell impact

Nothing publicly disclosed at the time of publication shows a worm, a mass-exploitation campaign, or a reliable cross-platform exploit. But researchers have proven the following:

Denial of service: Public PoC authors report the process crashes on unpatched Node.js, per the repositories described above. An attacker can take down any service that decodes Brotli from users.

Code execution under the Node.js process: Imperva showed this on one image and architecture, with repeated attempts. An attacker’s code would run with the permissions of the Node.js process and could steal data.

Memory disclosure: Vercel says researchers showed memory disclosure and command execution in the Node.js process on unpatched 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Even when code execution fails, leaked memory can expose data such as credentials.

How to detect Node2Shell

Sysdig Secure customers who use managed policies now have detections to identify and respond to Node2Shell. A Threat Intelligence entry shows where the exposure is, and runtime rules catch exploitation and the attacker activity that follows.

Threat intelligence

The Sysdig Threat Intelligence feed has published a Node2Shell entry. It lists the hosts and workloads that run a Node.js version below the fixed releases 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4, or an end-of-life line. Select the host or workload count to open a filtered search of the affected assets.

Runtime detectionExploitation is rarely clean. Failed attempts crash the Node.js process, and Imperva’s own demonstration needed several tries. The new managed rule Node.js Process Crash Followed by In-Place Program Execution, in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, correlates a Node.js crash with suspicious program execution that follows it in the same workload. This is the pattern of a Node2Shell exploitation chain.

If the exploit succeeds, the attacker can run commands as the Node.js service user. Common next steps include an interactive shell, a malware download, cryptomining, or theft of secrets and cloud tokens from the container. The managed policies that Sysdig Secure enables by default already alert on this kind of activity. Customers have coverage even if the exploit itself goes unseen.

How to mitigate Node2Shell

Patch

Update Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1. Imperva says only a Node.js update fixes the decoder.

Upgrade Bun to 1.4.4 or newer wherever it runs.

Rebuild container images from a patched base, then verify with node --version in the running container. A floating tag like node:24 stays on the old version if you rebuild from a cached image, so run docker pull first. Move your Dockerfile pin to 24.22.1 or later.

Check package managers before assuming. Homebrew still shipped node 26.12.0, node@24 24.22.0, and node@22 22.23.3 about 10 hours after release.

Replace Node.js 20 and older with 22.x or 24.x. No fix will ship for them.

Reduce reachability while you patch

Disable request decompression where you can. In body-parser, express.json({ inflate: false }) rejects compressed bodies with a 415. Test your clients first. This also rejects gzip.

Reject Content-Encoding: br on request bodies at the proxy or load balancer where your clients don’t send it. Brandefense proposes this as its own suggestion, not vendor guidance. Test it before relying on it. It does not cover responses your services fetch.

Audit fetch calls to servers you don’t control, and any direct use of createBrotliDecompress().

Layer a WAF if you have one. Imperva says it added WAF rules and advises limiting untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths. Treat this just as a layer and not as a fix.

Contain the blast radius

Run Node.js services as an unprivileged user and keep secrets out of the process environment wherever possible. Code execution lands with the permissions of the Node.js process.

Monitor web-facing Node.js processes for shell spawns and unexpected outbound connections.

Across the estate

Inventory every Node.js runtime: containers, CI runners, serverless functions, build servers, and tools that ship their own Node.js.

Conclusion

Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli. Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability.

The timeline, however, is the real warning. In the case of Node2Shell, a public repository tracking the CVE appeared five hours after the fix shipped, and a working PoC was public within a day. Since this flaw sits in a native library that Node.js and other software bundle, each must ship its own fix. Therefore, security teams should also expect more of them to be discovered — in the native libraries under the runtimes — on an increasingly short clock.

For security teams, this week’s work is inventory, then patching in order of reachability, then least privilege for whatever remains unpatched. A runtime sensor will not see the overflow, but it will catch what a successful exploit does next. That’s what makes post-exploitation behavior the backstop worth paying attention to.

articles.title: Detecting and mitigating ZDI-CAN-33367 and five other Linux flaws
articles.context: The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first
articles.full_text:
This blog was originally published on October 24, 2026.

As of October 28, there are four important updates to note:

AlmaLinux has shipped a fixed kernel for AlmaLinux 9 (5.14.0-687.60.1.el9_8), which also covers CloudLinux 9. Patched kernels for 8 and 10 were in testing as of Oct 23.

KernelCare’s EL10 rebootless patch shipped on October 23, with EL9 shipped on October 26, and EL8 is ready for release. Debian and Ubuntu work is in progress with no date.

CloudLinux 7 hybrid and 8 fixes are in beta, and the upstream fix has been accepted but has not reached mainline.

The Hacker News lists ZDI-CAN-34076 with a CVSS score of 8.6, we previously did not have this rated.

A working root exploit for a Linux kernel bug is now public, before it has a CVE or a merged fix. On October 20, 2026, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent one report, a bug in the ConnMan network manager, to the public ConnMan mailing list. On October 21, ZDI sent five reports to the Linux kernel security team and copied public mailing lists on every one. The reports included reproduction details, showing that several had no patch attached and no fix in any released kernel. Two of the Linux flaws have been rated as CVSS 9.0.

None of the six bugs has been assigned a CVE ID yet, and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported as of the publication of this blog. However, security teams should work to get detections and mitigations in place now. TuxCare has reproduced the public proof of concept (PoC) for ZDI-CAN-33367 from the ZDI report. Exploitation leads to root access on current Ubuntu, Debian, and AlmaLinux distributions.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) reviewed the batch of Linux vulnerabilities and ranked the reports by how much each should affect what defenders do today. This report explores what was disclosed, who may be exposed, what runtime visibility can detect for each bug, and what defenders can do while patches are pending.

Timeline

Date

Event

Sept. 30, 2026

ksmbd maintainer Namjae Jeon writes a fix for an SMB1/SMB2 dispatch race, credited to a different reporter

Oct. 20–21, 2026

ZDI sends six reports to the kernel security team with public lists copied

Oct. 21, 2026

The ksmbd fix is committed to the maintainer's ksmbd-for-next branch

Oct. 21, 2026

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher asks the reporter to test his Linux 7.5 branch against ZDI-CAN-33549

Oct. 22, 2026

A v2 patch for skb_zerocopy() (ZDI-CAN-33367) is posted to netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet

Affected versions

Exposure risk varies greatly across the reports. One affects the mainstream distributions TuxCare tested, including Ubuntu, Debian, and AlmaLinux releases. Two affect only hosts running ksmbd, the in-kernel SMB server. Another affects only VMware guests.

Organizations should review their inventory before deciding how to prioritize these vulnerabilities.

Report

Component

Impact

Exposure

Fix status (as of Oct 22)

ZDI-CAN-33367

skb_zerocopy()

Local privilege escalation (LPE); public PoC. CVSS 7.8

Hosts that allow unprivileged user namespaces and load the specific networking modules the PoC needs

Patch posted to netdev, not merged

ZDI-CAN-33774

ksmbd protocol dispatch

Remote, pre-authentication; PoC leaks heap / crashes. CVSS 9.0

Hosts running ksmbd

Fixed in the ksmbd maintainer tree, not in mainline

ZDI-CAN-33549

ksmbd SMB Direct

Remote heap overflow; needs RDMA and a writable share. CVSS 9.0

Hosts running ksmbd with SMB Direct, an RDMA interface, and a writable share

Maintainer believes a 7.5-branch fix covers it, unconfirmed

ZDI-CAN-34068

vmwgfx (VMware guests)

LPE. CVSS 8.8

Linux guests on VMware

No patch

ZDI-CAN-34076

nvmet

Information disclosure

Unknown

ZDI-CAN-32005

ConnMan DNS proxy

Userspace stack overflow, not a kernel bug

Not a kernel-level bug

Out of scope

ZDI-CAN-33367

Fix status

A small patch, “net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()”, is on netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet and tagged for stable. It has not been merged.

How the bug works: Dirty Frag again

Earlier this year, Dirty Frag (CVE-2026-43284) showed defenders how an unprivileged user could get the kernel's IPsec ESP code to decrypt in place over pages that belong to the page cache. Those pages back a file the user can only read, and decryption writes the attacker's bytes into the cached copy of that file. Targeting a setuid binary or /etc/passwd this way gives the attacker root without ever opening the file for writing.

The Dirty Frag fix marked those shared pages with a flag and taught ESP to copy before decrypting when it sees the flag. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a gap in that fix.

skb_zerocopy() moves the same pages into a new socket buffer but does not carry the flag across. ESP never sees the flag, decrypts in place, and the write lands in the page cache. According to TuxCare and Safeguard, the code path dates to kernel 3.14.

Not the first gap

The Dirty Frag fix only works if every piece of networking code that moves those pages around carries the flag along. Since May, the kernel's CVE team has published six follow-up CVEs where some other path lost it:

Frag-copy and shift helpers: CVE-2026-43503

Coalescing: CVE-2026-46300

IPTFS: CVE-2026-53363, CVE-2026-64566

An error-handling helper: CVE-2026-80977

Another error path inside skb_zerocopy() itself: CVE-2026-90049

CVE-2026-90049 is a different bug in the same function, so a kernel carrying its fix is not fixed for ZDI-CAN-33367.

Exploitation

The PoC needs unprivileged user namespaces and a handful of networking modules: nlmon, nft_queue, nfnetlink_queue, cls_u32, act_pedit, act_mirred, and esp4. It does not need a Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) leak, or any capability the user doesn't already get inside their own namespace.

Each step of exploitation is a system call that can be made by an ordinary user process:

Unshare into new user and network namespaces, then write sysctls.

Bring up an nlmon interface.

Install XFRM state over netlink.

Add an nftables NFQUEUE rule.

Attach a tc pedit action with a redirect.

splice() into a socket on 127.0.0.1, which triggers the in-place decryption over the page cache.

Impact

TuxCare reproduced a root shell on AlmaLinux 8–10, CloudLinux 9–10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. AlmaLinux was rooted with the Dirty Frag fix installed. CentOS 6 and 7 kernels are not vulnerable. The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Both CVSS 9.0 reports are in ksmbd, the in-kernel Server Message Block (SMB) server. Samba is not ksmbd.

If your file servers run smbd, neither report applies to you. To check whether ksmbd is running anywhere, look for the ksmbd kernel module, the ksmbd.mountd userspace daemon, and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445.

ZDI-CAN-33774: The dispatch race

ksmbd decides per request whether it is handling SMB1 or SMB2. If an attacker packs a burst of short SMB1 packets and an SMB2 packet into the same TCP write, the worker threads can run an SMB2 handler over SMB1 data and read past the end of the shorter buffer. This works before authentication. The public PoC leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel. ZDI describes a write-past-buffer path that needs share access and labels the bug as remote code execution (RCE), but nothing public shows code execution as of this blog’s publication.

Maintainer Namjae Jeon says the bug is already fixed, and his tree bears that out. Commit 68f410faedaf ("ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU") was written on September 30, credited to a different reporter, and describes exactly this race. It is queued in ksmbd's ksmbd-for-next branch and has not reached a released kernel.

ZDI-CAN-33549: SMB Direct

An integer underflow in the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) transport turns a crafted buffer descriptor into a heap overflow of up to eight KB. The bar is higher than for 33774. The host needs an RDMA-capable interface (hardware, or the rxe software driver), a client that negotiates SMB Direct, and a writable share. The public PoC crashes the kernel.

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher believes a fix already in his branch for Linux 7.5 covers it. As of this writing, that hasn't been confirmed. Ubuntu builds SMB Direct support; Debian does not.

ZDI-CAN-34068

ZDI-CAN-34068 is an out-of-bounds write in vmwgfx, the kernel driver for VMware's virtual GPU, rated as LPE (CVSS 8.8). Only the title is public. Kroah-Hartman's reply on dri-devel points to the dirty-tracking code. There is no patch.

The exposure is narrow. vmwgfx only binds to VMware's SVGA virtual display adapter, so the bug only matters on VMware guests: vSphere and Workstation VMs, and VMware-based virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI). In Sysdig TRT testing, it does not reproduce on Lima or EC2 instances, which don't present that device.

ZDI-CAN-34076 and ZDI-CAN-32005

ZDI-CAN-34076 (nvmet) is an uninitialized-memory information leak in the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target's Get Log Page handling. Only the title is public, and the kernel team has said nothing can be done until details arrive.

ZDI-CAN-32005 (ConnMan) is a stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager's DNS proxy. It is a userspace bug, not a kernel bug, and is outside the scope of this post.

Detection

The four bugs that are the most impactful right now differ in what a syscall-level runtime sensor can observe:

ZDI-CAN-33367. The sequence of the exploitation is distinctive. The process unshares into new user and network namespaces, writes sysctls, brings up an nlmon interface, installs XFRM state over netlink, adds an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attaches a tc pedit action with a redirect, and then splice()s into a socket on 127.0.0.1. Nothing legitimate does all of that from a single unprivileged process. Of the four, this is the easiest one to detect.

ksmbd (33774 and 33549). A sensor can see that ksmbd is exposed: the module loads, ksmbd.mountd starts, and 445 is listening. It can see what an attacker does after code execution, once something spawns a process or touches files. It cannot see the race or the overflow itself. Runtime detection is the backstop.

ZDI-CAN-34068. The trigger is DRM ioctl() calls on the vmwgfx device node, made by a local process. That narrows where to look, but GPU ioctls are noisy on any desktop or VDI guest, so treat them as context for an investigation, not as a signal on their own.

Sysdig Secure customers are covered by a new runtime rule in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, Page Cache Poisoning via Spliced File Pages to Loopback, which matches the syscall patterns as seen for ZDI-CAN-33367. Work on exploits for the other flaws in this disclosure continues, and the Sysdig TRT is writing detection rules for them as the techniques become clear.

Independently of the entry point, customers also keep post-exploitation coverage, which detects the effects of a successful exploit rather than the route in.

Recommendations

ZDI-CAN-33367

Patch as soon as your distribution ships the skb_zerocopy() fix. A kernel carrying only the CVE-2026-90049 fix is not covered.

Restrict unprivileged user namespaces. Setting user.max_user_namespaces=0 (or kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 on Debian) should block the public PoC, though TuxCare notes it has not yet validated this against the PoC. The cost is real: rootless containers, some browser sandboxes and some build tooling depend on user namespaces, so scope it to hosts that don't need them.

Avoid relying on Ubuntu's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. The PoC got past it through the AppArmor profile of a container launcher package.

Block the nlmon and act_pedit modules where you can. Denying them breaks this PoC, although TuxCare cautions it may not close every path to the bug.

Enforce seccomp RuntimeDefault on Kubernetes pods. The exploit starts by creating a user namespace, so containers that can call unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) are in play. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks that call, but Kubernetes pods run Unconfined unless you set RuntimeDefault per pod or cluster-wide using the kubelet --seccomp-default option. This is a good week to make it the cluster default.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Inventory where ksmbd runs. Samba users are unaffected.

Unload ksmbd and block the module on hosts that don't need it.

Restrict TCP 445 to trusted networks where ksmbd must stay.

Disable SMB Direct unless your storage network depends on RDMA.

ZDI-CAN-34068

Inventory Linux guests running on VMware, and watch for the vmwgfx patch.

Disable 3D acceleration, or keep the vmwgfx module from loading, on guests that have no use for it.

Across all Linux flaws

Track the reports by ZDI ID and component name until CVEs are assigned.

‍

Conclusion

ZDI's decision to copy public lists put reproduction details for six bugs in front of attackers before several of them had fixes. As defenders know, a lack of an assigned CVE ID does not mean a lack of exposure. Only one of the six, ZDI-CAN-33367, combines a public root exploit, broad distribution exposure, and a fix that hasn't yet merged. It is the seventh path found to drop the Dirty Frag flag, reopening a bug class whose protection has already leaked six times since May 2026. The two ksmbd reports carry the highest scores, but they only matter where ksmbd — not Samba — is running.

For defenders, the practical takeaway is that this week's work is about exposure, not scanners. It’s also important to note that the bugs differ in what defenders should actually watch. The ZDI-CAN-33367 exploit runs as an ordinary user process through a distinctive sequence of systems calls, so teams can catch it in motion. The ksmbd bugs run inside the kernel worker threads with no attacker process on the host, so controlling exposure is key.

Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix.

articles.title: PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619): Detecting unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP core
articles.context: To provide additional recommendations for security teams and create runtime detection coverage for Sysdig Secure and open source Falco users, the Sysdig Threat Research Team...
articles.full_text:
This blog was originally published on October 22, 2026.

As of October 28, there are four important updates to note:

CISA added both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109691 to its KEV Catalog on October 26.

We previously stated there were exploitation attempts. Exploitation has since been confirmed.

Multiple researchers have estimated the number of potentially vulnerable internet exposed hosts between 1.3 and 1.9 million.

Some downstream vendors impacted by these vulnerabilities include Cisco and Palo Alto Networks.

On October 21, 2026, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, dubbed PHP2Shell, were fixed in two emergency releases from the PHP project. The two CVEs group four related memory-safety bugs, and both vulnerabilities have a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit them to run code on a PHP server with HTTP requests alone. Multiple working proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits are circulating, and the researchers who reported the vulnerabilities said AI models helped in both discovery and exploit development.

Researchers reported the bugs to PHP in August 2026, PHP started a coordinated fix in September, and coordinated disclosure was set for October 22. Then, on October 20, the CVE identifiers and exploit details leaked to Hacker News and social media. PHP published an advance notice the same day and moved the release forward by one day, to October 21 at 14:00 UTC.

Exploitation did not wait for the patch. Amazon Threat Intelligence saw a PHP2Shell attempt against its MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure. Cloudflare reported early attacks on October 21 at 07:43 UTC, more than six hours before the fix shipped. watchTowr reproduced the bugs and reported active exploitation attempts against each.

The vulnerable code dates back to PHP 5.4, released in 2012. The bugs live in the PHP engine, not within any application. For that reason, any WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla site with clean application code is still exposed.

To provide additional recommendations for security teams and create runtime detection coverage for Sysdig Secure and open source Falco users, the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed PHP2Shell exploitation. The findings are outlined below.

Affected PHP versions

PHP version

Status

What to do

5.4-7.3

End of life, with no fix from the PHP project.

Move to a patched branch.

7.4, 8.0, 8.1

No official update released. The PHP security team published minimal source backports only for these versions.

Use a vendor-patched distribution package or move to a supported branch.

8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5

Fixed in branches 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12

Update to the fixed release or later.

In addition to the version number, there are three additional factors to consider for potential exposure to PHP2Shell:

Distribution packages: Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches before release. Vendors often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number, so check the vendor advisory and not only php -v. Any package reporting an old version should be patched.

Affected SAPIs: Every PHP installation that serves web requests. This includes Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates mod_php as the highest risk. A SAPI is how PHP connects to a web server, so if PHP answers HTTP requests in any form, it is in scope.

Default configuration: Vulnerable. There are no specific settings needed to be exposed.

Root cause

A PHP worker reuses its memory from one request to another. When a request goes over memory_limit, PHP hits a fatal out-of-memory error and destroys the request heap. The worker survives, and continues to the next request.

The flaw is that PHP does not clear global pointers into the request heap after a fatal out-of-memory error, so a later request on the same worker uses stale pointers into freed memory. All four bugs share this root cause.

CVE-2026-109618: Session upload progress

Use-after-free in the unserializer. Session upload progress decodes session data while PHP parses a multipart/form-data upload. It keeps bookkeeping in the unserializer's global state. An out-of-memory error destroys the request heap, but this global state stays published.

Remote memory disclosure. Upload progress also stores the session ID in a global pointer. An out-of-memory error can leave that pointer dangling. A later multipart request on the same worker reaches the upload-progress cleanup before session initialization resets the pointer. PHP then URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into the PHPSESSID response cookie and sends them to the client.

Session upload progress is enabled by default. It runs during request parsing, before any application code, and even if the application never calls session_start(). Authentication and application filters do not stop it.

CVE-2026-109619: Fatal-error backtrace and OPcache

Use-after-free in fatal-error backtraces. PHP keeps the backtrace of the last fatal error in a global. An out-of-memory error destroys the request heap but does not clear that global. The next request on the worker finds a pointer into the previous request's memory.

OPcache type confusion. While OPcache persists a compiled script to shared memory, an allocation failure at the wrong moment leaves internal slots inconsistent across workers. One worker then interprets data with the wrong type.

Impact

PHP2Shell is a pair of unauthenticated remote code execution flaws in the PHP engine itself. Because they sit below the application and trigger before any application code runs, the exposure is every internet-facing PHP server on an affected version, and the impact ranges from silent theft of other users’ secrets to full code execution on the workload, with a path onward to the host.

Unauthenticated remote code execution, no credentials. Any client that can send HTTP requests to a vulnerable PHP server can run code as the web-server user. No login, application bug, or user action is needed.

Exposure of every PHP application, not just popular or common ones. The bugs are in the engine, so even a minimal application on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Leaked secrets from other users’ requests. The memory disclosure works on its own, without RCE. It returns freed process memory to an unauthenticated client. That memory can hold data from other requests the same worker handled: credentials, session tokens, API keys, and even TLS private keys.

Container compromise and a path to the host. A PHP container is a common internet-facing workload. Code execution there gives the attacker the container's service account, mounted secrets, and network position. From there, a kernel LPE such as Copy Fail or Dirty Frag can lead to the host.

Detecting PHP2Shell with Sysdig Secure

Sysdig Secure customers using managed policies have detections to help them identify and respond to this active threat. The Sysdig TRT has already published a Threat Intelligence entry for PHP2Shell in Sysdig Secure, and Sysdig vulnerability management detects vulnerable PHP versions across images and hosts. Existing runtime detection rules also cover post-exploitation activity.

Threat intelligence

Sysdig Secure customers already have a PHP2Shell entry in the Threat Intelligence feed. The entry summarizes the flaw, the fixed versions, and the interim mitigations. It also shows how many hosts and workloads in your environment are impacted. Select the count to open a filtered search of the affected asset.

Vulnerability management

Sysdig vulnerability management detects CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 across your environment:

Images: Pipeline and registry scanning flag images that ship a vulnerable PHP runtime installed through the OS package manager, before they reach production.

Runtime workloads and hosts: Running workloads and hosts are matched against the new CVEs automatically. No rescan is needed.

Distribution backports: Matching uses vendor advisories, so a patched distribution package is not reported as vulnerable only because of its upstream version number.

Prioritization: Filter on workloads where the PHP package is in use, and start with internet-facing ones.

Runtime detection

The Sysdig TRT built two layered runtime rules for PHP2Shell and validated them against a working exploit. They ship as managed rules in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics and Sysdig Runtime Notable Events policies. The two rules are PHP Web Worker Killed by Fatal Signal and PHP Web Worker Crash Followed by Shell Execution.

A successful PHP2Shell attack gives the attacker a command line, and from there attackers do what they do after any web RCE. They open a reverse shell, download and run a tool, start a miner, steal cloud credentials, or try a kernel LPE to get root. Sysdig Secure already detects this post-exploitation activity with managed rules in the policies that are enabled by default. Most of these rules match the behavior, not the parent process, so they work the same way whatever PHP runtime serves the application.

Detecting PHP2Shell with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP requests. It cannot see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. There are many possible detection strategies, such as detecting shell processes from php workers, but noise often poses a major challenge. As we showed before with Sysdig Secure, many existing post-exploitation detection strategies apply.

Recommendations

Update PHP on every server: Move to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to a vendor-patched package. This is the only complete fix. Application code cannot fix this.

Restart every PHP worker after you patch: Old workers keep running the vulnerable code.

Mitigate with the interim settings if you cannot patch today: PHP states that these settings reduce the risk but do not remove it:

Set memory_limit=-1 through php_admin_value, so applications cannot override it. Enforce request size limits at the web server or proxy instead. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config. Do not rely on ini_set() or .user.ini.

On PHP 8.5, also set fatal_error_backtraces=0.

Restart every worker, and verify the values through a web request, not the CLI.‍

Block multipart/form-data at the edge if uploads are not needed: This blocks the session upload-progress path and the memory disclosure. It does not cover every bug, and it breaks file uploads and some checkout forms.

‍Audit your environment: Find every affected host and workload, and start with internet-facing ones. Sysdig Secure customers can use the Threat Intelligence entry and Vulnerability Management findings. ‍

Investigate dating back to October 17: Exploitation began before disclosure. Check for web shells, new cron jobs, new accounts, and shells spawned by web server processes.‍

Rotate secrets: Because of the memory disclosure, even if you see no sign of code execution, secrets should be rotated for exposed servers.‍

Enable default runtime policies: Use detections for post-exploitation behavior such as known threats, threat intelligence matches, and behavioral anomalies. For internet-facing web applications, alert on shells and suspicious commands spawned by the web server. The Sysdig Runtime Threat Detection, Sysdig Runtime Threat Intelligence, and Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policies catch the post-exploitation stage. For internet-facing PHP, customers should also enable the Sysdig Runtime Notable Events policy, or at least its rules for shells and suspicious commands spawned by web servers.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell is composed of four memory-safety bugs under two critical CVEs in PHP core, the most widely deployed web runtime. Exploitation began before the fix existed, and PHP has carried the vulnerable code since 2012.

It is the third high-impact flaw this year in old, widely trusted core code, following Copy Fail and Dirty Frag. Like those vulnerabilities, PHP2Shell was found with AI assistance. Defenders should approach these vulnerabilities with an “assume breach” mindset, as exploitation can begin before a patch exists. Patch first. Then, until every worker is patched and restarted, use the interim settings, edge filtering, and runtime detection to close the gap.

articles.title: CVE-2026-35273: SSRF to RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft
articles.context: On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group
articles.full_text:
On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group. TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative first reported this CVE to Oracle on June 10, 2026, following an investigation I conducted with Minh Giang and Lucas Miller of TrendAI Research. Although Oracle issued a patch under a single CVE, we reported three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components. We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue.

In this blog post, we will walk through each of these vulnerabilities, starting with a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. We will also review the validateClient method that Oracle introduced to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. Spoiler alert: the SSRF allows attackers to make requests that satisfy this validation and access endpoints vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE).

Overview

There are two main components involved here, both served as individual Oracle WebLogic applications.

The first, the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB), is part of Oracle’s Environment Management Framework. This component implements the validateClient method, ensuring only trusted clients can reach PSEMHUB functionality. Because this is an internal management interface, it makes sense that Oracle would restrict access to its web endpoints. However, this also means it’s a prime target for attackers looking to pivot from their existing, low-privileged access.

The second, the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), contains functionality for exchanging messages between the PeopleSoft server and remote systems. This is accomplished using a set of Listening and Target Connectors.

One such connector is the HttpListeningConnector, which translates data from inbound HTTP requests into the format supported by the specified Target Connector before routing the request to the desired URL. In this chain, attackers specify the HttpTargetConnector.

The diagram below shows how an attacker like ShinyHunters can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise PeopleSoft systems. Notice that the attacker cannot simply hit the PSEMHUB functionality directly:

Bug 1: PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery (ZDI-CAN-31816)

Now let’s take a look at how the PSIGW SSRF provides attackers with a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. An example malicious request to PSIGW shows just how powerful this is for an attacker. We control the URL to hit AND the full payload to send!

At [1], the attacker sends a POST request to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector

At [2], the HttpTargetConnector handler class is specified

At [3], the target is PeopleSoft on the loopback interface at http://127.0.0.1:8000, satisfying the validateClient logic

At [4], the full POST request payload is specified in the Data field, to be forwarded to the target URL at [3]

The HttpTargetConnector handler appears below. Note there is no validation to ensure this traffic is legitimate and bound for a valid target. I've done my best to pull out the important parts of this 800+-line function. If you want a fun side quest, go decompile this for yourself and check it out. I hope you like spaghetti!

At [1], retrieve the target URL from the attacker's request

At [2], create an httpObj using the URL from [1]

At [3], retrieve the HTTP method (POST) and apply it to the httpObj from [2]

At [4], send the content data seen in the Data tag of the network request. This content is sent as-is using the HTTP parameters configured in the httpObj

To fully understand why this SSRF is valuable, here is the validateClient method I mentioned earlier:

At [1] and [2], the validateClient method pulls the hostname and IP of the requesting client

At [3], a file path is built to the /envmetadata/config/allowedhosts.properties file, which contains the list of hosts allowed to access functionality protected by validateClient

At [4], the server checks if the allowedList set contains any entries. The first time this path is hit, the set is empty, so execution continues into the client list refresh block

At [5], that allowedhosts.properties file is read and iterated over

At [6] and [7], each allowed host is added to the allowedList set, including the default localhost entry alongside the server's resolved hostname and IP address

At [8] and [9], if the requesting host is found in the allowedList set, validateClient returns true

We can see the localhost entry in the default allowedhosts.properties that ships with PeopleSoft:

While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB. Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.

Bug 2: PSEMHUB External Control of File Path (ZDI-CAN-31818)

Now that the attacker can make requests to the PSEMHUB endpoints using the PSIGW SSRF, let's see how they can turn that into RCE.

The first path to code execution uses an External Control of File Path vulnerability in the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler, which is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem.

However, callers of the command control both the file contents AND the absolute file path on disk to which that content is written. Here’s an example of the request made to PSEMHUB. Note that, in practice, each parameter value is a form-encoded serialized Java object. For clarity, I’ve decoded and formatted it here:

At [1], we see the request is being made to PSEMHUB’s central routing hub

At [2], note that the request is made to the loopback address 127.0.0.1. Since this request originates from localhost, the validateClient check is satisfied

At [3], the web shell contents are specified in the m_line parameter

At [4], the absolute path where the contents will be written is specified in the m_targetFile parameter

Looking at the handler for this request, we can see that no validation is performed to ensure that m_targetFile points to a legitimate log directory:

By writing this shell to the PSEMHUB WAR path, the attacker achieves immediate remote code execution in the context of the PeopleSoft service account.

Here's how those bugs look when chained together:

Bug 3: PSEMHUB Deserialization of Untrusted Data (ZDI-CAN-31817)

Using any file write primitive (like the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand seen above), an attacker can write a malicious XML file inside the [docroot]/envmetadata/data/environment/ directory. When the PSEMHUB HubServlet class initializes next (after a system or service restart, for example), it triggers a code flow that ultimately deserializes this XML file. Because this vector does not require writing a JSP web shell, it is less likely to be noticed by standard detection methods.

Specifically, on initialization, the PSEMHUB HubServlet class calls startServerPeer in the com.peoplesoft.pt.environmentmanagement.hub.Server class:

At [1], HubMBeanPersistance.getInstance() is called, which triggers the private constructor for that class

At [2], env_dir_path is set to <context_root>/envmetadata/data/environment/, which contains the malicious XML file placed by the attacker

At [3], all files from this folder are loaded into a list variable fl

At [4] and [5], the absolute path for each file in that directory is built

At [6], XMLDecoder is instantiated for each file

At [7], the content of the malicious XML placed by the attacker is deserialized

Java's XMLDecoder instantiates and configures the objects described in the XML during parsing, so the attacker's payload executes before the cast to Environment throws an exception.

Conclusion

The combination of the powerful PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery primitive alongside the decision to allow access to PSEMHUB via the loopback address by default renders the validateClient protection ineffective. Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft.

The impact of SSRFs can sometimes be overlooked, especially if they have no standalone information disclosure impact. Under the right circumstances, however, the humble SSRF can open the door for complete compromise.

You can find me on Twitter at @bobbygould5, and follow the team on Twitter, Mastodon, LinkedIn, or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

articles.title: OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.

articles.title: Node.js Brotli Decoder Out-of-Bounds Write Threatens Remote Code Execution Across All Supported Versions
articles.context: No authentication is required to exploit this issue when the target processes attacker-controlled compressed data
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary:

A high-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) was disclosed affecting Node.js across all supported release lines (22.x, 24.x, 26.x), allowing attackers to achieve remote code execution via malformed Brotli-compressed data processed by node:zlib or fetch(). Due to the potential for crashes, memory disclosure, and code execution in cloud workloads, immediate patching is required.

About CVE-2026-111497

The issue originates from the bundled Brotli decompression library, where an invalid block switch declaring only one block type is not properly rejected, leading to an out-of-bounds write past the decoder buffer boundary. By sending specially crafted Brotli-compressed HTTP responses or request bodies, attackers can trigger memory corruption and crash target applications, potentially achieving remote code execution. No authentication is required to exploit this issue when the target processes attacker-controlled compressed data.

Affected Systems

The following components are affected: the Brotli decoder bundled in Node.js, exposed through node:zlib decompression APIs and the built-in fetch() function when handling Brotli-compressed HTTP responses (Content-Encoding: br). Node.js versions prior to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 are vulnerable, as are upstream Brotli library versions prior to 1.2.1, 1.1.1, and 1.0.10. Node.js 20.x and earlier have reached end-of-life and will not receive patches. Any application decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data is at risk, including cloud workloads, serverless functions, and container images running unpatched Node.js.

The same security release also addresses three additional high-severity issues. CVE-2026-106069 and CVE-2026-105483 allow TLS hostname verification bypass via non-canonical IP address formats (octal, fullwidth digits) that circumvent tls.checkServerIdentity() checks. CVE-2026-105482 is a DNS resolver flaw where embedded NUL bytes truncate domain names, enabling resolution of attacker-chosen domains. In total, the release fixes 10 vulnerabilities: four High, three Medium, and three Low severity.

Remediation

Users should upgrade immediately to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, and rebuild container images on patched base images. There is no reliable in-app workaround for the Brotli flaw; setting Accept-Encoding: identity does not prevent fetch() from decompressing Brotli responses. Node.js 20.x users must migrate to a supported release line. For the TLS issues, an interim mitigation is to reject hosts where net.isIP(host) returns 0 but net.isIP(url.domainToASCII(host)) returns non-zero. For the DNS issue, reject names containing NUL characters before passing them to dns.resolve functions.

Risk Impact

At the time of writing, a public proof-of-concept published on October 22 achieved code execution only on a deliberately weakened test build; on standard production builds it caused a crash and limited memory read. No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments where applications process Brotli-compressed data from untrusted sources.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to crash Node.js processes and cause denial of service, read sensitive memory contents from the application, and potentially achieve full remote code execution, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or infrastructure compromise across cloud environments.How Orca Can Help

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable Node.js versions, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the alert view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: Exploitation Attempts and Remediation Trends
articles.context: When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each
articles.full_text:
Last week, we published a report describing two major vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Since then, alongside much of the security industry, the Wiz Research team has been monitoring for related activity in the wild and reviewing publicly available exploit code. So far, we have observed a limited number of exploitation attempts in our telemetry and have not identified a publicly available proof of concept (PoC) demonstrating complete, general end-to-end exploitation against an arbitrary target. Some partners have, however, privately disclosed to us exploits that work against a variety of targets and we continue to experiment internally. Videos demonstrating our successful exploitations are available at php2shell.com.

This post summarizes what we have observed in terms of remediation efforts and exploitation attempts across real world environments and in our own honeypot data to date and shares findings from our ongoing investigation into these activities.

We will continue monitoring developments and update this post as new evidence emerges.

Observed exposure trends

Following PHP2Shell’s public disclosure on October 21, 2026, Wiz telemetry has recorded an approximate 67% decrease in the daily number of distinct Internet-exposed machines vulnerable to PHP2Shell over the past few days. Separately, among vulnerable Internet-exposed machines, the proportion running PHP version 7.3 or earlier fell from 8.3% to 5.7% over a period of five days. This measures the share of the observed population running older versions that did not receive official backports.

During this period, the number of significantly affected organizations - defined here as those with at least one exposed and vulnerable instance - fell by approximately 47.9% (see graph below). For reference, our data shows that PHP itself is in use by 65% of organizations in our dataset.

Together, these observations are consistent with organizations collectively reducing their exposure through a combination of patching, upgrading, retiring affected machines and restricting internet access (note that this data shows the overall trend, but does not establish the relative contribution of each remediation strategy; scan coverage and size of observed population can also affect the overall reported numbers over time).

Exploitation attempts observed by Wiz research

We have so far observed the following types of activities in this context:

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism, with techniques matching those of public PoCs.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities that instead relied on session poisoning and a separate local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in the application.

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism

We observed two variants of an open source exploit kit targeting PHP-based software. Neither completed the exploit chain in the attempts we captured. The older variant encountered request-size limits or failed to produce the expected memory-exhaustion condition. The newer variant did consistently exhaust PHP’s memory, but failed to obtain the memory addresses needed to continue.

Variant 1: the legacy chain

The first request to our PHP-CGI honeypot came from 3.37.227[.]134. It matched the kit’s older chain, found under archive/legacy-8m/exploit.py and its accompanying stage scripts. The first full exploit stage used a multipart body containing 1,005 parts, including a field named big filled with approximately 12 MB of padding:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=SSSSSSSSSSSSSSSSS Content-Length: 12655437 [1,005 parts] 1001 x p0000 = "x" 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "pwn" 1 x f (file) = "A" x 64 1 x big = "B" x ~12 MB

According to the kit’s notes, this stage attempts to exhaust memory during a session reset, leaving the session state available for a later request.

On our honeypot, it failed before reaching that code. The declared request size exceeded the configured 8 MB post_max_size limit, so PHP skipped processing the multipart body and logged:

POST Content-Length of 12655437 bytes exceeds the limit of 8388608 bytes

The author has since moved this chain into the kit’s archive directory.

A later attempt against Roundcube

In a later attempt, 103.151.172[.]95 sent a longer sequence from the legacy chain. It included stalled connections intended to occupy other Apache workers.

When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each. These requests didn’t trigger the memory exhaustion flow required. So there is no evidence that this attempt reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition.

Variant 2: the current chain

Most IP addresses we captured used the newer chain, built from pure/mk_a1.py and pure/mk_leak_b.py. We observed this variant in multiple attempts.

This variant progressed further: its first stage consistently caused PHP to exhaust its memory. The following stage, which attempts to leak process memory, failed in every run we captured.

The server logged a fatal error indicating that PHP reached its limit, for example:

Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 81920 bytes) in Unknown on line 0.

Keeping requests on the same worker

The chain depends on consecutive exploit requests reaching the same Apache child process. To increase the chances of that happening, the kit attempts to occupy the other workers with incomplete requests. Each connection declares a large body, sends a single byte and stalls:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-Length: 1048576 x

One address, 178.249.214[.]6, opened 399 of these connections alongside 400 GET requests before sending the exploit stages. The address is a VPN exit node, which limits what we can infer about the source.

Stage A1: triggering memory exhaustion

A1 is a chunked multipart request containing a null-byte session ID, 860 empty file parts with long, deeply nested array names and several groups of padding fields:

POST /?q0=v&q1=v&q2=v&q3=v&q4=v HTTP/1.1

Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=CCCCCCCCCC Transfer-Encoding: chunked [1,060,211 bytes, 974 parts] 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 860 x files[R00000KKKK...][a][a]... (file, empty) 14 x f0000xxxx... = "vvvvvvvv" 78 x b0000 = "B" x 8000 20 x u00 = "U" x 4000 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "k" x 4000

The request is designed to exhaust memory during session handling at a point that can leave the session ID pointing to freed memory.

Every A1 request we captured returned HTTP 500, accompanied by a PHP error matching:

Allowed memory size of 67108864 bytes exhausted ... in Unknown on line 0

This confirms that A1 reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition on our honeypot. It does not, by itself, confirm that the stale session state needed by the next stage was preserved.

Stage B1: attempting the memory leak

B1 followed roughly a second later. It sent another chunked multipart request containing PHPSESSID=a, PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=k0and two large padding fields.

If this request reaches the same worker before PHP resets the stale session state, PHP can write reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The kit then extracts heap and libphp addresses from that cookie to prepare the final exploit stage.

We observed no such leak. In all but one run, the connection closed without a response. The remaining run returned a normal 32-character session cookie. None of the sources sent the final exploit stage.

Why the leaks may have failed

The failed leaks highlight a broader challenge: building a generalized exploit that works reliably across PHP versions and deployment configurations is difficult. The kit’s B1 layout was calculated for the official php:8.4.26-apache image with a 128 MB memory limit. Other instances like our Roundcube honeypot ran the same PHP version from a different build, with additional extensions and a 64 MB memory limit. These differences can affect heap layout and memory reuse, potentially preventing the leak from working as expected.

Reliable worker pinning adds another challenge. Consecutive exploit requests must reach the same Apache child process while the required session state persists. Request timeouts, network latency and worker availability can disrupt this sequence. In our own testing, request timeouts combined with network latency were enough to prevent the chain from completing over an internet connection.

So far, we have not identified a publicly available, generalized solution for either worker pinning or information leaking across different deployments. Simply copying public PoCs and running them at scale does not address the work needed to turn a configuration-specific exploit into a reliable operational kit. We expect these barriers to diminish over time: some threat actors have the expertise needed to adapt the chain and build more robust tooling.

Other attempts

We also saw failed exploitation attempts from 15.204.59[.]70 and 162.35.99[.]94, but these scanners did successfully exploit Adel Karimi's honeypot, which was a likely contributing factor to CISA’s decision to include PHP2Shell in their KEV list.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities

We also observed tools labeled as PHP2Shell exploits that did not actually attempt to exploit either vulnerability. The earliest such traffic, from 85.11.187[.]35, matched a Go port of “Chain A” from WoYinDao/CVE-2026-109618-CVSS-9.2-Critical.

The tool used a longstanding session-poisoning technique, attempting to write PHP code into a session file through the upload-progress feature. The request below is abbreviated:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> User-Agent: Go-http-client/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----php2shell-golang PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = <?php echo "PHP2SHELL_XBu4Je"; system($_GET["c"]); ?> PHPSESSID = <attacker-chosen ID> f (file) = "Z"

It then attempted to execute that code by including the session file:

GET /lfi_sink.php?c=id&f=/tmp/sess_SUjKIKy3Rr6QsaJ1Ik7Rme8h3n HTTP/1.1

Crucially, lfi_sink.php is a vulnerable endpoint supplied by the PoC’s lab environment. The tool assumes that this endpoint exists on the target; without it or an equivalent local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability, the chain cannot execute code.

A padded variant triggered our memory-exhaustion detection, but we observed no successful code execution. Despite the PHP2Shell branding, this activity relied on an unrelated technique and a vulnerable application endpoint.

Conclusion

We have not yet observed successful end-to-end PHP2Shell exploitation in our own telemetry. However, Adel Karimi’s public report and supporting data provide the most robust public evidence we have seen to date, correlating exploit traffic, memory disclosure and subsequent code execution on his honeypots. Notably, those targets used a favorable single-worker Apache mod_php configuration, so the findings do not establish reliability across other deployments.

Our observations show that triggering memory exhaustion alone is not enough to complete the exploit chain. Differences in PHP builds, memory limits and worker behavior can prevent subsequent stages from working. The challenge for opportunistic attackers is turning currently available public PoCs into similarly reliable operational tooling or developing it on their own. In our view, PHP2Shell remains a risk in both the short and long term and applying the PHP security updates or remediating through other means therefore remains essential.

articles.title: HTTP2Shell Vulnerability: How Should Security Teams Assess and Reduce Exposure?
articles.context: Aqua Team October 27, 2026 Updated: October 29th, 2026 TL;DR: The HTTP2Shell vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) is a critical flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression decoder that...
articles.full_text:
How is Aquasec addressing HTTP2Shell?

Aquasec has reviewed the impact of HTTP2Shell on its own components and confirmed that the affected Brotli library was present in certain Aquasec Enforcer images.

However, our security analysis determined that the vulnerable decoding functionality is not used by Enforcer components. The Enforcer does not decompress Brotli data, meaning the conditions required to exploit HTTP2Shell through the affected decoder are not present in the assessed Enforcer execution paths.

Our assessment included examination of both source code and released binaries to verify that the vulnerable decoder is not invoked during Enforcer operation.

Although the vulnerable library was not reachable through Enforcer functionality, we have released an updated Enforcer versions for both Update 47 and Update 45 LTS containing the corrected Brotli package.

Aquasec Enforcer 2022.4 U47 SP2 (2022.4.951.5) and 2022.4 U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 (2022.4.880.50) are now available. We recommend that customers upgrade to this release to remove the vulnerable dependency and address associated scanner findings.

Customers looking for additional information about affected versions, our technical assessment and upgrade guidance can refer to the Aquasec Support Knowledge Base and the U47 SP2 release documentation or the U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 release documentation

articles.title: Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams’ external chat creation feature to target employees for initial access into organizations, new research by Arctic Wolf has found.

The researchers said they had observed over 400 incidents in which the function was abused, with “highly consistent” IT-support impersonation tactics deployed by the malicious actors.

The attack chain is rapid, with payload execution reached in under 15 minutes from when a victim engages with the initial social engineering message.

The attackers often target multiple victims within short windows of time, which suggests the use of automation.

“Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise,” the Arctic Wolf researchers wrote in the report published on October 26, 2026.

The researchers did not identify the perpetrators behind these attacks. However, it noted that the use of the external Teams chat as an initial access vector has been a tactic deployed by ransomware groups including Black Basta.

Threat Actors Establish Legitimate-Looking Teams Identities

Arctic Wolf noted that the external Microsoft Teams chat function has become an effective platform to launch social engineering, with attackers able to make themselves appear legitimate to users.

Teams’ external access is turned on by default, meaning any Teams user in another Microsoft 365 tenant can find, chat with, and call an organization’s employees, provided both tenants allow external access.

In the observed incidents, the threat actors established external Teams identities through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Between 30-40% of the cases involved default onmicrosoft[.]com tenant domains, which do not require verification and can be provisioned within minutes.

The attackers typically selected a support-, IT-, admin-, network-, or helpdesk-themed word as the tenant name, optionally suffixed with the number 365, to appear as an IT-support worker.

In addition, threat actors used fake first names, such as “IT Service Desk – Liam”, to make it appear as though the message came from a real member of the organization’s service desk.

In a small number of cases, legitimate company names were included in the sender’s tenant name to increase their credibility.

In a “significant number” of the attacks the target’s email was flooded with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations within minutes, a tactic known as mail bombing.

The attackers then sent a Teams “IT support” message moments later to offer to resolve the very same problem the attacker just created.

Following the initial contact, the attackers’ next aim in most cases was to obtain hands-on-keyboard access through legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools, most frequently Quick Assist, which is built into Windows and therefore requires no installation.

When attackers seek persistence beyond the initial call, they pivot to a commercial RMM tool, such as AnyDesk and ScreenConnect.

These RMM tools can enable to attackers to execute a PowerShell payload and undertake lateral movement across the organizations network for purposes such as ransomware.

In some cases, the user was instructed to run the PowerShell command and launch the downloaded file.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-48356 Adobe Commerce and Magento Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111497 Google Brotli Unchecked Return Value Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.

Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.

Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.
