articles.title: [remote] PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) - PHP core versions after v5.4 - RCE
articles.context: txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab
articles.full_text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3 """PHP2Shell RCE chain for PHP 8.5.11 apache/mod_php. Usage: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --rce 'id>/var/www/html/proof.txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab. Its default endpoint is ``/index.php`` and is configurable with ``--path``. With no ``--rce`` it stops after reproducing the overlong ``Set-Cookie`` disclosure. With ``--rce [COMMAND]`` it composes two distinct PHP memory-safety mechanisms. Bare ``--rce`` runs the documented default and verifies ``/proof.txt``; a custom command is delivered without claiming that its execution was verified. 1. The A1/B1 disclosure is derived from 9bie's cross-request session-state chain. An upload-progress request reaches an OOM bailout before request state is safely reset; a later request in the *same mod_php child* consumes the stale ``PS(id)`` and encodes an attacker-forged ``zend_string`` into the session cookie. This is strongest-fit **CVE-2026-109619** behavior: request- owned session globals outlive their backing request heap. OOM is the producer, but the security boundary crossed by this stage is request lifetime. This is mechanism-based attribution, not a CNA reassignment of any individual public PoC. 2. The optional final sink is adapted from Cookiengineer's OOM RCE. Multipart amplification exhausts the stock 128 MiB heap while ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i()`` has counted but not initialized its final ``HashTable`` bucket. Same-request shutdown walks the incomplete bucket into a forged object, a libphp-only ``jump_fcontext`` ROP chain, and ``zif_system``. This is the incomplete-state/cleanup mechanism of **CVE-2026-109618**. Worker discovery, chunked transfer, prefork saturation, the full-pool scrub, and the clean holder rebind are delivery/affinity techniques, not additional CVEs. The scrub exists because the validated Apache environment can retain children already marked for graceful retirement when its IPv6 listener wakeup fails; without it, a second invocation may place A1 and B1 in different processes. The post-scrub repin is concurrent so VPN latency cannot recreate an idle-surplus window. Debugger mappings were used only to calibrate and independently verify the constants below; successful end-to-end runs derive their live bases from the HTTP cookie. Validated exact environment (2026-10-23) ======================================== This profile is intentionally build-specific. articles.title: A patched PHP server can still be a compromised one by Lucie Cardiet
articles.context: Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad...
articles.full_text:
On October 20, details of two critical flaws in PHP leaked online before the fixes were ready. PHP, the scripting language behind a large share of the web, moved its patch release up a day and shipped it on October 21. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed php2shell), let an attacker run commands on a web server through PHP itself, with no login needed.

Patch now. CISA added both flaws to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on October 26. That advice is right, and it leaves a gap. This post is about the gap.

Attackers were testing the flaw before the fix existed

Fixes are out for PHP 8.2 to 8.5,and PHP says PHP 8.1 and older will not get updates. One estimate counts about 884,000 such servers still online, a rough figure from a single source.

Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw early attacks, and the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned organizations to update immediately or take systems offline. How many real servers were taken over is still unclear. Amazon says it does not know whether the attempts it saw would have worked outside a honeypot.

On October 23, CrowdStrike and Flare still reported only probing and failed attempts, many of which crash PHP rather than give an attacker control. The next day, Perplexity's Adel Karimi recorded successful remote code execution on a honeypot, and on October 26 CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, with a federal patch deadline of October 29. Karimi's test used a deliberately favorable setup, so it shows the flaw works, not how often attacks like it succeed.

Every flaw has been out there for a while before anyone announces it

A flaw becomes news on the day it is announced, not the day it appears. PHP's own maintainers first spotted signs of this problem in a 2024 audit, and attackers reached it before the public did.

We have seen this pattern before. When Log4j hit in December 2021, Vectra wrote that the first sign of an attack was hard to spot and that the safest assumption was that at least one server in an estate was already compromised. Other flaws in the software your business runs are very likely in the same position today: known to someone, announced to no one. Patching deals with the ones you hear about. It cannot help with the rest.

The PHP servers you miss matter most

PHP runs WordPress,Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, hosting control panels, and a lot of software that never mentions PHP. The servers you know about will get patched. The ones you do not know about are the ones attackers find first, because nobody is watching them.

Appliances and management interfaces that ship PHP are the likeliest place an attempt becomes a compromise, and they are rarely monitored like web servers. Flare, relaying one researcher's report, says some ship PHP without address randomization, which removes the main obstacle for an attacker. Ask your vendors which of their products include PHP.

No team patches everything on the day a fix ships. Knowing which servers face the internet, and which hold the most valuable data, turns a backlog into a short list of decisions, including which services to switch off until they are fixed. On any server you suspect was hit, save logs and a snapshot of memory before restarting, because a restart erases traces.

‍

What happens after a PHP server falls

An attacker who gets code running through PHP usually does not need malware. The web server already has a shell, a network connection and access to files, so they can use the tools already installed on the machine to look around, find credentials and move from one system to the next. Nothing looks wrong, because the web server is doing web server things with slightly different commands. That is the first of the three detection gaps I write about: nothing looks wrong.

What changes is where the server talks to. A web server that has served the same pages for years suddenly reaches places it never did before, calls out to unfamiliar addresses, or starts talking to internal systems. That behavior shows up in network traffic, not in patch status. A view of the network is how you see what a server is actually connecting to, whether or not anyone is watching the server itself.

What Vectra AI can and cannot see

Vectra AI is not really concerned about what the initial attack vector is. What we see is what happens afterward.

PHP is the story today. Next week it will be something else: another flaw, a phone call to a help desk, someone on the inside. What we look at does not depend on which door was used. We watch what a system does once an attacker is inside, so we do not need the way in to be known or the flaw to be published. That matters most when the entry point is unknown or the vulnerability has not been announced yet.

Uncovering Potential PHP Servers and Shadow IT

One of the challenges in securing PHP infrastructure is knowing where it exists in the first place. Forgotten applications, unmanaged servers, and shadow IT can create security blind spots, even after known vulnerabilities have been patched.

Vectra AI's PHP Server Visibility dashboard provides an additional investigative tool to help security teams identify potentially overlooked PHP servers using indicators observed in unencrypted HTTP traffic, such as .php endpoints and PHPSESSID cookies. Analysts can then investigate whether these hosts are also receiving externally originated encrypted traffic, helping prioritize potentially exposed systems for further investigation.

The dashboard is not intended to provide a complete inventory of PHP servers. It can only identify systems exhibiting observable PHP-related indicators, and encrypted traffic or limited network visibility may leave some servers undiscovered. Instead, it acts as an assistant to existing asset discovery and threat-hunting workflows, helping analysts uncover potential shadow IT, investigate exposure, and identify systems that warrant closer examination, even after patching.

Detection rules for known php2shell exploit attempts

Vectra Match now contains rules to detect the PHP2Shell attacker behaviors when proper visibility is provided to the attacker traffic. They flag known exploit attempts in network traffic when that traffic is visible to us, so they catch attempts at the door, while the detections above catch what follows. An attempt is not a compromise. A match is a reason to look at that server, not proof that it was taken over. This is available for all Vectra Match customers.

The rules, by ET rule number:

2072548: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Handler-mismatch Session Injection (CVE-2026-109619)

2072549: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Header Amplification OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072550: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Nested Empty File Control OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072551: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Chunked Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072552: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Binary URL-Encoded POST for $_POST Corruption (CVE-2026-109618), commented out in the rule set, so off by default

2072553: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072554: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Code Injection in Filename (CVE-2026-109619)

2072555: ET HUNTING PHP Generic Upload Progress Session Manipulation, a hunting rule, not an exploit rule, so treat a match as a lead

2072556: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Multipart Part Count (CVE-2026-109618)

2072557: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Empty Multipart File Controls (CVE-2026-109618)

What a compromised PHP server reveals about your resilience

The old measure of success was whether attackers get in. The better one is how far they get. Patching, a sound network design, splitting the network into zones, least privilege and knowing which systems carry your most important business processes all limit that distance. The network record can show whether anyone came through the door before it closed, and where they went next.

The three gaps are walked end to end in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks white paper.

articles.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot
articles.context: While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains...
articles.full_text:
Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.

The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.

Two lessons from this event apply well beyond this one vulnerability:

An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug. Coordinated disclosure is still the right model. But defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation. With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory.

The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons. In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.

For security leaders, this changes several working assumptions:

For critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours. A 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.

Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17th.

Invest in detections that don’t rely on a signature for a specific CVE. The first exploitation will often come before those signatures exist.

How AWS helps protect customers

AWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.

Immediate recommended actions

Upgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues.

Consider blocking multi-part file uploads in PHP deployments that cannot be patched immediately, but determine how this would affect your application prior to deploying.

Look for POST requests with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS string in form uploads.

Review web server logs for suspicious activity.

Check for unexpected process execution or file modification on web application servers.

See how to use AWS Web Application Firewall to help reduce your exposure while you patch in our blog post Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

If you have questions, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or reach out to AWS Support.

CJ Moses

CJ Moses is the CISO of Amazon Integrated Security. In his role, CJ leads security engineering and operations across Amazon. His mission is to enable Amazon businesses by making the benefits of security the path of least resistance. CJ joined Amazon in December 2007, holding various roles including Consumer CISO, and most recently AWS CISO, before becoming CISO of Amazon Integrated Security September of 2023.

Prior to joining Amazon, CJ led the technical analysis of computer and network intrusion efforts at the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division. CJ also served as a Special Agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). CJ led several computer intrusion investigations seen as foundational to the security industry today.

CJ holds degrees in Computer Science and Criminal Justice, and is an active SRO GT America GT2 race car driver.

articles.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: PHP Vulnerable to Unauthenticated RCE Attacks
articles.context: *October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours...
articles.full_text: *October 26, 2026: This advisory has been updated to clarify language describing exploitability and potential impact.*October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours following disclosure.IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell,” were publicly disclosed. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. The PHP security team has released emergency patches and strongly encouraged all PHP users to update immediately. These flaws reside in the PHP core language runtime and successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve remote code execution on any server running a vulnerable version, potentially enabling unauthorized access, data theft, or further system compromise. Given PHP's pervasive deployment across web infrastructure globally - including applications like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, as well as embedded devices and similarly overlooked public-facing platforms - the potential attack surface is significant. The vulnerabilities could enable automated exploitation of exposed, vulnerable PHP deployments without authentication or user interaction. The vulnerabilities therefore may be attractive targets for exploitation.ThreatLabz analysis indicates that attackers began rapidly targeting these vulnerabilities following public disclosure, highlighting the need for organizations to patch vulnerable PHP deployments immediately.Zscaler’s security team has analyzed this issue across both production and corporate environments and has ruled out any impact to Zscaler Cloud Platforms, products, distributed components, services, or our enterprise environment, as detailed in the Trust post. RecommendationsOrganizations running PHP should take the following actions:Patch immediately: Upgrade PHP to one of the fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Linux package maintainers received patches in advance and may already have updated packages available. PHP packages for most Linux distributions may also include the patches backported to previous versions of the software, so consult the release notes for your specific installation to ensure your systems are covered.Deactivate unpatched instances: Consider fully disabling services for any PHP instance that cannot be immediately patched. While this may seem overly cautious, any unpatched instance could be targeted by opportunistic adversaries and result in shell-level access to the vulnerable host. Inventory PHP deployments: Conduct an immediate inventory of all PHP installations across your environment, including standalone servers, vendor appliances, bundled software (WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce, Shopware), and hosting panels (cPanel, Plesk, etc).Migrate off EOL branches: Organizations running PHP 5.4+, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1 must migrate to a supported branch immediately. No official binary patches will be released for these versions.Isolate EOL instances that cannot be immediately migrated: Migrating EOL instances is strongly recommended. If this is not possible, isolating unpatchable applications from the internet and other untrusted networks may provide some level of protection. This should be considered a high-risk mitigation and reserved only for business and mission-critical applications while implementing aggressive monitoring of these instances.Monitor for exploitation: Audit web server logs (including but not limited to Apache, Nginx, etc.) for unusual segmentation faults, crash dumps, or abnormal memory usage patterns that may indicate active exploitation attempts.Mitigate risk through PHP settings: While not a definitive fix, mission critical applications that cannot be disabled or immediately patched may benefit from reviewing and tightening memory_limit and max_execution_time settings in php.ini to avoid triggering OOM conditions. Consult additional guidance regarding mitigations through setting session.upload_progress.enabled = Off and disabling multipart uploads at the service edge. ThreatLabz Observes Exploitation Attempts Within 48 HoursThreatLabz observed scanning activity and possible exploitation attempts targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities using multiple attack tools and exploitation methods, including RCE payloads, PHP object injection, and named exploitation frameworks, indicating rapid, in-the-wild exploitation attempts.In the first 48 hours after the PHP2Shell disclosure, Zscaler’s global decoy mesh observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IPs targeting 70 organizations. As a rapid response measure, a new detection rule for PHP2Shell exploitation has been pushed to all Zscaler Deception customers.Attack chainAutomated scanning activity observed by Zscaler suggests attackers may be attempting to use a two-stage PHP2Shell exploitation chain, as shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Notional exploit chain consistent with scanning and exploit attempts observed by ThreatLabz.Stage 1: State setup and fatal triggerThe attacker sends a crafted multipart/form-data POST request containing:A PHPSESSID field to associate the request with a known session, making the session filename (sess_[PHPSESSID]) predictable.The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field to force PHP to begin session bookkeeping during multipart parsing, populating vulnerable global state pointers and writing attacker-controlled data into the session file.A file attachment whose filename= parameter contains either PHP code or a serialized object string.A body sized or structured to exhaust memory (CVE-2026-109618) or trigger a fatal error (CVE-2026-109619).When the fatal condition is triggered, longjmp() aborts the request, freeing per-request memory but leaving stale global pointers.Stage 2: Heap reclaim and code executionThe attacker immediately sends a second request to the same worker process. This second request contains the attacker's payload, sized and aligned to reclaim the freed memory slots. When PHP processes the new request and references the stale global state before re-initialization occurs, it reads and executes the attacker-controlled data, achieving arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker process.Zscaler Deception telemetry findingsThreatLabz observed malicious POST requests targeting the PHP2Shell exploitation path across multiple tools and stages of the attack chain. Every observed request is a multipart/form-data POST targeting PHP endpoints, specifically /, /index.php, /api/endpoint.php, and /app/upload.php.Exploitation payloads observed1. ShellFlow PHP2Shell named exploit toolThe most forensically significant artifact is the presence of a multipart boundary string that explicitly names the exploitation tool. This indicator should not be considered durable, as an adversary can trivially replace the known strings with something less obvious. At this time, the ShellFlow tool uses a known boundary value, so it is a useful indicator for detecting the unmodified tool. The exploit tool request is shown below. POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----shellflow-php2shell ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" sf618_ec172709c8b74601 ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" shellflow_poc ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="poc.bin" Content-Type: application/octet-stream AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA[...15485 bytes total...]The multipart boundary shellflow-php2shell identifies the attacking tool by name. articles.title: Arctic Wolf Labs: Finding, Prioritizing, and Patching PHP2Shell Exposure
articles.context: On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race...
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race between defenders and attackers. The flaws are tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together they’re known as PHP2Shell. Both carry a 9.2 rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 scale. For both vulnerabilities, Arctic Wolf’s Aurora® Agentic SOC helps organizations rapidly identify affected assets, correlate exploitation signals across the environment, and accelerate investigation and response before attackers can establish persistence.

An unauthenticated attacker can use either flaw to run code on a vulnerable server. On Wednesday, October 21, the PHP project released patched versions. PHP2Shell shows how AI is changing the threat landscape. Attackers can now find and weaponize old flaws in widely used technology faster than ever before. Arctic Wolf recommends treating every PHP installation that serves web requests as at-risk presently. Internet-facing Linux web servers without endpoint monitoring carry the highest risk of quiet compromise.

Patching remains the recommended remediation. Security teams should assess exposure immediately, identify likely attack paths, and segment critical systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment. If attackers exploit PHP2Shell, Aurora Agentic SOC is designed to detect the activity that follows, including webshell deployment, unauthorized command execution, persistence attempts, and lateral movement, enabling rapid investigation and response before attacks can escalate.

Overview and Impact

All PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk. That includes PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates the risk highest for mod_php. In PHP’s demonstrated exploit, an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, and control panels like cPanel and Plesk. Many vendor applications bundle PHP without saying so, which makes the affected assets hard to find. Bundled standalone binaries such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe on Windows are easy to miss.

Understanding the Root Cause

CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. PHP can stop while internal request data is only partly set up. Request cleanup may then treat that invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale state flaw. Request-owned internal state can survive after its memory is freed. A later request on the same worker may use that stale state before normal setup resets it. The PHP session upload progress feature is one confirmed path to this flaw, and it’s enabled by default.

Guidance for Arctic Wolf Customers

Inventory every system that runs PHP. Include package-based installs, containers, appliances, and hosting panels. Include vendor software that bundles PHP. Include continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) images.

Identify the PHP branch and package source on each system.

Update to the patched version or confirm your vendor has backported both fixes. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Restart every affected service. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache, NGINX upstream pools, application workers, and containers.

Rebuild container images from patched upstream bases. Patching only the running containers leaves the image exposed.

Move end-of-life PHP to a supported branch.

Record the patched version, vendor advisory, restart time, and validation evidence for each host or image. If a workload can’t be patched right away, document compensating controls and an approved exception with an expiry date.

Patched versions

PHP branch

Support status

Patched version

Action

8.5

Active support

8.5.12

Update immediately

8.4

Active support

8.4.27

Update immediately

8.3

Security fixes only

8.3.36

Update immediately

8.2

Security fixes only

8.2.35

Update immediately, then plan an upgrade

8.1 and older

End-of-life

None from the PHP project

Upgrade or get fixes from your vendor

The PHP project no longer releases updates for 8.1 or older. Some distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes, so check with your vendor.

Audit commands

Use these commands to find PHP packages and confirm that your vendor backported both fixes.

Platform

Command

Ubuntu or Debian

dpkg -l | grep php

Ubuntu or Debian

apt changelog php8.3-cli | grep -E “CVE-2026-109618|CVE-2026-109619”

RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, or CentOS

rpm -qa | grep php

RHEL, Rocky Linux, or AlmaLinux

rpm -q php-cli –changelog | grep -E “CVE-2026-109618|CVE-2026-109619”

Alpine containers

apk info | grep php

Use stopgaps to reduce exposure while you patch

Configuration changes such as memory_limit or session.upload_progress.enabled are not remediation. PHP states that only an update is a complete solution. The required fix is a patched PHP runtime or a vendor package that explicitly backports both fixes.

If you can’t update right away, PHP lists measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths. These measures do not make an installation safe.

For CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration.

Set a low post_max_size. PHP suggests 8M for applications without uploads and 32M for those with uploads. Keep upload_max_filesize below it.

Enforce request size, field count, and header limits at the web server or proxy.

Skip RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA because they can trigger the vulnerable allocation failure.

For CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or in an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Then restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts.

How Arctic Wolf Labs turns telemetry into outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global SOC telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base. Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This means customers gain coverage against PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance

As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments. Arctic Wolf Labs’ initial investigation has identified numerous scanning efforts as well as malicious exploitation attempts, including passing wget requests to retrieve both ELF and Golang binaries associated with commodity malware.

How the Aurora Superintelligence Platform keeps customers protected

The Aurora Superintelligence Platform helps organizations reduce PHP2Shell risk before and after exploitation. Aurora Vulnerability Management identifies and prioritizes affected assets using live exploit activity and threat intelligence, helping security teams focus remediation efforts where risk is highest.

PHP2Shell vulnerability detections in Aurora Vulnerability Management

The Aurora Agentic SOC monitors the behaviors attackers rely on after exploitation, including webshell deployment, suspicious processes spawned by PHP or web servers, malicious command execution, persistence activity, and lateral movement.

Together, these capabilities help organizations quickly identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation, detect malicious activity, investigate potential compromise, and contain threats while vulnerable systems are being patched. As the threat evolves, Arctic Wolf continuously incorporates new intelligence across the platform to strengthen proactive cyber risk remediation and detection and response capabilities for all customers.

articles.title: Keep Calm, and Patch PHP2Shell
articles.context: With a widely available patch for supported versions and the lifeline thrown for some legacy code, threat actors will weaponize these exploits against unpatched and end of life...
articles.full_text:
Keep Calm and Patch PHP2Shell

October 21, 2026

Justin Timothy

With contributions by the GuidePoint Security GRIT team

BLOG

10 min.

How to Respond to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

*Note: This is an actively developing situation and the information from this blog is accurate as of writing. Please refer to PHP’s official guidance for any newly released information and additional patching and mitigation recommendations.

The newly released ‘PHP2Shell’ vulnerabilities have become a hot topic hitting the desks, feeds and wires of every cybersecurity professional around the world. Starting October 20th, leaked details, disputed PoCs, conflicting exploitation reports and a patch that was scheduled but not yet released started circulating among security professionals online.

TL;DR – LPHP2Shell is a critical, highly exploitable set of two vulnerabilities that could potentially affect a massive percentage of internet facing websites. The patch is available and the time to patch is now.

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively nicknamed “PHP2Shell”, are critical severity vulnerabilities that require immediate attention.

Patches are available for supported versions of PHP. PHP supplied Linux distributions and LTS vendors the patches in advance. Experts recommend isolating or decommissioning systems running versions older than 7.4.

It’s important to patch internet-facing systems first, rebuild containers that contain PHP, restart all affected systems after patching and conduct retrospective threat hunts to ensure no threat actors slipped through before the patches were applied.

The instinct during these types of high-impact vulnerability disclosures is to either panic or wait for certainty. Panic can lead to uncoordinated patching and inconsistent workarounds. Waiting means the exploit code is circulating before you hit your change window.

It wasn’t until PHP released their official post announcing the two CVEs and the mitigation options that the world was able to definitively understand the impact and start implementing patch management strategies.

This is why a balanced approach works best: act on what’s confirmed, prepare for what’s coming and make deliberate decisions about the tradeoffs you’re accepting.

What We Know About PHP2Shell

All PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed are affected by these vulnerabilities. PHP considers the risk highest for mod_php, where the demonstrated exploit achieves unauthenticated remote code execution before application code runs. Both CVEs have been rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0 by PHP.

CVE-2026-109618: RCE via OOM Corruption

PHP handles out-of-memory (OOM) conditions, unwinding straight out of the current execution context and aborting the request. In certain early-request contexts, request-scoped memory is reachable before it has been fully initialized.

If any allocation fails in that window, the non-local exit skips the initialization and PHP’s error path does not account for the half-built state. The request shutdown routine then reads or branches on that memory. The failing allocation does not need to be related to the corrupted memory, so the trigger is generic: any OOM during the window is enough.

Several OOM-induction strategies trigger it consistently, which makes exploitation reliable and leads to Remote Code Execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109619: RCE Via Stale Global State

PHP workers are long-lived and reused across requests and they keep some global state (error, session, object and extension data) that points to memory belonging to a single request. That state should be cleared before the request’s memory is freed. A fatal error can stop an operation before it cleans up.

Examples include running out of memory, hitting the execution time limit or a failed compile. A later warning during shutdown can also refill error state that was already cleared. The request’s memory is then freed while the worker still points to it, which is a use-after-free. When the same worker handles its next request, early steps that run before normal setup (input, configuration, session and error handling) can read, free or act on that stale pointer.

With a carefully crafted memory layout, an attacker can turn this into RCE, meaning they run their own code on the server. Exploitation takes two separate HTTP requests handled by the same worker: the first leaves stale state behind and the second uses it.

PHP2Shell encompasses two critical-severity vulnerabilities in one of the most widely deployed server-side runtimes on the internet. A patch has now been made available and we encourage all organizations to patch where possible.

Why PHP2Shell Deserves Your Attention

Not every vulnerability warrants immediate attention; however, this one does. The characteristics, including the potential impact and the exploitability demand quick action.

The parsing layer is the attack surface: Initial reporting indicates that the PHP2Shell vulnerability triggers during multipart/form-data parsing, before your application code executes. CMS maintenance modes, security plugins, authentication layers… none of it matters once it’s under attack. The request body gets parsed by PHP itself and that’s where the flaw lives.

The affected footprint is potentially enormous: PHP powers a significant portion of global websites with their server-side language. It’s embedded in WordPress, cPanel, WHM, Laravel-based internal tools, hosting panels, appliances and countless containerized microservices. Many organizations running PHP don’t think of themselves as PHP shops.

End-of-life PHP versions won’t get a fix: PHP 8.1 and earlier are considered end-of-life by the vendor. Any system running a legacy PHP version will not receive an official patch. If the claims about the vulnerability affecting versions as far back as PHP 5, many systems may face the need for rapid upgrade or decommissioning to ensure security.

The exploit interest is high and the details are public: The advisories are linked, the root causes are documented and the confirmed attack paths are described. The window between “patch available” and “weaponized exploit code circulating” is narrowing. We know from experience that threat actors weaponize large scale, public exploits within 24-48 hours of their disclosure.

How to Patch PHP2Shell

PHP has released the following versions that have addressed the vulnerabilities: PHP 8.5.12, PHP 8.4.27, PHP 8.3.36 and PHP 8.2.35.

Source downloads are available on php.net. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, so check your vendor for updated packages.

Patching alone does not fully mitigate the possibility of exploitation. Keep in mind exploitability and follow this recommended execution sequence to reduce the highest risks first:

Patch internet-facing systems first: With systems that face the internet, the attack surface is remote and unauthenticated. Internet-facing PHP hosts are the front line. Secure them before all others to close the widest gap.

Confirm the fix through package changelogs, not version strings: Distributions frequently backport security fixes without changing the upstream version number. A system reporting PHP 8.4.26 might already contain the fix if the distribution backported it. Check the package changelog or the distribution’s security advisory for confirmation.

Restart everything: Patching the binary on disk doesn’t protect running processes. Restart PHP-FPM, Apache modules and every long-running PHP process. This includes queue workers, schedulers and daemons. Without a restart, these processes continue running the old, vulnerable binary.

Rebuild and redeploy container images: If PHP runs in containers, updating the host package isn’t enough. Rebuild images with the patched PHP version and redeploy. Every running container based on the old image remains vulnerable.

Watch your distribution’s timeline: Not every package repository will have the fix today. The volunteer-run Remi repository (widely used on RHEL-based servers) will not publish updates on October 21st. PHP’s advisory urges Remi users to switch to distribution packages or build from source so the fix can be applied immediately.

What to Do If You Can't Patch PHP2Shell Immediately

PHP’s guidance is clear: the only complete solution is an update.

PHP has published specific interim measures that reduce exposure to confirmed attack paths. These mitigations are not equivalent to patching. They mitigate the risk of exploitation, but they do not eliminate it completely.

The multi-part rejection workaround remains valid as an additional layer for both CVEs. Rejecting requests whose Content-Type contains multipart/form-data at the web server, before they reach PHP, is still a strong stopgap. Cover all HTTP methods, not just POST (PHP 8.4+ parses multipart bodies on other methods) and apply it to every virtual host and default server that passes requests to PHP. This breaks file uploads until removed.

For CVE-2026-109618 (OOM corruption):

Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can’t override (e.g., php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration). Verify that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don’t require file uploads, post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Enforce limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count and nesting depth, including for requests without a usable Content-Length.

Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause vulnerable allocation failure.

For CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state):

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. The setting needs to take effect before the parser runs.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.

Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors or @ does not help.

The Systems That Won't Get an Official Fix (But Might Get Help)

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life, so normally, those versions would not receive updates. Notably, PHP published minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 to help organizations building from source or without access to an LTS vendor. This is not a full-support commitment. However, it is a valuable lifeline for teams that can compile from source and need to close the gap.

For systems that can’t be patched or compiled from backports (and especially for anything older than 7.4) the guidance from multiple regulatory boards and industry experts stands: isolate internet-facing PHP systems from public networks or take them offline entirely. That’s a hard conversation for teams running legacy applications on unsupported PHP versions and it’s a conversation that needs to happen today.

With a widely available patch for supported versions and the lifeline thrown for some legacy code, threat actors will weaponize these exploits against unpatched and end of life systems.

After Patching: Hunt Backwards

Patching closes the door, which reduces your risk going forward. However, it doesn’t guarantee that a threat actor wasn’t able to slip through the cracks while you were busy patching. A retrospective threat hunt based on these behavior signals can help you eliminate the possibility of infiltration:

PHP worker child processes spawning shells or download utilities (PHP-FPM, Apache or other PHP workers)

Unexplained worker crashes or segmentation faults in PHP-FPM and web server logs (plausible side effects of memory-corruption exploitation attempts)

Unusual multipart/form-data requests from October 20th, 15:00 UTC onward, particularly to endpoints that don’t accept uploads

New or modified files in web roots, upload directories, plugin directories and mu-plugins

Changes to .user.ini files or the auto_prepend_file setting

Persistence indicators: new cron entries, systemd units, Supervisor entries, SSH authorized_keys additions, newly created application admin accounts or unexpected outbound connections from PHP service accounts

A clean result doesn’t rule out compromise, but it does indicate that the available behavioral indicators didn’t fire. That’s a meaningful data point. That said: preserve your logs. Web server and PHP logs from October 20th, 15:00 UTC onward are your forensic baseline. Log rotation, redeployment and container rebuilds can destroy the evidence needed for a compromise assessment. Back them up before patching changes anything.

Stay Tuned for Updates

GuidePoint Security’s GRIT team is actively tracking PHP2Shell and its impact. We will provide updated advisories, emerging exploit techniques and confirmed indicators of compromise as they become available. If PHP workers are spawning shells, unexpected files appear in web roots or you discover persistence mechanisms on a PHP host, the GuidePoint Security Incident Response team is ready to help.

FAQs

What is PHP2Shell?

PHP2Shell is the collective name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) disclosed on October 20, 2026. Both are rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical) and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on PHP web servers. CVE-2026-109618 exploits out-of-memory corruption during request processing and CVE-2026-109619 exploits stale global state that persists across requests within the same PHP worker process.

What PHP versions are affected by PHP2Shell?

All PHP installations serving web requests are affected, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP considers mod_php the highest-risk configuration. Patched versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive official patches, though PHP published minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Unconfirmed reports indicate the vulnerabilities may affect versions as far back as PHP 5.

How do I patch PHP2Shell?

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Source downloads are available on php.net and Linux distributions and LTS vendors received patches in advance. After updating, restart PHP-FPM, Apache modules and all long-running PHP processes such as queue workers and schedulers; these continue running the old binary until restarted. Container images must be rebuilt and redeployed with the patched PHP version. Confirm the fix through package changelogs or vendor advisories rather than version strings, since distributions often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.

What should I do if I can't patch PHP2Shell immediately?

PHP’s official position is that only a full update is a complete solution. Interim measures that reduce exposure include: rejecting requests whose Content-Type contains multipart/form-data at the web server before they reach PHP (covering all HTTP methods, not just POST); setting memory_limit=-1 to remove the controllable OOM trigger for CVE-2026-109618; and setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 for CVE-2026-109619. For systems running PHP 8.1 or earlier that cannot be patched or compiled from PHP’s source-backports, the recommended action is isolation from public networks or taking them offline.

How do I detect PHP2Shell exploitation on my servers?

As of October 21, 2026, no vendor-published indicators of compromise exist yet, so detection relies on behavioral hunting. Look for PHP worker processes spawning shells or download utilities, unexplained worker crashes or segmentation faults in PHP-FPM and web server logs, unusual multipart/form-data requests (especially to endpoints that don’t accept uploads) from October 20, 2026 onward, new or modified files in web roots and upload directories, changes to .user.ini files or auto_prepend_file settings and new persistence indicators such as cron entries, SSH authorized_keys additions or unexpected outbound connections. Preserve web server and PHP logs from October 20 onward before patching or redeploying.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: How to Protect Vulnerable PHP Workloads While Patching
articles.context: Aquasec provides vulnerability detection and runtime controls to help identify exposure and restrict supported unauthorized activities while customers apply security updates
articles.full_text:
How does Aquasec protect PHP workloads?

Aquasec enforces security policies inside running workloads, allowing security teams to restrict supported unauthorized actions without depending exclusively on vulnerability specific signatures.

Four runtime control areas are particularly relevant to PHP workloads.

Restrict unauthorized process execution. Runtime policies can restrict PHP workloads from launching unnecessary shells and download utilities such as `sh`, `bash`, `curl` and `wget`. This can interrupt certain attempts to execute additional commands or retrieve malicious payloads.

Prevent unauthorized executable changes. Aquasec Drift Prevention can block execution of executable files that were not present in the original container image. This helps restrict newly introduced malicious binaries, although it does not independently prevent a PHP script from running through the existing interpreter.

Restrict unauthorized network activity. Appropriate runtime network controls can restrict unnecessary outbound connections and help limit certain reverse shell activities or communication with attacker controlled infrastructure.

Protect application files. File integrity monitoring can detect unauthorized modifications to sensitive application directories. File modification restrictions can prevent changes when properly configured, including changes to PHP web roots where malicious scripts might be introduced.

The effectiveness of these controls depends on workload coverage, policy configuration and the attack technique. In enforcement mode, validated policies can block supported unauthorized actions. They should not be represented as complete protection against either PHP2Shell vulnerability, particularly the reported memory disclosure path.

articles.title: Limits of Java Certificate Bypass: Fingerprint Blocklist Insights
articles.context: TL;DR Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked
articles.full_text:
TL;DR

Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked.certs rejected the listed certificate encodings but accepted re-encoded versions that still validated in the tested configurations.

We reproduced the behavior with ECDSA- and RSA-signed intermediates associated with the eMudhra incident. Each re-encoded certificate had a different SHA-256 fingerprint.

The results apply to the JDK versions and trust-store configurations tested. Follow current vendor guidance and verify the protections in the runtimes and trust stores you deploy.

A certificate blocklist can reject a known-bad certificate and still miss another encoding of it.

We saw this while examining Java's response to the eMudhra certificate incident. The mitigation uses SHA-256 fingerprints to identify compromised intermediate certificates. But a certificate’s fingerprint is calculated from its exact encoded bytes.

During an AI-assisted review, Sonatype Research Labs asked Opus 5.5 whether Java's exact-fingerprint blocking could be bypassed. The AI model flagged that exact-byte matching might leave room for equivalent certificate encodings.

We confirmed the behavior for both ECDSA and RSA certificates: re-encoded intermediates had different SHA-256 fingerprints, yet still validated in our Java trust-store tests. This points to a limit in exact-fingerprint blocking: it can identify the certificate bytes it knows about without necessarily covering every equivalent encoding.

Here, we’ll explain how the re-encoding works, what the tests show, and what teams should check before relying on a certificate blocklist as their only mitigation.

How It Started: eMudhra Certificates Compromised

Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authority keys were compromised on October 20, 2026, allowing anyone who obtained a key to create certificates that could be trusted as part of a chain to a trusted root. Browser and platform vendors responded with blocks and trust-store changes.

This also prompted a Java mitigation: add the affected intermediates to blocked.certs. Our research began with a narrower question: does that fingerprint-based block reject every valid encoding of those certificates?

How Exact-Fingerprint Blocking Works

A certificate is a structured document: it contains information such as the subject, public key, issuer, validity period, and a digital signature. In Java, blocked.certs identifies certificates by their SHA-256 fingerprints. The fingerprint is calculated from the certificate's encoded bytes, so even a small change to those bytes produces a different fingerprint.

This makes fingerprint blocking precise, but the match depends on the exact encoding in the blocklist. If a certificate can be re-encoded and still pass signature validation, the new encoding may have a different fingerprint and may not match the listed entry. To test whether an alternate encoding could still validate in practice, we examined two signature formats: ECDSA and RSA.

Changing the Encoding Changes the Result

We tested two certificate chains from the eMudhra incident advisory: one with an ECDSA-signed intermediate and one with an RSA-signed intermediate. For each, the reproduction added the original intermediate's SHA-256 fingerprint to a copy of a JDK's blocked.certs file, changed the intermediate's encoding without its private key, then checked whether the chain still validated.

The two encoding changes were:

ECDSA: The script changes the signature value from s to n − s, another valid representation of the signature.

RSA: It removes the NULL parameter from the outer signature algorithm identifier. The signature over the certificate data remains unchanged.

Both tests produced the same result:Java rejected the original chain whose intermediate fingerprint was listed, but trusted the chain with the re-encoded intermediate, whose fingerprint was different. After the relevant roots were removed from the copied JDK’s trust store, both chains were rejected.

Verify the Mitigation in Your Runtime

Teams should verify certificate mitigations in the Java runtimes and trust stores they deploy. Removing the relevant roots rejected both chains in our tests, but it can also interrupt legitimate TLS connections. Before changing a trust store, identify dependent services, test their certificate chains, and monitor for TLS failures after deployment.

Follow current vendor guidance and document any exceptions. These results cover only the JDK versions and trust-store configurations we examined, so validate the controls separately for other runtimes and TLS paths in your environment.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Makes PHP Inventory and Patch Ownership Urgent
articles.context: As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet
articles.full_text:
Updated October 23, 2026: PHP disclosed a related follow-on issue, CVE-2026-115560, involving an unlikely remote code execution (RCE) vector under unusual session settings. PHP recommends disabling session.upload_progress.enabled until the next regular bugfix release. See our research and recommendation in Sonatype Guide for more details.

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is the name being used for two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

PHP says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, with the highest risk in Apache configurations using mod_php. Fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Organizations should inventory PHP across their environments, prioritize internet-facing systems, monitor for suspicious activity, and apply the update through PHP or the relevant distribution or product vendor. If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

On October 23, 2026, PHP disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate follow-on RCE issue. Temporarily disable session.upload_progress.enabled as PHP recommends, then apply the complete PHP fix when available.

PHP2Shell Is Two Critical Flaws in the PHP Runtime

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP's internal request handling. Because PHP is used in websites, applications, and products, affected installations may be managed by different teams or supplied through different vendors.The urgent work is to find those systems, establish who owns each one, and verify that the fix reaches every deployment.

Sonatype's PHP2Shell Security Event tracks current guidance and response recommendations.

CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory handling: PHP may interrupt a request while internal data is only partly initialized, then handle that data incorrectly during cleanup.

CVE-2026-109619 involves a stale global state that can persist after its underlying memory has been freed.

PHP says CVE-2026-115560 can occur when an application configures session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, switches it to php at runtime before calling session_start(), and leaves session upload progress enabled. PHP had already listed disabling upload progress as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619. This setting does not cover every affected path, and that a PHP release containing the complete state-reset patch is the reliable remediation.

Under affected conditions, the flaws can allow a remote attacker to execute code without authentication.

Ilkka Turunen, Sonatype's Field CTO, puts the operational priority plainly: "The immediate priority is clear accountability: know where PHP is used across your services and products, who owns remediation, and how quickly fixes can be deployed."

The Hard Part Is Finding Every PHP Installation

Organizations may know that their public websites use PHP but have less visibility into internal portals, older services, appliances, or software that bundles its own runtime. Different teams may also install and maintain PHP through separate operating system distributions, hosting providers, or third-party vendors.

Turunen expects remediation to extend beyond visible websites and services. PHP is bundled into other products and remains in older environments, creating what he calls "a long tail of environments needing to apply this patch."

A complete response starts with an inventory that connects each runtime to an owner and a patch path. Teams should identify:

Which internet-facing and internal systems run PHP.

The PHP version and how it is supplied or maintained.

Which applications, containers, images, appliances, and products include a PHP runtime.

The business or service owner responsible for remediation.

Whether a fixed package is available from PHP, the operating system distributor, hosting provider, or another vendor.

Include systems that are easy to overlook: older applications with little traffic, test environments that remain reachable, and deployments maintained outside the central platform team. An incomplete inventory can make an organization believe remediation is finished while vulnerable installations remain online.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. PHP says some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported fixes, and it has also published source backports for selected older branches. Organizations using these versions should confirm the status with their distribution or vendor, or plan an upgrade to a supported release. Do not assume an upstream version number alone tells you whether a vendor-maintained package includes the fix.

Patch, Verify, and Monitor Across the Estate

PHP says updating to a fixed release is the only complete solution. Temporary controls can reduce exposure to specific attack paths, and a web application firewall can add protection for traffic routed through it. Cloudflare reported deploying protections and seeing attack traffic aimed at its customers, while urging users to patch.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, the UK National Cyber Security Centre advises organizations to consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated. If it must remain available, assign an owner and document interim protections and a reassessment date.

The discovery and response also highlight the role AI is playing in vulnerability research. The Wall Street Journal reported that Calif and Wiz researchers used AI tools during a PHP source-code audit, and that developers, researchers, and distributors coordinated on fixes after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure.

As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet."

What Organizations Should Do Now

PHP2Shell is a test of whether organizations can find, own, and update the software running across their environments. PHP has published fixes, but a release only reduces risk when the update reaches every affected runtime, including those inside products and services maintained by other vendors.

Organizations should:

Inventory systems running PHP, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Monitor internet-facing PHP systems for suspicious activity.

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or apply the relevant vendor backport. Include products and services that bundle PHP.

Check PHP, distribution, and third-party vendor advisories for updates, especially when running PHP 8.1 or older.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

For ongoing details and links to current advisories, see the official PHP security advisory.

Written by Sonatype Research Team

Sonatype's Research Team is focused on bringing real-time, in-depth intelligence and actionable information about open source and third party vulnerabilities to Sonatype customers.
