articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.context: Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in PHP
articles.context: Overview On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP
articles.full_text:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges.

CVE

CVSSv4

Description

CVE-2026-109618

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via OOM corruption

CVE-2026-109619

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via stale global state

All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs.

The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon.

Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles.

Multiple public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are now available. Rapid7 researchers have reviewed these and observe that each demonstrates RCE only against a specific combination of operating system, PHP version, and web server, and none appears to be broadly reliable. Rapid7’s own research supports this. Our attempts so far have produced a working exploit only under narrow lab conditions, and exploitation depends on assumptions that are unlikely to hold on internet-facing instances. We are continuing to investigate approaches that could improve portability, but have not yet developed a reliable, general-purpose exploit. Rapid7 has not observed exploitation in the wild, though there are multiple reports of exploitation attempts, which is expected for a vulnerability of this profile. The situation is evolving quickly, and a more portable exploit technique could emerge at any time. The current difficulty of reliable exploitation should be treated as a window to patch rather than a reason to delay, and Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis.

Update #1: On October 26, 2026, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA set the remediation due date to October 29, 2026, for affected Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies and directs them to follow the associated BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements. Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis and investigating for prior compromise.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling

According to the OOM advisory, PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM.

Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. The advisory reports RCE over HTTP with default PHP input and memory limits, including multi-worker prefork deployments. PHP-FPM terminates a worker when startup fails, preventing that particular sequence. Source analysis supports FPM susceptibility after successful startup, but the advisory reports no complete FPM exploit for this CVE. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior, and memory layout.

CVE-2026-109619: Use after free across requests

PHP can reuse a worker process to handle multiple HTTP requests. The stale-state advisory describes internal state that still points to memory freed at the end of an earlier request. A later request handled by the same worker can access that stale value before normal initialization clears it. Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset.

The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start().

The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition.

Mitigation guidance

PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions:

PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35

PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36

PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27

PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement, or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source.

Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation.

PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment:

For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit.

For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern.

Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length. If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP.

Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path.

For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting, display_errors, log_errors, or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe.

For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and stale global state advisory.

Rapid7 customers

To learn how to use Rapid7 capabilities to find systems affected by these vulnerabilities and for answers to common questions, read the PHP2Shell documentation.

For Rapid7 Customers with questions regarding Rapid7 products and their usage of PHP please consult this page.

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with remote unauthenticated vulnerability checks, available in a dedicated release that followed the regular October 21 content release.

Rapid7 has also released authenticated scan checks for both the Scan Engine and the Agent for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as part of the October 22 content release.

Authenticated, package-based checks are now available for a variety of Linux distributions. These checks evaluate installed distribution packages, so they can recognize backported fixes that keep the original upstream PHP version number. Run an authenticated scan with this content release to use them. For the full list of checks and supported distribution versions, read Rapid7’s PHP2Shell documentation, where package-based coverage for other distributions will be added as their fixes are published.

In a dedicated October 23 content release following the regular release, Rapid7 has released coverage for CVE-2026-115560, published on October 23 by the PHP Foundation. A mitigation technique is available, but no patch has yet been published. Exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 relies on non-standard configuration.

Current scope for authenticated coverage: Windows, macOS and Linux. Remote unauthenticated coverage provides coverage regardless of web-server OS.

Velociraptor

A Velociraptor Artifact Generic.Applications.PHPInventory is available to inventory PHP installations on Windows, Linux and macOS for remediation scoping. This artifact allows for the collection of package versions, common binary and module paths, and running PHP processes.

Updates

October 21, 2026: Initial publication.

October 21, 2026: Updated to reflect availability of vulnerability checks.

October 22, 2026: Updated the Overview section to include Rapid7’s findings on a PoC and the Rapid7 Customers section to include a link to the FAQ documentation.

October 23, 2026: Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to describe authenticated coverage, Linux distro backported coverage, and more.

October 27, 2026: Updated the Overview to note that CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to the CISA KEV catalog. Updated Rapid7 customers section to reflect added Windows support.

articles.title: “Next Exploit Opportunities”: How a Threat Actor Used AI to Help Plan and Execute Multiple Types of Cybercrime Activities
articles.context: Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks...
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

“Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing [sic],” the threat actor typed. The conversation was with one of several AI assistants that the actor was using to get advice on planning and executing a variety of cybercrime activities.

Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks across multiple campaign types.

Unit 42’s investigation into the actor’s operational environment and activities makes two things clear:

The attacker used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, suggesting they didn’t have the skills these activities would have required before the advent of readily available AI tools.

Despite some apparent bumbling, the actor had an impact, attacking a number of targets in India, including universities. The actor recovered thousands of records revealing personal information and mapped multiple organizations’ attack surfaces.

The attacker’s conversations with jailbroken AI tools included getting step by step advice on how to set up a fraudulent Voice over IP (VoIP) operation. One assistant “helpfully” generated a document including a “NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES” section, outlining planned followup attacks.

Unit 42 identified and investigated this threat actor's operational environment. There, we determined that they had weaponized an AI assistant across several types of cybercrime, including:

Credential theft and data exfiltration

VoIP telecommunications fraud

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

Command-and-control (C2) operations

An actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) as a secondary tool, both with safety controls disabled. The actor ran an AI-generated brute-force campaign against an Indian university’s website. The actor also achieved a confirmed intrusion against a second university, where they exfiltrated a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students.

The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders). Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Multiple, unrelated actors are independently adopting the same Hermes + DeepSeek combination. This suggests we may be witnessing an increasingly prevalent toolchain of choice for cybercriminals adopting AI-enabled capabilities. We assess a key driver is low safety friction at low cost: DeepSeek models are inexpensive and easy to access, and readily jailbroken with a simple system-prompt override.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced IP Defense

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Cortex Cloud

Idira Privileged Access Manager (PAM)

Idira Identity and Access Manager (IAM)

Idira Secrets Manager

The Unit 42 AI Security Assessment and Unit 42 Frontier AI Defense service can help identify and mitigate complex AI-enabled risks.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

AI, Credential Theft, Cryptocurrency

Technical Analysis

We identified evidence that the threat actor leveraged AI systems for a wide range of criminal activity against multiple target networks, primarily in India. The criminal activity included:

Planning for VoIP fraud

Credential theft targeting several organizations

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

C2 payloads

Credential Theft and Data Exfiltration

WordPress Brute Force

The actor used AI-generated reconnaissance to conduct a methodical attack against an Indian university's online education platform. The actor’s enumeration reports exhibit structured formatting (executive summaries, severity ratings, systematic endpoint categorization) consistent with AI-generated output. The attack progressed through four stages:

Subdomain enumeration: The actor identified 12 subdomains including the main WordPress site, a learning management system (LMS), student portal and administration dashboard

WordPress REST API enumeration: The actor extracted 13 active user IDs with real names via post author fields and author sitemaps, bypassing the Cloudflare Web Application Firewall (WAF) that blocked direct user endpoint access

Targeted brute force: A generator script produced a brute force tool with 117 usernames (derived from the enumeration) and 28 common passwords

Credential brute force: The actor’s tool flagged one WordPress login as valid

Figure 1 shows an excerpt from the actor's WordPress REST API enumeration report (stage 2).

Figure 2 shows output from a brute force attempt that recorded a candidate credential (stage 4).

University Database Exfiltration

The actor exfiltrated a MongoDB database from a second Indian public university. The exfiltration tooling wrote a manifest alongside the dumped collections, recording the following data:

Admin credential obtained: An administrator account with a weak password

Exfiltrated records: Thousands of student records (diploma, undergraduate, postgraduate) and faculty records containing PII

Infrastructure exposed: Cloud load balancing, edge routing, database services, and a third-party cloud storage service account

E-Commerce Enumeration

The actor enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform, extracting:

A storefront API token

Three admin email addresses

Two phone numbers

Payment merchant IDs

The attack report is a suspected large language model (LLM)-generated document, including a NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES section outlining planned follow-up attacks.

VoIP Telecommunications Fraud

We also identified evidence that the actor was developing VoIP (Voice over IP) fraud infrastructure, using the alice Hermes profile as an AI-powered advisor. Evidence included:

Advisory conversations

A detailed technical knowledge base

Carrier research

However, the absence of call logs, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) traces or active call routing suggested the operation was still in a planning or early setup phase.

With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, alice provided detailed, actionable criminal methodology through conversations and a comprehensive fraud knowledge base ingested into the bot. The actor developed a planned approach following an established VoIP fraud model:

Establish a legitimate front: Register a US limited liability company (LLC) with an employer identification number (EIN) to qualify as a telecommunications provider. The knowledge base includes detailed guidance on:

Forming LLCs in Wyoming or Delaware as a non-US resident

Obtaining an EIN without a Social Security number via the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) fax

Completing Federal Communications Commission (FCC) registration

Obtain carrier access: Contract with legitimate VoIP carriers to purchase call routing capacity (SIP trunks).

Traffic mixing: Route approximately 70% legitimate call traffic alongside 30% fraudulent calls to stay below carrier compliance audit thresholds.

Bypass caller ID authentication: Circumvent STIR/SHAKEN, the FCC-mandated caller identity verification framework. In the advisory conversations, alice covers bypass techniques and Calling Line Identification (CLI) spoofing.

Monetize: Generate revenue with the 30% fraudulent traffic through toll fraud and other non-compliant routes. Least-cost routing (LCR) optimizes per-minute costs across carrier tiers.

Figure 3 shows an excerpt from an alice conversation including the actor asking and DeepSeek advising on fraud traffic ratios and carrier evasion.

The pandarouter profile handled carrier research. The excerpt below in Figure 4 illustrates how the actor used it to investigate a wholesale VoIP carrier for regulatory vulnerabilities and past fraud.

Other Operations

Command and Control

The threat actor’s infrastructure maintained a listening port for a Python-based C2 listener supporting Windows reverse shell connections. Supporting payloads include:

A Base64-encoded PowerShell reverse shell delivered via VBScript

A QubesOS VM setup script with SSH and ncat

Multiple Windows shell variants

Wi-Fi Password Cracking

The actor developed an automated Wi-Fi password cracking process. A Linux (Kali) device the actor labeled Pi placed within range of target Wi-Fi networks captured Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) authentication material (PMKID or EAPOL handshakes) from nearby access points.

The server collected these hashes over an SSH tunnel and dispatched them to Vast.ai cloud GPU instances for cracking, with results automatically reported back to the actor via Discord webhooks. This technique requires physical proximity to the target networks, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Credential Scanning Toolkit

We also identified a large Go-based credential-scanning toolkit. This toolkit scrapes webpages and extracts exposed credentials, including:

.env values

S3 signed URLs

Google Cloud service account keys

Content delivery network (CDN) API keys

Private keys in log files

A companion Python script scrapes domain lists for scanning.

Cryptocurrency Reconnaissance

The actor scraped the top 500 ETH holders and major token holders via the DeBank API, producing intelligence files that documented 45 cryptocurrency whales with net worth figures. We assess this was likely for future targeting, but we were unable to identify any follow-on activity during this research.

Tool Design and Infrastructure

The threat actor used a single US-based server (162.243.3[.]92) to host multiple core services, including:

The Hermes Agent framework

A C2 listener

A Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) proxy

Several supporting components

Our analysis of the actor’s logs and test scripts indicates that they experimented with various LLMs, including GLM 5.2 by Zhipu AI and other models accessed through OpenRouter. Ultimately, they chose DeepSeek V4 as the backend for operations.

The actor's test scripts show repeated attempts to defeat model safety controls with a prompt-level override. Although GLM 5.2 is an open-weight model that has been reported as weakly guarded, the actor built a dedicated script to send the override to GLM 5.2 and flag refusals. This is evidence of resistance the actor worked to overcome.

The actor ultimately operationalized DeepSeek V4, consistent with the minimal safety controls observed in the Chinese-speaking activity we previously reported. Figure 5 shows an example of the system prompt the actor used to override model safety controls (from the actor's model-testing scripts, e.g., test_batch1.py).

Table 1 summarizes the actor's AI tool configurations.

Table 1. AI tool configurations.

Figure 6 shows a flowchart that illustrates the actor's infrastructure and how the AI tools interconnect.

The Hermes Agent served as the actor's primary interface, controlled via Telegram direct messages. The actor maintained three Hermes profiles as specialized AI modes, each running as a separate Telegram bot gateway spawned from the operator's session (Table 2).

The actor configured four additional profiles (dev, check, vuln, deploy) in a shared Telegram group. While we did not observe any chat artifacts for these profiles, the naming suggests the actor used AI to assist with development, validation, vulnerability testing and deployment automation functions.

The Cursor IDE was configured through a proxy script named cipher-proxy.sh that set environment variables to enable full agent mode and bypass its permission and sandbox controls. The configuration and the AI-generated scripts on the host shown below in Figure 7 suggest the actor used it for code development.

Attribution

We assess the actor is a financially motivated, multi-domain criminal operator with no prior reporting. The actor is English-speaking with informal, frequently broken grammar. The alice bot's stored memory describes the actor as a “gamer, OSINT, VoIP entrepreneur” claiming to hold a US LLC and EIN. Figure 8 below shows text from the pandarouter bot's stored memory, which is more candid.

Conclusion

This case illustrates how AI lowers the skill barrier for cybercrime. The actor used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, but still achieved notable impact. They recovered more than 5,200 PII records and mapped multiple organizations' attack surfaces. AI enabled a single actor to operate across diverse attack types (credential theft, VoIP fraud, Wi-Fi cracking, cryptocurrency targeting) that would traditionally require distinct skill sets.

The VoIP fraud planning demonstrates a particularly notable use of AI as a domain expert. With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, the actor's bot profiles provided detailed, actionable criminal guidance.

This guidance included specific fraud-to-clean traffic ratios, carrier audit thresholds to stay below and operational security measures to avoid detection. The model's minimal safety controls allowed it to function as an on-demand criminal advisor, enabling the actor to acquire operational expertise through conversation rather than experience.

Combining these findings with our previous reporting on a Chinese-Speaking threat actor leveraging the Hermes + DeepSeek toolchain points to growing uptake of this combination among cybercriminals.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
articles.context: Core PHP engine flaws enable remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure across the web.
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.

PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.

These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, putting every affected website in immediate risk.

Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.

On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine.

These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.

Overview

In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.

Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.

PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.

Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.

We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Google, Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel, and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.

The Vulnerabilities

All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

Below you can find a table that demonstrates what type of impact was demonstrated by each of the bugs we reported to PHP. The applications listed below are targets we chose for the RCE demonstrations. They are representative targets - exploitation does not require one of these CMSs, as the vulnerable code is in PHP itself.

Tracking ID

Bug

What an attacker can achieve

What we demonstrated

CVE-2026-109618

Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

Remote process-memory disclosure

Corrupt process memory and execute code

Unauthenticated disclosure of PHP worker memory

Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla

Application-agnostic remote memory disclosure

CVE-2026-109619

Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

OPcache type confusion

Corrupt process memory and execute code

Corrupt shared PHP state and execute code

Pre-authentication RCE on Drupal

Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress

While this blog covers only four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs) that follow this problematic pattern, there are other tracked, and likely untracked, variants of this issue in the PHP codebase. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release.

Impact

We combined these vulnerabilities into a single exploit script, php2shell, and demonstrated that it could execute code remotely without authentication on deployments of WordPress (wordpress:latest), Drupal (drupal:latest), and Joomla (joomla:latest), using their latest container images at the time of testing.

These platforms illustrate the impact, but the vulnerabilities are in PHP itself. Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Separately, we demonstrated that attackers could read sensitive data from the PHP process’s memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys, without needing to achieve remote code execution.

Demonstrations of PHP2Shell with Wordpress, Joomla, and Drupal:

The AI inflection point

The vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Turning these flaws into working exploits required chaining multiple bugs and accounting for how PHP allocates and reuses memory across requests. Memory bugs are notoriously complex; differences in PHP versions, configurations and application behavior can break assumptions the exploit depends on. An attack that works against one deployment may need substantial adjustments to work against another, each requiring further analysis, testing and debugging. Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale.

With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts. With testing and debugging tools, models can analyze failures and iterate on adjustments, reducing the specialist effort required for each target. This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets.

We used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research. Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.

Using Gemini 4 Argon, the team at Wiz has shown why frontier AI is a game-changer for cyber defense. For over a decade, these critical vulnerabilities remained unaddressed because vulnerability discovery and exploitation were incredibly complex. We're pleased to see Gemini 4 Argon help defenders bridge that gap, finding vulnerabilities and helping patch them.

Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind

Industry-level collaborations

Prior to public disclosure, Wiz Research worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI on discovery, coordination and patch verification. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately.

A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application. PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.

Technical deep dive

Bug: Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

PHP's Session module can decode session data during upload-progress handling in the same pre-initialization window. The decoder stores request-owned bookkeeping in BG(unserialize). A fatal allocation failure can interrupt this path, destroy the request heap and leave the unserializer's global state published.

On a later request handled by the same worker, PHP can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live unserializer bookkeeping. The stale state becomes a powerful memory-corruption primitive. We combined it with the memory disclosure to remove address uncertainty and achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.

The WordPress, Drupal and Joomla chains are representative demonstrations. The underlying primitives exist at the PHP engine level and can affect any PHP application running on a vulnerable version.

These issues execute below the application layer, so application logs may contain little context. Until systems are patched, defenders should pay particular attention to unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These signals can guide an investigation. Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation.

Bug: Remote process-memory disclosure

PHP parses RFC1867 multipart requests during request startup, before normal module initialization has completed. Session upload-progress handling can initialize Session state at this early stage and publish a session ID in PS(id). An out-of-memory error can abort the request before cleanup completes. PHP then destroys the request heap and may leave PS(id) pointing to the freed allocation.

A later multipart request handled by the same worker can reach the upload-progress cleanup path before normal Session initialization resets that pointer. PHP trusts the stale pointer and length as a live zend_string and URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The attack works even when the application never calls session_start(), making the issue application-agnostic. We demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of an attacker-sized region of live worker memory containing data from outside the attacker's request.

Bug: Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

In affected versions, PHP retains the backtrace of the most recent fatal error in EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace). A fatal out-of-memory error can destroy the request heap without undefining that executor-global value. The worker survives with a global that still points to memory from the previous request.

If the same worker emits a diagnostic early in the next request, it can access the pointer before the executor reinitializes that state. PHP then destroys or updates the dangling backtrace and follows attacker-reclaimed memory. The resulting cross-request use-after-free can be developed into controlled memory corruption. We demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against Drupal using this primitive.

Bug: OPcache type confusion

OPcache persists compiled PHP structures in shared memory and assigns indices into per-worker runtime-pointer maps. Workers coordinate those indices through a shared frontier. During zend_accel_script_persist(), PHP advances the process-local CG(map_ptr_last) frontier. It publishes the corresponding shared frontier only after persistence completes. An allocation failure between those two events leaves the process-local advance in place and partially persisted objects referring to slots that the shared state still considers available.

When another worker later reuses one of those slots for a different runtime object, stale shared metadata resolves to a pointer of the wrong type. The mismatch creates a cross-worker type confusion and corrupts shared OPcache state. We used this primitive to build an unauthenticated RCE chain against WordPress.

There are other variants outside of these four bugs. While we initially reported these four to PHP, through this research we realized the vulnerability is deeply rooted in the PHP codebase and will require a comprehensive fix. Other variants should also fold under the same two CVEs.

How Can Wiz Help?

Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intel Center advisory for PHP2Shell, which includes built-in coverage for agentless and runtime vulnerability detection, exploitation detection via Wiz Defend and Sensor, and automatic response policies, alongside remediation and threat hunting guidance.

Sensor customers using the newest version (1.0.12768) can also enable a built-in response policy to automatically terminate processes exhibiting behaviors typical of PHP2Shell exploitation:

Conclusion

With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated. It marks an AI inflection point. The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit. With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. Vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. These same capabilities also give defenders a chance to uncover and fix flaws that have survived years of scrutiny.

Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research, with Argon making a particularly significant contribution to finding and helping to remediate the vulnerability.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: systematically finding flaws in existing software and catching new ones before they reach production. Our coordinated efforts with PHP, OpenAI and Calif advance that goal, applying AI to strengthen the software foundations we all share.

Responsible disclosure timeline

August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.

August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.

August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.

August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.

September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.

October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.

October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.

Stay in touch

Hi there! We are Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

Watch the Threat Briefing Webinar

articles.title: Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability
articles.context: The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability
articles.full_text:
Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release.

All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed session.upload_progress.name are not covered by the WAF rule.

The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability.

More information to follow.

October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell. The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic.

Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation, OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell.

Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic.

Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives.

To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability.

Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog.

The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users.

What we know about the vulnerabilities

PHP is used by almost 70% of websites. The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet.

The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released.

An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker.

The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens:

Vulnerability

What goes wrong

CVE-2026-109618

PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid.

CVE-2026-109619

A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data.

These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update.

Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix.

New rules

For Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). Free customers don’t have to take any actions to enable the protection. To override the ruleset behavior, you can refer to our documentation.

To analyze blocked requests, visit Security > Security Analytics > Events. Filter by the rule IDs in the table above and inspect the matched request, action, and path. Copy prompt to fix!

# Security task: check and fix "php2shell" (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) Two critical PHP runtime vulnerabilities were disclosed on 2026-10-21 (CVSS v4.0 9.2). They allow unauthenticated remote code execution, data exposure and DoS through crafted HTTP requests. Exploitation is already happening. The bug is in the PHP runtime itself, so updating app code, frameworks, WordPress or plugins does NOT fix it. Official advisory (treat as source of truth, re-fetch it in case it was updated): https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5 - GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618, RCE via OOM corruption) - GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state) **Fixed upstream versions:** 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35 **Affected:** every PHP install that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed). mod_php has the highest risk: a demonstrated exploit triggers before any application code runs. ## Rules - Do NOT guess. If you can't confirm a version or setting, say so. - Ask me before changing anything on production or shared infrastructure, restarting production services, or editing deploy config. Read-only discovery is fine. - Don't stop at the first finding. Inventory everything, then report. ## Step 1: Inventory every place PHP runs Search the current repo/workspace AND any machines/containers I have access to: - Repo: `*.php`, `composer.json`/`composer.lock` (check `require.php` and `config.platform.php`), `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `.php-version`, `.tool-versions`, `.devcontainer/`, CI files (GitHub Actions `setup-php`, GitLab CI `image:`), IaC (Terraform, Ansible, Helm, k8s manifests), PaaS config (`app.yaml`, `Procfile`, Platform.sh, Laravel Forge/Vapor, etc.). - Base images: list every `FROM php:*`, `FROM wordpress:*`, `FROM bitnami/*`, `FROM serversideup/*`, `FROM dunglas/frankenphp*` and similar, with tags. - Running hosts/containers (if accessible): `php -v`, `php-fpm -v`, `php -i | grep -i "server api"`, `apachectl -M | grep -i php`, `docker ps` + `docker exec <c> php -v`. - Note the SAPI for each (FPM / mod_php / CGI / FrankenPHP / LiteSpeed / CLI-only). - Note long-running workers (Laravel Octane, RoadRunner, Swoole, FrankenPHP worker mode). These are relevant to the stale-state bug. If no PHP is found anywhere, tell me clearly and stop. Nothing else is needed. ## Step 2: Decide if each instance is vulnerable For each instance, classify it as PATCHED / VULNERABLE / UNKNOWN: - Upstream builds: vulnerable if below 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 on that branch. - **PHP 8.1 and older are EOL upstream:** vulnerable unless a vendor backport is confirmed. - **Distro packages (Debian/Ubuntu/RHEL/Alpine/etc.)** often backport fixes WITHOUT bumping the upstream version, so `php -v` alone isn't enough. Check the package changelog for the CVE IDs, e.g. `apt changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]"` or `rpm -q --changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]"`. - If PHP comes from `rpms.remirepo.net`: the advisory says it will not have same-day updates. Flag this and recommend distro packages or building from source. - Managed hosting / shared hosting / PaaS: mark UNKNOWN and tell me to ask the provider. ## Step 3: Fix (only after I approve the plan for prod) 1. Upgrade PHP to a fixed version (or the vendor-patched package): - Bump Docker base image tags to a fixed patch release, rebuild, redeploy. - Update CI `php-version` pins. - `apt`/`dnf`/`apk` upgrade of the distro PHP packages. - 7.4 / 8.0 / 8.1 built from source: the PHP security team published minimal backport branches linked from the advisory. Otherwise upgrade to a supported version. 2. **Restart EVERY PHP worker** (FPM pools, Apache, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Octane/ RoadRunner/Swoole). Old processes keep running vulnerable code until restarted. 3. Verify each instance afterwards (version + changelog check) and report the evidence. ## Step 4: Temporary mitigations (ONLY if patching isn't possible right away) These reduce exposure but do NOT make the server safe. Apply them in php.ini / the FPM pool / server config (not `ini_set()` or `.user.ini`) and restart every worker: - CVE-2026-109618: - `memory_limit=-1`, set non-overridably (e.g. `php_admin_value`), and confirm nothing re-applies a finite limit. - Low `post_max_size` (8M with no uploads, 32M with uploads), with `upload_max_filesize` below it. - Enforce request size / field count / multipart part count / header limits at the web server or proxy, including requests without `Content-Length`. - Use container/cgroup memory limits. Do NOT use `RLIMIT_AS`/`RLIMIT_DATA`. - CVE-2026-109619: - `session.upload_progress.enabled=0`. - On PHP 8.5: `fatal_error_backtraces=0`. - Remove invalid/deprecated per-request settings that emit diagnostics early (hiding them via `error_reporting`/`display_errors`/`@` does not help). - Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and timeouts. - If the site sits behind Cloudflare: confirm the WAF Managed Ruleset is deployed in **block** mode (Free plans get the Managed Free Ruleset automatically). This is defense in depth, not a replacement for patching. ## Step 5: Look for signs of compromise (read-only) Since exploitation started before disclosure, check what you can access: - PHP-FPM/Apache error logs for segfaults, "Allowed memory size exhausted", or worker crashes, especially clustered around unusually large POST/multipart requests. - Recently modified or unexpected files in web roots (webshells), new cron jobs, unexpected processes or outbound connections from PHP users. Report anything suspicious. Do not delete evidence. ## Final report Give me a table: location | how PHP is provided | SAPI | version | status (PATCHED/VULNERABLE/UNKNOWN) | action taken or needed. Then list: - What you changed (files, commands), what still needs my approval, and anything that needs a hosting provider. - Mitigations applied as stopgaps and when they should be removed. - Any compromise indicators found.

articles.title: Q3 2026 Threat Update: Attackers Are Exploiting Vulnerabilities Within 3 Days
articles.context: Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-...
articles.full_text:
Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days.

For security teams already managing growing vulnerability backlogs, this creates a difficult question: How do you reduce exposure when attackers can exploit vulnerabilities before your next patching window?

Rapid7's Q3 2026 research brings together vulnerability intelligence, ransomware activity, APT tracking, and underground forum intelligence to show where attacker activity is concentrated.

The exploitation window has narrowed, big time

Rapid7 tracked 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities this quarter, down 7% from Q2 but still 19% higher than the same period last year.

The number of newly exploited vulnerabilities isn't growing at the same rate as disclosures. The more pressing concern is how quickly attackers exploit the vulnerabilities they choose. On average, exploitation occurred just three days after public disclosure. The report also found that 80% of tracked exploitation occurred within 14 days and 90% within 30 days.

That timeline creates a serious challenge for organizations relying on fixed remediation schedules. It also reinforces the need to distinguish between vulnerabilities that are theoretically severe and those that pose an immediate, exploitable risk.

The report examines the exploitation timeline in greater detail, including the vulnerability characteristics that make certain exposures particularly attractive to attackers.

Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction

Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities tracked, 34 (79%) required no authentication or user interaction.

This provides attackers a potential path into exposed systems, no stolen credentials or malicious content interaction necessary. An internet-facing service with an exploitable vulnerability may require immediate attention, particularly when an attacker can reach it without authenticating.

This makes attack surface visibility and contextual prioritization essential. Security teams need to understand which systems are externally accessible, which vulnerabilities are actively exploited, and whether existing controls can prevent or limit compromise.

A CVSS score alone won’t give you the answers. The report explores the characteristics of exploited vulnerabilities and why understanding reachability is critical to reducing risk.

AI is taking on a more operational role in attacks

In Q3, 8% of the threat reporting tracked by Rapid7 cited AI as an operational component. The research identifies a shift from using AI primarily to help draft content or code toward supporting tactical decisions and execution within attack campaigns.

In the documented cases, human operators continued to select targets and determine objectives, but relied on AI assistance for technique selection, target assessment, and adapting when an attack step failed.

The report also examines how threat actors split malicious objectives across multiple AI sessions to evade provider safeguards. There are serious implications for detection in these findings. AI-enabled attacks also reinforce the value of monitoring and quickly adapting to attacker behavior rather than relying exclusively on known malware signatures or threat actor identities.

The report provides additional context on how AI appeared in tracked campaigns and what defenders should monitor.

The next step: Prioritize exposure before attackers exploit it

Q3's findings reveal a challenge that vulnerability counts alone can’t explain. Attackers exploited 43 newly tracked vulnerabilities this quarter, yet the average exploitation window was just three days. Meanwhile, underground forum monitoring identified 41 posts advertising RDP or network access, demonstrating continued interest in selling access to compromised environments.

Security teams must account for both the vulnerabilities attackers can exploit directly and the access they can obtain through other means.

Start by identifying externally accessible assets and the vulnerabilities affecting them. Prioritize known exploitation, unauthenticated access paths, and systems supporting critical business functions. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, assess compensating controls and detection coverage.

The latest Rapid7 Quarterly Threat Landscape Report brings together vulnerability research, ransomware intelligence, nation-state activity, and dark web monitoring to help security teams understand where threats are concentrated and what to address first. Download and read it now.

articles.title: Sizing the PHP exposure window for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with VirusTotal
articles.context: On October 20, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, fixing two critical vulnerabilities rated CVSS v4
articles.full_text:
On October 20, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, fixing two critical vulnerabilities rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). Hours before the release, technical details leaked publicly. They point to the session.upload_progress feature, which has been part of PHP since 5.4.0 and is enabled by default. The community quickly converged on an interim mitigation: set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini.

That leaves defenders with two questions: how big is the exposed surface, and where should they start? We used Internet Scanning in VirusTotal to answer both.

Note: Official details, affected versions and fixed versions are published by the PHP project with the release. The figures below describe the Internet-facing PHP footprint, not confirmed vulnerable hosts.

Most PHP servers don't say they are PHP

VirusTotal fingerprints roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP (port_service_cpe:php), about 3.8 million of them with at least one port open today. Only around 1.1 million of those announce a version in an HTTP header such as X-Powered-By: PHP/8.3.35.

In other words, roughly four out of five PHP servers hide their version (expose_php = Off, stripped headers, reverse proxies). VirusTotal still identifies them as PHP through other signals: the application on top (WordPress, Laravel, Nextcloud...), PHPSESSID cookies and framework-specific headers. If you only search for a version string, you only see the fraction of the problem that volunteers it.

The version picture: the long tail of end-of-life PHP

Among the servers that do disclose their version, the split is stark:

~272K run a supported branch (8.2 to 8.5), the only branches that receive security fixes from the PHP project.

~758K run an end-of-life branch between 5.4 and 8.1. These branches have session.upload_progress enabled by default and no longer receive security fixes. PHP 7.4 alone accounts for ~187K IPs and PHP 5.4 for ~119K.

~88K run PHP 5.2 or 5.3, which predate session.upload_progress.

Being up to date doesn't buy much time either: about 85K IPs run the exact releases published on September 24 (8.3.35, 8.2.34, 8.4.26 and 8.5.11), the latest available before this fix.

What runs on top, and where

Apache (~2.9M) and nginx (~1.48M) are the web servers most often seen on PHP hosts, followed by LiteSpeed (~90K). On the application side, WordPress dominates with ~538K IPs, followed by Laravel (~141K) and Nextcloud (~107K). Webmail (Roundcube) and database admin panels (phpMyAdmin) add another ~25K high-value targets.

The geography is concentrated: the United States accounts for ~920K PHP hosts with at least one open port, and a handful of cloud and hosting providers (AWS, DigitalOcean, Alibaba, OVHcloud, Hetzner) concentrate a large share. That concentration is good news for remediation: a few providers that push a configuration change or a WAF rule can cover a lot of ground.

Going beyond the web port

PHP rarely travels alone. ~394K PHP hosts also have port 22 open (SSH by default), ~233K port 3306 (MySQL) and ~68K port 3389 (RDP). Those co-exposed services are useful for something else: identifying the exact build behind the web server.

The leaked material references LiteSpeed lsphp82 8.2.34 builds for Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04, and notes that HTTP headers alone don't tell those builds apart. The OpenSSH package on port 22 does. With the bracket syntax, every condition is pinned to its port:

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"PHP/8.2.34" port_service_version[22]:"9.6p1 Ubuntu"

Of the ~3.5K IPs whose banners show both LiteSpeed and PHP 8.2.34, about 500 also have port 22 open. Across all PHP 8.2.34 hosts, the OpenSSH package on port 22 matches Ubuntu 24.04 on 269 IPs, Ubuntu 22.04 on 112 and Debian 12 on 65. For a defender, that is the difference between "patch everything" and "these are the machines that match the leaked target profile, patch them first". Keep in mind that port 22 reveals the host operating system: PHP may still run inside a container built on a different base image.

Adversaries run PHP too

The exposed surface also includes attacker infrastructure. Around 5.7K PHP hosts with at least one open port have five or more detections in VirusTotal, 729 of them disclosing PHP 8.x. One of them is an old acquaintance: the NOX Stealer panel (rebranded as BOMBAY) on 5.175.221[.]206:8443, which we profiled in our Internet Scanning post, runs nginx 1.24.0 with PHP/8.3.33.

What the VirusTotal corpus saw

The leak left traces across VirusTotal. The archive referenced in the write-up was first submitted at 02:29 UTC on October 21, less than 15 minutes after the first submission of the write-up URL. By the time of writing, 21 crowdsourced reports covering the vulnerabilities had been ingested as collections. Following entity:collection collection_type:report "CVE-2026-109618" is the fastest way to keep up with new reporting as it appears.

What to do now

Patch. Upgrade to the fixed release of your branch (8.2, 8.3, 8.4 or 8.5) as soon as it is available on php.net or through your distribution.

Plan the EOL migration. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive security fixes. If you are on 5.4 to 8.1, upgrade the branch or check whether your distribution or vendor ships a backport.

Disable upload progress until you patch. Set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini (or the pool configuration) and reload PHP-FPM, Apache or LSAPI. It only breaks upload progress bars that rely on the feature. Community analysis suggests it may not cover every vector, so treat it as a stopgap, not a fix.

Filter multipart at the edge. Where an application doesn't need file uploads, block or inspect multipart/form-data requests before they reach PHP. Cloudflare shipped emergency rules to its Managed and Free rulesets on October 21, and its CTO stated that they cover known payloads, while stressing that only updating PHP fully protects a site.

Make sure the WAF can't be bypassed. Edge rules only help if the origin is not directly reachable. Search your own ranges in VirusTotal (for example, entity:ip port_service_cpe:php asn:<your ASN>) to find origins that expose PHP directly to the Internet.

Don't rely on hiding the version. expose_php = Off hides the header, not the vulnerability.

Note: All counts in this post were taken on October 21, 2026. For large result sets VirusTotal returns estimated totals that vary between runs, so we report the median of seven runs, rounded. Port modifiers without a port in brackets match per IP, not per port: port_service_cpe:php port_status:open means PHP was fingerprinted on the IP and at least one of its ports is open.

articles.title: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Leaked Ahead of Scheduled Security Patches
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Two vulnerabilities that could affect the servers underlying many websites have been disclosed ahead of the planned security patches, leading major cybersecurity authorities to urge users to prepare for remediation.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ were scheduled to be disclosed on October 21 at 2pm GMT.

However, a user named ‘petecooper’ published a post on the Hacker News forum on October 20 revealing the vulnerabilities’ CVE identifiers, which were supposed to be kept secret until the patches are available.

The post, now deleted, claimed that two maximum-severity (CVSS rating of 10.0) PHP remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities would be disclosed on October 22.

It also said that both vulnerabilities affected PHP versions dating back to PHP 5 and that exploiting them could allow remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data.

These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

Following the petecooper post, WatchTowr confirmed that CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were scheduled to be disclosed later.

The disclosure was also scheduled to happen alongside the PHP security team releasing patches for both vulnerabilities.

Leaking information on critical vulnerabilities and some of their characteristics, such as the range of affected versions, ahead of an available patch can lead malicious actors to exploit them, for instance using reverse engineering techniques.

CERT-EU Urges PHP Users to Prepare for Patching

In a security bulletin, published on October 21, the PHP security team confirmed it was working on patches, which were scheduled to be released at 2pm GMT on October 21 – not on October 22 as claimed by the Hacker News forum user.

“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild,” they added.

In addition, the PHP team allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.2 rather than the maximum-severity score suggested by the individual sharing the leak.

Several cybersecurity authorities, including the Computer Emergency Response Team of the EU (CERT-EU) and th UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) also released emergency advisories, warning of upcoming patches for the two vulnerabilities.

These authorities advised organizations to prepare for immediate patching of affected assets.

“Where immediate patching is not feasible, organizations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available,” CERT-EU added.

Inferring from PHP’s pre-release builds, Kevin Beaumont, an independent security researcher, said on Mastodon that fixed versions will likely be the following:

8.5.12

8.4.27

8.3.36

8.2.35

Update 4pm BST: The PHP security team has now published a security advisory for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 which can be found here.
