articles.full_text: Title: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform 10.7.5- JSP command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform (CTP) from Parasoft (United States), a closed-source commercial continuous-testing product bundling environment management, service virtualisation and test-data management, distributes an em web application running on Tomcat 10.1.57 with the Jasper JSP engine and Java 17 inside the vendor's own container image, and contains three composing first-party defects that yield unauthenticated remote code execution in two HTTP requests: an unfiltered ObjectInputStream over an uploaded backup archive (CWE-502, primary), a licensing filter that decides whether to run at all by testing the raw un-normalised request URI (CWE-436, primary and co-equal, with CWE-863 as its authorisation consequence), and a remember-me authentication service that hands an anonymous request an authenticated administrator principal when no external security provider has been configured (CWE-287, enabling gate). Defect one, the licensing filter: EMLicenseFilter is 175 lines and reads request.getRequestURI() raw at line 165, testing it at line 166 against exemption clauses including endsWith("about"), endsWith("welcome"), endsWith("forgot"), endsWith("notlicensed"), contains("/resources/") and contains("/images/"), none anchored by a separator or segment boundary, with a further branch at lines 167 to 171 that reassigns the entire exemption set rather than accumulating into it when the request accepts JSON. That test has exactly one consumer in the class, shouldNotFilter() at line 47 calling isLicenseRequired() at line 48, so a matching URI suppresses the whole doFilterInternal() body rather than weakening one decision, taking with it the /tdm/api/v guard at line 99 and the unlicensed-instance redirect to /em/license at line 118. Because a servlet container strips semicolon-delimited path parameters from each segment before servlet mapping, filter and router disagree about the identity of one request, and a target of /em/database/restore;welcome is exempted by the filter while still being routed to the restore handler. Defect two, the sink: com.parasoft.ctp.core.database.backup.AbstractDatabaseBackup, a class of 518 lines and 19,851 bytes, wraps the uploaded database.ser zip member at line 111 with new ObjectInputStream(in), reads an int at line 112 and calls readObject() at line 117 casting the result to TableMetadata, nine lines above the getConnection() call at line 126, so the cast constrains nothing (the gadget executes during the call and the ClassCastException is thrown afterwards) and no database needs to exist, be reachable or accept the supplied parameters for the payload already to have run. The caller is the web-layer controller EMDatabaseController, 1359 lines, whose restore handler at lines 707 and 708 takes a StandardMultipartHttpServletRequest and hard-compares zip member names against the literals "version.txt" at line 725 and "database.ser" at line 733, a shape check that says nothing about content. The absence of a filter is a corpus-wide artefact measurement rather than an inference: ObjectInputStream appears in 68 files with 149 occurrences in the core tree and in 3 files in the web layer, readObject appears in 81 files, and ObjectInputFilter appears in 0 files, jdk.serialFilter in 0 files and serialFilter in 0 files, three zeros across a class name, a system property and its short alias against a positive control of 81 files containing readObject. Two sibling readObject() calls on the same class of untrusted stream sit at lines 323 and 435 of the same class, in a row-draining and a row-binding routine, read from source and not detonated, named so a fix covers the class rather than the call site. Defect three, the fail-open gate: EMRememberMeServices is 483 lines and, at line 140 to 142, returns null when an Authorization header is present, then at line 146 fetches PSTSecServiceClient.getInstance() and at line 148, when that client is null, returns createAuthenticationToken("admin", "admin", EmUserInfo.Role.ADMIN, request), which registers new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN") inside a Spring Security User whose authenticated flag is true, so the resulting principal is a genuinely authenticated administrator rather than the container's anonymous principal and satisfies the authenticated() matcher that CTPSecurityWebConfig line 283 demands for /database. Neither hop is an unprotected route, /database being explicitly matched to authenticated() and the images allow-list being /images/welcome/* rather than a widened glob, so the accurate description is not that the endpoints are unauthenticated but that the product mints an administrative principal for an anonymous request. CsrfSecurityRequestMatcher is a 28-line class whose anchored exemption alternation at line 19 includes /database, so the state-changing POST needs no CSRF token. The write primitive is a HashSet forcing hashCode() on a TiedMapEntry wrapping a LazyMap whose factory is a ConstantTransformer holding attacker bytes and whose decorated map is an aspectjweaver SimpleCache$StoreableCachingMap with an absolute folder field, reaching writeToPath(folder + File.separator + key, bytes). That class was read at the bytecode level for four facts: folder is declared private final String, is not transient, and the class declares no readObject of its own, so it is populated by the inherited HashMap.readObject path through defaultReadObject and both writer routines read it with an explicit getfield that the compiler has not inlined; writeToPath is getfield folder, StringBuilder, separator, key, store, with no forced extension appended to the key, an assumption that had to be disproved at the bytecode level because it would have removed any execution surface, and the value passes a checkcast to a byte array so the content is any bytes at all; validation is absent in every form, with zero occurrences of File.getName(), Path.normalize(), getCanonicalPath(), startsWith(), a regular expression or a length truncation in that write path, keys carrying slashes or relative traversals both working, and an absolute destination reachable because concatenation with an empty folder yields a leading double separator that POSIX treats as a valid absolute path; and the gadget does not fire on deserialization alone, because HashMap.readObject reconstitutes entries through putVal, which is package-private, final and not overridden, so it bypasses the overridden put containing the write, which is why the TiedMapEntry to LazyMap to Map.put prefix is needed to force a virtual dispatch. The only content constraint anywhere is that the bytes must not equal the four-byte sentinel IDEM, and the published carrier sets storingTimer to Integer.MAX_VALUE to suppress the index file the caching map would otherwise write alongside the payload. The execution sink is the product's own container configuration: conf/web.xml declares the Jasper jsp servlet and its mapping at lines 274-275 and 448-450, and webapps/em/images/ is inside the deployed web application root the mapping covers, writable by uid 1000 as drwxrwxr-x parasoft root, and exempt from the licensing filter by the contains("/images/") clause at line 166, so fetching the written page needs no bypass of its own and the product compiles it into work/Catalina/localhost/em/org/apache/jsp/images/<stem>_jsp.java and .class. A second independent execution sink was also detonated and is recorded so a fix removing JSP compilation does not close half the problem: WEB-INF/classes/com/parasoft/rest/api/core/docs/templates/ is the FreeMarker template root, its prefix from an init-param in webapps/em/WEB-INF/web.xml at lines 206-207 with FreeMarker 2.3.34 through jersey-mvc-freemarker 3.1.12, and because freemarker.template.utility.Execute is on no restriction list the new() built-in is usable, a template performing 7*119 returning 200 with a 4-byte body containing 833 and a template invoking Execute with id returning 200 with a 61-byte body containing the full identity string. Measured chain: one anonymous multipart POST to the restore path carrying a semicolon-welcome suffix, with no cookie, no Authorization header and no CSRF token, returning HTTP 500 with the product's own 119-byte "An error occurred while applying changes to the database configuration" message, which is the success signature rather than a failure because readObject() precedes getConnection(); the product log then carried one occurrence per run of a stack trace naming AbstractDatabaseBackup.restore(AbstractDatabaseBackup.java:114) with "class java.util.HashSet cannot be cast to class ...TableMetadata" and a java.lang.ClassCastException, counted at 2, then 4, then 6 across runs, and distinguishable from a malformed payload which produces a ClassNotFoundException instead. One anonymous GET of the written page then returned 200 with a 538-byte body containing a per-run marker with a 12-hex nonce, JSP_EVAL=42 from server-side evaluation of the expression 6*7, proving evaluation rather than source echo, SIZE_SELF=1372 agreeing with the length of the payload the client built, which proves byte-exact content control, the identity string uid=1000(parasoft) gid=1000(parasoft) groups=1000(parasoft), an ls line showing the page owned by the product's own service account, a /proc/1/status line reporting Uid: 1000 1000 1000 1000, and two /etc/passwd lines read by the product process. Two end-to-end detonations of the two-hop chain are recorded as successful, and two intermediate iterations failed inside the client script rather than against the product. No vendor-supplied credential, no licence installation or forgery, no outbound connection, no DNS or RMI callback, no cross-version payload adaptation, no memory corruption and no privilege escalation is involved: the upstream libraries carrying the gadget are carriers and not the root cause, executing a jsp page is the product's own configuration, and the landing identity is the product's unprivileged service account, uid=1000(parasoft), confirmed three ways (id inside the executed page, the written file's ownership and mode, and the product process's own /proc/1/status read from inside the container rather than through a container runtime which would report root regardless), with root not reached and not claimed. CVSS: 9.8 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, recomputed from the vector with the CVSS 3.1 base formula rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - ((1 - 0.56) x (1 - 0.56) x (1 - 0.56)) = 0.914816; Impact for Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 (AV:N) x 0.77 (AC:L) x 0.85 (PR:N) x 0.85 (UI:N) = 3.887043; base = min(5.873119 + 3.887043, 10) = 9.760161; rounded up to the nearest tenth = 9.8. AV:N because the chain is two ordinary HTTP requests to TCP listeners the product serves itself over HTTP 8080 and HTTPS 8443, both accepting connections from outside the container, with no shipped reverse proxy, WAF or management-plane separation in front of em, and the loopback publication of the test port being the research testbed's containment rather than a product restriction. AC:L because there is no timing window to win (this is the steady factory state, not a first-run race), no host-specific reconnaissance, no memory-layout condition, no database reachability requirement (the readObject at line 117 runs before getConnection at line 126), no outbound callback and no cryptographic work; the only condition is a configuration state the vendor's own image is in when no external security provider has been configured. PR:N because no credential belonging to anybody is supplied or consumed, the authenticated subject being manufactured by the product itself for an anonymous request. UI:N because no administrator action, browser session, induced click or human upload step exists anywhere in the chain. C:H, I:H and A:H describe compromise of the product, its managed data and its availability, and do not depend on the landing identity being privileged, nor rise if a deployment runs the platform as root, which was not measured. Scope Unchanged, with Scope Changed considered and rejected on an argument stated here so the call cannot be read as a scoring maneuver: the rejected S:C variant of the same metrics, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H, computes to 10.0 from ISS 0.914816, Impact for Scope Changed 6.128026, Exploitability 3.887043 and 1.08 times their sum capped at the maximum, so the reading rejected here is the higher one and rejecting it lowers the published number from 10.0 to 9.8. It is not two authorities because the filter, the deserialising controller, the security service, the web application root and the JSP mapping all belong to one deployed application in one JVM, the platform being a single product with several routers rather than several products; because executing a page inside its own web application root is the documented intended behaviour of the shipped container configuration, so the transition from write to execution crosses no boundary the product defines; and because the executed code carries the product process's own uid in that process's own filesystem view, entering no other account, machine or security domain. Three labelled conditional readings accompany the published score and none replaces it. Conditional A, external security provider configured and the attacker holding any valid account, is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.8 High (Exploitability 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.62 x 0.85 = 2.835255, Impact 5.873119, base 8.708373 rounded up), since the security matcher for the restore path is authenticated() rather than hasRole("ADMIN") so low privileges suffice while the licensing gate is still bypassed and the sink still unfiltered; this deployment state was not detonated, and it is the reading an operator of a configured deployment should work from because it depends on no unverified capability. Conditional B, external security provider configured with the subject supplied by an offline-forged session cookie, is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 9.8 Critical, arithmetically identical to the published score, and is a static and structural inference that was never verified: the platform signs its remember-me cookie PST_LT_FEATURES_INFORMATION, whose signed plaintext takes the form user:expiry::localAddr:"rememberMeAuthenticated", with a key that is a compile-time string literal and a signature scheme, bcrypt, that carries no secret, so anyone holding the shipped class can compute a cookie offline, and forgery was exercised only in the unconfigured state where it buys nothing, while the combination of a configured deployment driven end to end with a forged subject has no run behind it at all; building a fake security provider to test it was deliberately abandoned because installing one would have manufactured the condition being measured. Conditional B is published so an operator of a configured deployment knows which exposure to check and so the vendor knows which mechanism to replace, never as a demonstrated capability and never as the headline score, and the published PR:N rests on the measured fail-open behaviour of the untouched image rather than on any forgery. Conditional C, listeners reachable only from a management network, is CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.8 High (Exploitability 8.22 x 0.62 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 2.835255, Impact 5.873119, base 8.708373), conditional on a deployment change that was not tested and downward rather than upward, so an operator who hardens the network position can see that it is worth one point of severity and fixes nothing else. No version-range claim is made: only CTP 10.7.5-SNAPSHOT was executed, obtained through the vendor's mutable parasoft/ctp:latest tag (image id prefix f99f7210fc67, from a saved copy of 997,805,056 bytes with md5 47946c7d1e7d99a00d6c90f4ae675f90), and in the Maven convention the product's own build system uses a -SNAPSHOT version marks an in-progress development line rather than an immutable released artefact, so a mutable tag cannot be mapped onto a released version range with the confidence a public affected-version list requires; the claim is that this build is affected and that any other build shipping the same AbstractDatabaseBackup and EMLicenseFilter source carries the same construction. CWE classification: CWE-502 primary and CWE-436 co-equal for the two root causes, CWE-863 and CWE-287 contributing for the authorisation and authentication gates, with CWE-321 and CWE-347 reported separately for the literal session-cookie signing key and its keyless signature scheme and CWE-22 reported separately for a sibling file-path primitive that is not part of this chain, none of the contributing items raising any metric of the published vector, and no upstream component blamed since the gadget libraries are carriers and the jsp execution is the product's own container configuration. Impact: unauthenticated remote code execution inside the product process from two ordinary HTTP requests, on a platform whose documented entry point for the same function is an administrator menu behind authentication and a valid licence. Before any command runs, the chain carries an arbitrary-path arbitrary-content file write as a primitive in its own right, the folder field, the map key (observed to accept both nested and relative-traversal forms) and the content byte array all living inside the serialized stream, with the only content restriction being that the bytes must not equal the four-byte IDEM sentinel. Execution as uid 1000 inside the product's JVM puts in scope the product tree under /usr/local/parasoft/ctp including the deployed em application (writable, which is how the page was created), the container's own conf/ directory holding server.xml and web.xml, and the Jasper work directory; the platform's HSQLDB database files, whose location and database user the bypassed configuration endpoint disclosed to an anonymous caller on its own, and through them every environment definition, system definition, virtual-service definition and test-data-management record the platform manages plus whatever credentials or connection strings it stores on behalf of the systems it virtualises; anything else on the host filesystem readable by uid 1000, measured concretely by reading /etc/passwd; and the product's own licence and security state, since arbitrary in-process code can rewrite configuration files and restart the application's view of them, which is why the unlicensed and unconfigured conditions an operator might rely on as compensating controls are not durable ones. There is no window: this is not a first-run race, a setup-mode condition or a state that closes when an administrator first logs in, the fail-open branch applying for as long as the external provider is unconfigured, the licensing bypass for as long as the filter reads raw URIs, and the sink unconditionally, and the chain was fired repeatedly against one instance with no state consumed in between. The cost to an attacker is one crafted multipart POST and one GET with no reconnaissance, no credential acquisition, no timing precision, no outbound infrastructure and no target-specific adaptation. Persistence that survives naive cleanup was measured rather than argued: after the dropped page and both of its Jasper compilation artefacts were deleted, the same URL still returned 200 with a body two bytes shorter than the first response, precisely because the ls command inside it could no longer find the file it was listing, the compiled servlet instance still being loaded in the JVM. An operator who deletes the file and the compiled class has therefore not removed the web shell; only a context reload or a JVM and container restart does. Also within reach structurally rather than by demonstration is the ability to overwrite the deployed application's own pages or class files, converting a single write into persistence surviving a restart, which was not performed and is flagged as an unexercised consequence of a proven primitive rather than as a measurement. Detection is weak by construction: hop 1 is a documented administrative function returning an ordinary 500 with the product's own configuration-error message, and hop 2 is an anonymous GET for a file under a static-assets path, so the strongest indicators are a request target containing a semicolon, a non-image file appearing under the deployed images directory, a compiled jsp stem under the Jasper work directory that the product does not ship, and the product log line pairing the restore frame with a cast exception naming a JDK collection class where backup metadata was expected. One caution for status-based monitoring: the licensing filter flushes its response output stream at line 113 before calling setStatus(403) at line 115, so licence refusals surface as HTTP 200 with a JSON body carrying status 403, and any rule keyed on HTTP status for licence failures will not fire at all. Verification boundary: live black-box HTTP verification against a running instance started from the unmodified vendor image in an isolated container sandbox with no setup step performed, plus source-level reading of the decompiled first-party classes and of the shipped conf/web.xml and webapps/em/WEB-INF/web.xml; it is not an emulation and not a protocol replica. The instance state was factory, unlicensed and with no external security provider configured, and that state was confirmed rather than assumed from a shipped-code fact about the pristine image and not a property of anything the researchers configured: requesting the provider-configuration endpoint at /em/pstsecconfig with an Accept header naming application/json returned 404 with a zero-length body, matching the controller's own getActiveConfig()==null branch, and it reproduced on two instances so it is not an artefact of one container. The client was Python 3.11.6 using only the standard library, run by an ordinary unprivileged user, and no packet left the sandbox at any point because the chain requires no outbound connectivity and none was available to it. Nothing was driven from a separate network host: the client ran on the same sandbox host as the container, reaching it through a published loopback port, so reachability from a second machine over a routed network is argued from the shipped listener topology (the container accepts connections on its HTTP and HTTPS ports from outside itself and the product ships no front-end proxy or filter of its own) and not demonstrated between two hosts, while every other claim in the chain, the bypass, the principal, the write, the execution, the identity and the persistence of the compiled servlet, was measured over real HTTP against a real product process. Only the factory configuration state was detonated; a deployment with the external security provider configured was not tested end to end and is scored as a conditional reading. Only one build was executed, with no older release, no newer release, no Windows variant and no differently configured instance fired at, so no cross-release and no cross-platform claim is published. Two legs are labelled inference and never presented as measurement: the forged session cookie in a configured deployment, and the JavaScript-engine evaluation path, whose capability layer was measured in isolation while its two reachability preconditions were never satisfied, so no claim about it appears in the rated chain or the impact section. Read from source but not separately detonated were the two sibling readObject() sites at lines 323 and 435 and the hardening of the other upload and zip-handling paths examined and ruled out; measured on shipped artefacts rather than over the network were the corpus-wide absence of any deserialization filter, the JVM's own --add-opens list read from its process command line, the absence of JDBC drivers among 238 jars, and the bytecode-level facts about the caching map's write path from single-class disassembly rather than a whole-library dump. Six negative controls were exercised, each removing a specific alternative explanation: hop 1 without the semicolon suffix returned 302 with Location /em/license; hop 1 with the backup part omitted returned 400 with 59 bytes; hop 2 against a never-written file in the same directory returned 404 with 762 bytes and the container's own "JSP file not found" page carrying an Apache Tomcat/10.1.57 footer, the run marker appearing once in the executed body and zero times here; the licensing-bypass read with the suffix but no semicolon returned 404 with 792 bytes, excluding a literal-suffix match; the identity endpoint with Authorization: Bearer garbage returned 401 with a zero-length body, showing the fail-open branch is specific to requests presenting no credential at all so the behaviour is not that authentication is off but that an absent credential is more trusted than a wrong one; and the /em/tdm/api/v2/servers resource without the bypass returned 200 with a 90-byte unlicensed body, excluding the possibility that the bypass variant's well-formed XML came from the fixed unlicensed path. Everything the client reported was re-verified from the target side rather than trusted from the script's output: the images directory's file count went 39 before the run, 40 immediately after and back to 39 after self-deletion, a single-file difference matching a single payload; the Jasper residue under work/ after cleanup was zero entries; a filesystem search for the run's marker leaf name under the product tree and under /tmp returned zero results; and the container was destroyed afterwards with its published ports confirmed free, leaving only a read-only reference instance running. Two classical gadget families were established dead on this target from the product's own process rather than from a guess, its JVM's --add-opens list covering java.base/java.lang, java.lang.reflect, java.io, java.util and java.util.concurrent plus java.rmi/sun.rmi.transport with no SecurityManager installed: a comparator-driven PriorityQueue chain with a bean comparator targeting TemplatesImpl was deserialized and did fire, the stack showing PriorityQueue.readObject:801 into heapify:734 into BeanComparator.compare:142, and was then stopped by the module system because java.xml does not export com.sun.org.apache.xalan.internal.xsltc.trax; and a JdbcRowSetImpl chain using autoCommit as the trigger with an rmi URL was stopped the same way, java.sql.rowset not exporting com.sun.rowset, confirmed independently by a native listener on the sandbox host receiving no inbound connection during a 25-second window. No JDBC driver of the commonly abused families is present either, a survey of all 238 jars finding no PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, Derby or H2 driver, so the JDBC-connection style of gadget has nothing to connect with, the platform talking to HSQLDB in-process, which is not the same surface; on a modern JDK with default module boundaries the usable gadget set is whatever lives entirely in the unnamed module, which is why the published chain has the shape it does. Classic zip-slip is closed in the live extraction helper whose entry-name checks are hardened, a second older zip utility in the tree has zero callers and is dead code, and the import path used by restore reads members into an in-memory map rather than extracting them to disk; the restore handler's own member selection is a hard comparison against two literals so no alternative member name can be smuggled in to change which bytes reach the stream. A file-API variant taking an extension parameter appeared to allow a traversal into a jsp suffix and is closed by two independent walls, the extension helper taking everything after the last dot so traversal sequences are discarded and the manager underneath using File.createTempFile so the JDK's own temporary-file machinery rejects a suffix containing a separator, the product even echoing back its own failure message containing the attempted suffix. The upload, temp and task endpoints under /em/tdm/api/ have no mounted handler at all although the generated WADL advertises paths that do not exist, which is a documentation defect and a trap for anyone mapping this surface from the WADL alone. The licensing bypass is not a skeleton key, which was measured rather than assumed: handlers performing their own licensing check are unaffected, the coverage-agent endpoints reading the license manager directly and continuing to return 403 with a 90-byte unlicensed body across all seventeen of their mappings even with the bypass applied, and a server-resource feature gate continuing to return 403 with a 94-byte body, so what the bypass unlocks is only what whose enforcement lives in the filter, being the whole /em/database subtree and the entire /em/tdm/api/v tree. Several additional first-party defects were measured on the same product and reported to the vendor separately with none folded into the published vector: the generic licence-gate bypass on its own, an authorisation bypass rather than an execution; the fail-open remember-me branch and an authentication provider that does not verify the submitted password at all, at PSTAuthenticationProvider.java:144, privilege granting rather than execution; the offline-forgeable session cookie with its literal signing key and keyless signature scheme, demonstrated only where redundant and not verified where it would matter; anonymous whole-database download and anonymous backup creation through both /em/api/v2/database/backups and /em/api/v3/database/backups, because the 213-line resource class backing them contains zero occurrences of checkLicensing() while the filter's exemption clause covers everything under /em/api/, the v2 variant being an undocumented twin of v3 that the shipped OpenAPI description does not cover and that was found by reading the routing table; anonymous arbitrary file read and anonymous arbitrary file delete through a temp-file handler building new File(tempDir, fileID) by pure concatenation from a query parameter with no base-name extraction or canonicalisation, measured with a passwd read returning the first line verbatim in a 47-byte body and with a DELETE that really removed a prepared file, being CWE-22 from the same unvalidated-concatenation family and not an execution; anonymous creation of database files in an arbitrary directory from a JSON connection URL passed verbatim into a JDBC file URL, measured as six new files appearing in a chosen directory, with the directory and base name attacker-controlled while the extension is fixed by the engine and the content is not, so it reaches no execution surface; twenty-eight hardcoded secret values of which seventeen participate in security decisions, being a shipped TLS keystore whose store password is the industry default changeit and appears in plaintext in server.xml at lines 110-112 (so every installation that did not replace the keystore shares one TLS key pair, checked once by listing the keystore with the documented password and succeeding on the first attempt with no brute-forcing), three hardcoded AES-128 keys in AES128Cipher.java at lines 41 to 43 that use the key as the IV removing the semantic-security benefit of an IV entirely, a literal Blowfish argument with iteration count 5 in NativeBlowfish.cc at line 36 used by the licensing subsystem to decode licence feature data, and a salt present as a string literal rather than generated material; a transactional-commit defect in which a malformed JSON body can leave orphaned rows because the checked exception thrown by the JSON library does not mark the surrounding transaction for rollback; and an inconsistent upload guard family, being header validation applied to only two of the seventeen files that set a content-disposition header, a zip validator testing only the extension, and a routine named canonicalize that performs a UTF-8 round trip rather than any path canonicalisation while being relied on as a path guard. The structural fact behind the unevenness is that the em application has four independent routing stacks behind one set of hand-written gates, / to the Spring DispatcherServlet, /api/* to a Jersey RestServletContainer, /tdm/api/* to TDMApiServletContainer and /services/* to CXF, with ten star-path servlet filters in conf/web.xml, so enforcement is not centralised and licence enforcement lives in two places at once, the filter and per-controller calls to checkLicensing(), of which 97 occurrences appear across 17 files against 31 routed Jersey resource classes, meaning 54.8 percent of routed resource classes perform any licensing check at all. Exactly one payload shape was executed for the published chain, a command capture plus a self-listing and a passwd read, and the dropped page deleted itself and its two Jasper compilation artefacts before the forensic refetch; nothing destructive was performed beyond the single written page, no product file other than that page was modified or deleted, and the container was destroyed afterwards. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/parasoft-ctp-unfiltered-deserialization-license-gate-fail-open-jsp-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/parasoft/ctp-10.7.5/unfiltered-deserialization-license-gate-fail-open-jsp-rce/exploit/parasoft_ctp_unfiltered_deserialization_license_gate_fail_open_jsp_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target address. It takes the target URL and the command either as positionals or as -t and -c, defaulting the command to id, and exposes every coordinate of the chain as an argument rather than a constant: --folder for the landing directory, defaulting to the product's own deployed images directory; --leaf for the page name, defaulting to a per-run nonce-based name; --json for the connection parameters, whose default names a loopback address on port 1 so the post-deserialization database attempt fails immediately and predictably; --version for the content of the version.txt zip member, defaulting to 93; --web-prefix for the application context path, defaulting to /em; --catalina-base and --work-dir for the container layout; --restore-path for the hop-1 target, defaulting to the database restore mapping carrying the semicolon suffix; --images-path for the hop-2 directory; --timeout, --retries and --retry-delay for request behaviour; --keep so the dropped page does not delete itself; --no-hop3 to skip the post-delete forensic refetch that establishes the servlet is still loaded; -k or --insecure for a self-signed certificate on the https scheme; --dump-payload to write the generated carrier to a path; and --selftest, which sends nothing at all. The self-test encodes the offline discipline: it rebuilds the carrier skeleton using the original values of its three patch regions and asserts byte identity with the archived 1,178-byte carrier whose md5 is 6099d3f5fd36e28d8934c2e4e6c95da6, then rebuilds with new values and asserts that the new folder, leaf and content appear verbatim, which is what makes the claim that this generator produces the stream proven against the product checkable by a reader with no target to shoot at. The carrier is a 1,178-byte stream containing 19 handles, all consumed, treated as an immutable skeleton with three marked patch regions, the leaf name, the content byte array length-prefixed and raw, and the folder path, leaving every class descriptor, serialVersionUID, field order and handle back-reference byte-for-byte untouched. The written page carries the operator's command base64-encoded and decoded with java.util.Base64 at request time so no quoting conflict can arise between the page source, the Java string literal and the shell, invokes it through ProcessBuilder with /bin/sh -c and the error stream redirected into the output stream with LC_ALL and LANG pinned to C so id and ls output is machine-readable, and prints a per-run marker, a server-evaluated arithmetic expression distinguishing evaluation from source echo, its own absolute path and size, the identity output, the delimited command output and, unless asked not to, the result of deleting itself and both Jasper compilation artefacts before the forensic refetch. The script refuses to fire at all if the target URL has no scheme, no host, a non-rooted path or a doubled slash in the path; that pre-flight validator exists because two of the four iterations of the client failed for reasons unrelated to the target, one producing a URL with no slash between context and path and raising a nonnumeric-port error before a packet was sent, and one producing a doubled slash that the container answered with 404 while its unit test asserted only that the URL was parseable, which it was, and so guarded the wrong property. The exploit installs, forges, modifies or clears no licence, uses no MITM, DNS hijacking, TLS interception, outbound connection or callback, attempts no privilege escalation and claims no root, does not persist through any startup mechanism or second page or account creation, and its cleanup report is a forensic finding rather than a guarantee, since deleting the dropped page and its compiled artefacts does not unload the servlet from a running JVM. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

articles.full_text: Title: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce CVE: pending Description: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E, version v2.2.44, the industrial wireless radio from ProSoft Technology, Inc. (United States) whose research designation is RLX-IH 24E, installs and executes code submitted over its management interface without performing any signature, hash or CRC check on it. The appliance is a closed-source embedded device and an OEM build of the MicroHard Systems IPx21 platform on the MHX-910 board design: an Intel IXP425 XScale processor, ARM big-endian, Linux 2.4.24-uc0, with static management pages under /usr/web and 57 ARM big-endian CGI programs under /usr/lib/cgi-bin/ served by boa over HTTP and boa_ssl over HTTPS. The classification is CWE-494, download of code without integrity check, with CWE-345 and CWE-347 co-equal, because the only authenticity check in the path is a non-cryptographic string equality and no signature is verified anywhere. CWE-434, CWE-73, CWE-250 and CWE-269 contribute. It is explicitly not CWE-78 and a command-injection remediation would not fix it: the shared platform helper SubProgram_Start at offset 0xbd5c splits its argument string on spaces with strtok into at most eight tokens and then calls vfork and execvp directly, so no shell is ever invoked and shell metacharacters are inert here. The upload hop is in usr/lib/cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi, routine HandleSubmit at offset 0x8d1c, with its formatting string at rodata offset 0x2b1c. On the file1 part of a multipart/form-data POST to /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi it calls cgiFormFileName and cgiFormTempFileName, builds the move argument with sprintf(buf, "%s /upgrade/upgrade/%s", tempfile, origfilename), runs SubProgram_Start("/bin/mv", buf), which must succeed, and then runs SubProgram_Start("/sbin/upgrade", origfilename). The client-supplied original filename is therefore used unmodified twice, once as the destination of the move and once as the installer's only argument, which makes the file extension and so the installer branch entirely the requester's choice. The handler applies no extension whitelist, no digest comparison and no path canonicalisation. The install hop is /sbin/upgrade, a short POSIX shell script shipped in the same package, running with the CGI's own privileges, which are root. It dispatches on ${FILE##*.} and its three consequential branches are: ".pkg", which tests gzip stream integrity with gunzip -t, unpacks with tar -xf into a staging tree, compares the appliance's PRODUCT_NAME read from /etc/MHX_CONFIG against a LOCK_NAME read from a lockfile inside the package itself, prints "Match image." on equality, executes ./pre, applies the inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C /, executes ./post, prints "Upgrade Successful" and then reboots unconditionally; ".passwd", which copies the upload over both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original; and ".factory", which copies the upload over /etc/db1, the configuration store holding the management interface's own transport flags, accounts and radio behaviour. The equality test is the only gate before code execution and both of its operands are available to the requester: the expected value is the compile-time platform constant IPx21PROSOFT recoverable by reading the shipped firmware once, and the asserted value is carried inside the package being installed. A package whose identity is validated against data carried inside that same package cannot be a source of assurance about it. The defect is the absence of an authenticity step, not a weak one, and strengthening the compatibility check would change nothing while both operands come from the same side. Impact: root command execution on the appliance from a single multipart/form-data POST followed by the product's own documented install sequence, with requester-authored shell code running both before and after an unconstrained archive extraction into the root of the filesystem. Attacker code reading the pre-execution state, an arbitrary rootfs write through the inner archive whose entry names are constrained in no way, and attacker code running post-write are all present in one request. The .passwd branch reaches the same privilege ceiling without executing anything, replacing both the live account database and its backup copy so that the device's own recovery path restores the modified database rather than the shipped one; since the factory admin entry is uid 0 with the restricted shell /bin/txtUI, an added uid-0 entry with /bin/sh converts an administratively restricted login into a general root shell at the next interactive login. The .factory branch lets a requester rewrite the device's security configuration, widening or narrowing the exposure of the surface they arrived through and surviving a later reconfiguration by the operator. Persistence is native to the product rather than improvised, because the install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. Availability is controlled at will, both by that reboot and by installing content that stops the device serving traffic, which for a radio carrying traffic between a process network and its field instruments is also a position on the path that traffic takes. Detection is weak by construction: every step is documented product behaviour, the request is an ordinary firmware upload, the response is the vendor's own success page, and a legitimate upgrade prints exactly the same "Match image." and "Upgrade Successful", so the usable indicators are post-hoc and filesystem-level, namely an installed package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair corresponds to no release the operator obtained, an unexpected file under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid-0 account whose shell is not the vendor's restricted interface. Verification boundary, stated exactly because it is narrower than the headline suggests, and because the classification above depends on it. The installer half of the chain was measured and the upload half was not. No HTTP request was ever issued at this product and no physical appliance was used at any point, so nothing here is an exploit run against a live device and it is not presented as one. What was executed is the firmware's own /sbin/upgrade, byte-for-byte unmodified, inside an isolated chroot sandbox built on a copy of the upgrade package's own root filesystem. A crafted .pkg printed "Match image." then "Upgrade Successful" and exited 0; the pre script left a marker proving it executed and wrote PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0 into a second marker, the post script left its own marker, and the inner archive applied an entry to the root of the filesystem. The uid marker is the load-bearing evidence: the payload wrote that value at runtime rather than having it read from a configuration file, so it is the executing identity and not an inference about it. The recorded landing identity is uid=0(root). A .passwd run replaced both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original with the uploaded text, proven by a pre-run digest of the pre-seeded database that no longer matched afterwards and by a marker line present in both copies. A negative control was run to establish that none of this came from the harness: a structurally identical package, same outer tar layout, same metadata files, same inner archive, same marker-writing scripts, with exactly one deliberate difference, LOCK_NAME=WRONGPRODUCT, was refused with "This unit doesn't support the image." and produced no markers anywhere. That control also isolates the product-string comparison as the single cause of refusal and makes the positive and negative runs mutually exclusive. Four substitutions existed in the harness and none in the code under test: an x86 busybox build supplied /bin/sh, tar, gunzip, mv and cp because the firmware's own copies are ARM big-endian and the host is not; a stub replaced the platform mhx utility; /etc/MHX_CONFIG was populated with the product identity the firmware itself ships; and /etc/passwd was pre-seeded with three factory-style entries for comparison. Two transcript lines, "logger: not found" and "mhx: not found", are absent helpers in the sandbox PATH and are not product behaviour. The run count is one positive .pkg run, one positive .passwd run and one negative control, in one sandbox on one host, each effect observed once, never repeated across sandbox builds and never performed on hardware. Not measured, and not claimed: the web server and its access control, because /bin/boa lives in the device base flash and is not contained in the system upgrade package, so the access control gating this CGI could be neither proved nor disproved from the artefacts available; the CGI binaries and the firmware's ARM helpers, for the architecture reason; the closing reboot, since the sandbox is a directory tree with no init, though the path up to it was observed; any privilege escalation, the chain starting from the administrative identity the product's own account database already grants uid 0; any reach into the radio baseband image RLX-IFH24E_v5089.mhx, identified but not exercised; and any impact on an attached control system, PLC or historian. Consequently the Type field above reflects the documented delivery vector, a network POST to a CGI on the management listener, and the Platform field reflects a firmware and hardware target; the part that was actually executed was the vendor's own installer acting on a supplied file, and a reader should weight the two halves of this chain differently. That is what the published advisory is written to allow. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, computed from first principles rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - (0.44 x 0.44 x 0.44) = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708; Base = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. AV:N because the entry point is a network service and the firmware's own default configuration record inside the shipped package enables the web interface on both transports, UI_Access_HTTP=B and HTTPS=B, with non-default values for the Telnet and SSH entries; that shipped record is the evidence for a default, and the Network classification comes from the transport the artefact establishes rather than from a reach we observed. AC:L because the chain is deterministic, with no race, no timing window, no memory-layout dependency and no on-path position, and the single piece of environment knowledge it needs is a platform string published inside the shipped firmware. PR:H because installing firmware is an administrative function, the handler is a maintenance CGI linked directly from the interface's own menu pages, and the only account model the package documents for that interface is a uid-0 admin entry with a password-change page and a configurable RADIUS mode; no lower-privileged principal was demonstrated reaching the handler. UI:N because once a session holds that privilege the move, the install, both script executions and the reboot all follow from one request with no operator action and no confirmation step in the recovered handler path. Scope Unchanged because the vulnerable component and the impacted component are the same appliance operating system, the CGI already running as root, the installer already running as root and the rootfs extracted by that same root process, so no authority boundary is crossed. Three readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: low privilege (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 8.8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach the maintenance handler, which was not tested; Scope Changed (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 9.1 and is rejected because an unproven boundary crossing may not raise a published score; high attack complexity (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 6.6 and is rejected because the control run isolates a wrong product string as the sole cause of refusal. Two of those rejected readings score higher than the number published, and the advisory says so itself. Two further readings are labelled conditionals and neither is the headline. An unauthenticated HTTP layer (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) would compute to 9.8 and was NOT demonstrated; it is a structural inference that applies only if the management listener does not gate the handler, and the binary that would answer that question is not in the package analysed. The supporting observation about the package is narrower and is weaker than that reading: none of the 57 shipped CGIs imports crypt, none parses or sets a session cookie and no login CGI exists in the directory, so the handler layer adds no authentication of its own, which says nothing about what the web server does before it forks a CGI. A factory credential still in place on a deployed unit would remove the need to discover any secret, but it was not demonstrated either, no authentication was performed against any appliance and no first-login behaviour was tested; under CVSS the metric prices the privilege level of the account used rather than whether its secret was public, so that reading leaves the vector unchanged at 7.2 and is published as a deployment amplifier for operators to assess. The factory password hash is deliberately not reproduced in this submission or in the advisory. No version-range claim is made: only the system upgrade package RLX-IFH24E_v2244.pkg was analysed, no other build of this model, no other version of the OEM IPx21 platform and no other product of either company is claimed as affected, although the upgrade path is a shared platform component rather than a per-product script, so a wider population of devices built on the same OEM platform plausibly shares the root cause, and that is stated as a likelihood rather than scored. Adjacent structural observations recorded in the analysis and deliberately excluded from this finding are a startup configuration that symlink-exposes /etc/MHX_CONFIG, /var/log/messages and /etc/system.debug into the web document root as configuration, syslog and debug views; a legacy debug CGI named request.cgi whose first-argument dispatch includes sending AT commands to the radio module, which was never executed and to which no AT command was sent; and SNMP community strings public and private shipped on the platform, which belong to the configuration plane. Public records were searched by product designation, by the RLX-IH name, by the OEM platform name and by the vendor name with no result describing this appliance and this root cause; the one record associated with the vendor's RadioLinx engineering-software line concerns a pseudo-random number generator in that software family, a different product and a different defect class, and records naming the platform manufacturer's own product families concern different platforms and different chains. Proof of concept, published unconditionally. The shipped script is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target: the target address, port, scheme, credentials, command, lock name, product name, uploaded filename, marker token and output path are all command-line arguments and default to inert values, the default target being loopback and the default payload command being true. It builds a gzip-compressed tar containing the file and lockfile metadata the installer reads, the pre and post scripts at mode 0755 and extract/upgradepkg.tar, and can either write that package to disk for inspection or carry it in a multipart/form-data POST under the part name file1. Its modes and the flags that matter: Build the package locally only, performing no network access at all: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --build-only --out demonstration.pkg Refuse a filename that would break the hand-off. The tool rejects any name containing a space or a path separator before it builds anything, because SubProgram_Start splits its argument string on spaces before execvp, so an extra token would change what /bin/mv is asked to do: --filename "payload.pkg" accepted --filename "pay load.pkg" rejected by the tool itself Build the negative control, for an operator who owns the hardware to confirm that the success path really is gated by the product string and by nothing else: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --control --build-only --out control.pkg Build the account-database variant as a local file, which is never sent unless --send is also given: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --passwd-mode --passwd-entry "marker:*:0:0:INERT-DEMONSTRATION-ENTRY:/root:/bin/sh" Deliver the built package to a management listener the operator owns and is authorised in writing to test, over HTTP or HTTPS, with optional HTTP Basic credentials: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 80 --user <user> --password <pass> python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 443 --https --user <user> --password <pass> The default payload is deliberately non-destructive: pre touches one marker file and writes the executing uid into a second, post touches a third, and the inner archive writes a single marker entry under the root of the filesystem. Nothing is deleted, encrypted or modified beyond those markers. The tool also prints the sha256 of what it built, so an operator can record the digest of a package before installing it, which is the one detection control that works after the fact. The script's own documentation carries a warning that applies to every reader of this submission: the network half of this chain was never exercised against an appliance, and running it against hardware you do not own or hold written authorisation to test will reboot and reimage that device, because a successful install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. PoC location in the public repository: product/prosoft-technology/rlx-ifh24e-v2244/unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce/exploit/prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish Full analysis, including the sink and source inventories with offsets, the end-to-end data flow marked at the line between measurement and inference, the verification transcripts, the negative control, the authentication boundary and its limits, the detection notes, the remediation set and the derivation of every one of the six CVSS readings: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce ProSoft Technology, Inc. was notified unconditionally through the mailbox its own website publishes for reporting a potential vulnerability, under a Security Assurance heading on its Quality and Environment page, with a copy to the North America technical-support address published on its Regional Technical Support page. The research is already public, no permission was asked for, no embargo was requested, nothing is withheld pending a reply and nothing is asked in return. No report was filed with any third party and no national coordination body was involved. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

articles.full_text:
The Latest Update

Insikt Group has published a TTP Instance for PHP2Shell covering public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, observed exploit activity, and recommended mitigations. As of 7 PM UTC on October 21, 2026:

Patch status: PHP released fixed versions on October 21, 2026: PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.

Exploitation status: While there are some reports of emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, the available reporting does not establish the full extent of successful exploitation or confirmed compromises (1, 2).

PoC status: Publicly available repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, although their effectiveness and relationship to the confirmed vulnerabilities vary. For example, security researcher J4ck3LSyN published two alleged PoCs but subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer UAF theory underlying their proposed exploitation sequences.

How It Started

On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. PHP initially withheld technical details and affected versions pending coordinated disclosure, warning that the release could be accelerated if vulnerability details leaked or exploitation emerged.

Ahead of the scheduled release, watchTowr reported reproducing CVE-2026-109618 and assessed that both vulnerabilities could enable remote code execution (RCE). Technical information subsequently leaked before coordinated disclosure, prompting heightened concern about potential exploitation. PHP shipped the fixes on October 21, alongside a PHP Foundation post about the release, which addressed the emergency release and improvements to PHP's security processes.

The “PHP2Shell” name comes from Wiz Research, which found the flaws with Calif and OpenAI and reported them to PHP in August. Wiz’s write-up covers the discovery and root cause in depth.

The Vulnerabilities

Both CVEs are memory-safety vulnerabilities involving PHP's handling of request memory during initialization, error handling, and cleanup. According to Wiz, out-of-memory (OOM) failures and stale internal state can expose freed or partially initialized memory, potentially enabling memory disclosure, memory corruption, and remote code execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109618: An OOM-related vulnerability involving partially initialized request memory. Wiz identified a use-after-free (UAF) in the session upload-progress unserializer and a related flaw that can disclose PHP worker memory. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla.

CVE-2026-109619: A stale-state vulnerability involving PHP globals that retain references to freed request memory. Wiz identified a UAF involving fatal-error backtraces and a separate OPcache type-confusion flaw. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against Drupal and WordPress.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP itself rather than a particular website application. Some exploitation paths involve PHP's session upload-progress functionality, which VirusTotal notes has existed since PHP 5.4.0 and is enabled by default. Because exploitation depends on the PHP runtime, server configuration, and reachable execution paths, even websites with secure application code may be vulnerable.

PHP identified the following affected and patched versions. Older, unsupported PHP branches are not covered by these release-specific fixes and should not be presumed unaffected.

Affected Versions

Patched Versions

8.2 releases before 8.2.35

8.2.35

8.3 releases before 8.3.36

8.3.36

8.4 releases before 8.4.27

8.4.27

8.5 releases before 8.5.12

8.5.12

Reports of Active Exploitation

Following the disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, multiple sources reported exploitation activity in the wild:

Patchstack received reports of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners by 07:34 UTC on October 21, ahead of PHP's security release.

Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht reported observing early attacks targeting the vulnerabilities. Cloudflare subsequently deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections against known exploit vectors.

Although these reports indicate early exploitation activity, publicly available evidence remains insufficient to establish the extent of successful compromise or characterize the techniques used in observed attacks.

Public Proof-of-Concept Exploits

Numerous public GitHub repositories have emerged around PHP2Shell, including projects advertising proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, vulnerability-testing tools, and defensive resources. Several claim to target CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 through memory-corruption techniques intended to crash vulnerable servers or achieve remote code execution (RCE). However, some rely on invalidated exploitation theories, and the existence of publicly available code does not establish that it successfully exploits either vulnerability.

Insikt Group's TTP Instance examines two PoC scripts published by security researcher J4ck3LSyN:

poc0_109618.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109618 through PHP's session upload-progress functionality, using a proposed memory-corruption technique to execute commands on a vulnerable server.

poc1_109619.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109619 through a related technique involving successive chunks of an uploaded file, similarly attempting to achieve remote code execution.

J4ck3LSyN subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer vulnerability theory underlying these proposed exploitation techniques but separately reported reproducing another memory-safety issue without demonstrating RCE.

Other publicly available repositories advertise PHP2Shell exploits, vulnerability-testing scripts, and demonstration environments. Some continue to describe the invalidated cached-pointer technique, while others claim to use different exploitation methods. At the time of this publication, Insikt Group has not independently tested J4ck3LSyN’s PoCs or other publicly available PoCs for accuracy or effectiveness.

Scale and Exposure

Two independent internet scans show how much PHP is exposed, but they count differently. Modat counts PHP services that report a readable version and were seen in the 10 days before October 20. VirusTotal counts IP addresses as of October 21, including PHP servers it identifies through signals other than a version string, such as the application, session cookies, and framework headers.

Modat: 4,384,302 PHP services on 1,886,612 unique hosts. About 79% of services with a readable version run a branch PHP no longer supports, and PHP 7.4, end of life since 2022, accounts for 878,761 services, more than any supported branch.

VirusTotal: About 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, of which only about 1.1 million disclose a version, so roughly four in five hide it. Among those that disclose their version, about 758,000 run an end-of-life branch from 5.4 to 8.1, compared with about 272,000 on a supported branch, and PHP 7.4 alone accounts for about 187,000.

Neither scan counts confirmed vulnerable hosts, but both point the same way: most exposed PHP runs on end-of-life branches that will not receive an official fix. Scans that rely on version strings miss most of the exposed surface, and running the latest release was no protection: VirusTotal counted about 85,000 IP addresses on the September 24 releases, the newest available before the fix.

Why This Matters

Millions of servers could be exposed: VirusTotal identified approximately 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, highlighting the potentially widespread reach of these vulnerabilities.

Even secure PHP applications are at risk: The flaws can allow unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, even when the application running on top of it has no vulnerabilities.

Secrets can leak without code execution: Wiz showed that the memory disclosure flaw can expose passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests.

The patch window collapsed: Details leaked hours before the release, and security researchers reported exploitation attempts before fixed versions were available (1, 2).

Many servers run outdated PHP versions: VirusTotal found that most PHP servers disclosing their versions were running end-of-life branches that no longer receive regular upstream security updates.

Compromise can spread past the web server: VirusTotal found about 394,000 PHP hosts that also expose Secure Shell (SSH), about 233,000 that expose MySQL, and about 68,000 that expose remote desktop protocol (RDP).

Logs may show little: Exploitation happens below the application layer, so application logs may record limited context.

Timeline of Events

The disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities unfolded over several weeks, beginning with their discovery in August 2026 and culminating in an emergency security release on October 21, 2026. However, vulnerability details became publicly accessible ahead of the coordinated release, prompting defensive preparations and reports of exploitation activity before patches became available.

The following timeline outlines key developments associated with the discovery, coordinated disclosure, early exploitation reports, and Recorded Future's response.

August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using AI-assisted research tools.

August 20, 2026: Wiz Research confirms unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against Drupal.

August 21, 2026: Wiz Research confirms unauthenticated RCE against WordPress.

August 24, 2026: Wiz Research privately reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team, initiating the coordinated disclosure process.

September 21, 2026: The PHP security team acknowledges the vulnerability reports and begins developing coordinated fixes.

October 20, 2026: PHP announces an emergency, out-of-band security release scheduled for October 21 to address two critical vulnerabilities.

October 20, 2026: Insikt Group publishes an initial intelligence note highlighting the upcoming PHP security updates.

October 20, 2026: Recorded Future develops Attack Surface Intelligence signatures to identify potential exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

October 21, 2026, 02:29 UTC: An archive containing leaked vulnerability information was first submitted to VirusTotal.

October 21, 2026, 07:34 UTC: Patchstack reports receiving notifications of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners, several hours before the scheduled security release.

October 21, 2026, 13:52 UTC: PHP releases security updates addressing both vulnerabilities, ahead of the previously announced 14:00 UTC release time.

October 21, 2026, 17:52 UTC: Insikt Group publishes a PHP2Shell tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTP) instance to support threat detection and analysis.

Notably, reports of exploitation activity emerged before the official security release, creating a brief period during which vulnerability information was circulating publicly while affected organizations lacked an official patch. As a result, PHP users may discover exploitation attempts that occurred prior to the official patch disclosure. Threat hunters should therefore extend their lookback period for exploitation attempts to before the vulnerability disclosures were published.

Recorded Future Independent Analysis

Recorded Future's Insikt Group analyzed the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, publicly available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, reported exploitation activity, and defensive measures. The resulting TTP Instance provides defenders with technical context and actionable guidance to help assess exposure, prioritize remediation, and identify potential attacks.

Public PoCs: Multiple publicly available GitHub repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits targeting CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These PoCs focus on exploiting PHP memory-safety flaws to achieve remote code execution, though their effectiveness varies, and some rely on exploitation techniques that were subsequently invalidated.

Exploit activity: Security vendors have reported emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, although the extent of successful exploitation remains unclear, and confirmed indicators of compromise (IoCs) remain limited. Insikt Group’s TTP Instance includes potential warning signs that defenders can monitor, such as unusual web requests, PHP errors, and suspicious server activity.

What You Need to Do Now

Organizations operating PHP-based applications should prioritize patching vulnerable systems, assessing their exposure, and monitoring for potential exploitation. Given reports of exploitation activity ahead of the coordinated security release, organizations should also investigate whether affected systems may have been compromised before patches became available.

Insikt Group recommends the following measures to mitigate the risks associated with PHP2Shell:

Prioritize Patching and Remediation: Upgrade affected PHP deployments to the appropriate patched versions, prioritizing internet-facing applications and critical infrastructure. Organizations running unsupported PHP versions should migrate to supported releases or obtain vendor-maintained security fixes. Ensure that remediation includes PHP components embedded in third-party applications, containers, and managed services.

Identify Exposed Assets and Validate Remediation: Inventory PHP deployments across organizational environments and assess exposure based on internet accessibility, configuration, and business criticality. Recorded Future customers should leverage Attack Surface Intelligence to identify potentially vulnerable internet-facing assets and validate remediation efforts.

Implement Compensating Security Controls: Where immediate patching is not feasible, restrict external access to vulnerable systems and implement applicable WAF protections, request filtering, and PHP configuration hardening. Ensure that origin servers cannot be accessed directly to bypass perimeter defenses. These measures may reduce exposure to certain exploitation techniques, but should not be considered substitutes for patching.

Monitor for Exploitation and Investigate Potential Compromise: Review web server, application, and endpoint telemetry for anomalous HTTP requests, PHP process failures, unexpected command execution, and other indicators of malicious activity. Prioritize reviewing activity beginning October 20, 2026, and investigate potentially compromised systems. Where compromise is identified, initiate incident response procedures and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

Recorded Future customers can access the Insikt Group PHP2Shell TTP Instance, Validated Intelligence Event, and Vulnerability Intelligence Cards® for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the Recorded Future Intelligence Operations Platform. Recorded Future will continue to monitor developments related to PHP2Shell and provide updated intelligence as additional information becomes available.

How Recorded Future Helps Prioritize Actively Exploited Vulnerabilities

PHP2Shell went from disclosure to exploitation in hours, which leaves little time to determine where you are exposed and what to fix first. Learn how Recorded Future helps teams prioritize the vulnerabilities attackers are exploiting
